Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with
Mr. Cliff Leeman
Reel 1
Interviewed by Milt Hinton

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS

I'm sitting here in 1979, I'm sitting here with my dear friend Cliff Leeman, and Cliff, for the record -- I know we're gonna have to do this anyway on paper, but I would like you to say your full name, your address, telephone number, Social Security number, and so it will be on record on the tape.

My name is Clifford Leeman, and I was born in Portland, Maine, 1913, September 10th. And my Social Security number is 120-07-0590. My residence for the last 27, 28 years has been 21-04 154th Street, Whitestone, New York 11357, and I've lived in the same house for 27 years.
Beautiful. And your parent's name was Cliff?

Well, my father's name was Merle, Merle Leeman. And my mother's maiden name was Margaret Webb -- W-e-b-b. They were both from Maine, my father was born in Portland, Maine, as was I. My mother, I believe, was born in Portland, Maine. I have that all in the family Bible. I have a real old Bible that goes back to the early 1800's, by the way.
What kind of work did your father do?
My father was a Teamster, as they

were called in the days before trucking. He owned his own trucking business, and my grandfather was a Temaster who had his own trucking business, but that was before mobile automobiles, or trucks -- and I was born -- I was in the middle of the city of Portland, Maine, with my grandfolks, after my father and mother divorced, and I was brought up by my grandfolks.
Why? Why was that?
My mother was a very talented pianist, and she -- why they broke up, I was only 5 or 6 years old, it was 1919, and I don't exactly know, except they were, as they say today, incompatible.

My mother then went on to have a career -- she went on to study the organ, and she was a very fine pianist as far as concert work, and especially she played in theatres, and what I heard of my mother, she played some ragtime, which I didn't know what it was at the time. Her approach to the piano, she made some rolls, piano rolls at one time -- and her approach to the piano, when she played personally, it sounded a great deal like a piano player, like a Ralph Sutton approach, or who was that fellow who used to be with the Bob Crosby band?
It was a 'Little Rock Getaway' approach, it was a heavy approach, I don't want to say she played like Bob Zurke
a man, but that was way, way back in the old days -- that's what people used to say, it was some old fashioned phrase, it was a very definite heavy approach.
Then she became an authoress.
When did you say your mother and father separated?
That was in 1918, during the war.

The reason for this is we're doing this for the Smithsonian Institute, and this is what we call Oral History, so that young people and people in America and throughout the world will know about great artists like you who have made a name, who have gone through and made a name for themselves in jazz and have been the pioneers of jazz, and you and guys like you -- and you certainly are one of the pioneers of this great American art form known as jazz.

So we're trying to do this so that long after we're gone, they will know about you and they will know what you did and the accomplishments that you did and hear in your own voice how you felt about your era and what happened. So it is very important that we know about your family and where you came from and what it was like. Is that clear as to what we're trying to do?
Because they had a great deal of influence on how I turned out to be a drummer.
Right, right. So we want to get that.

Now I'd like to get this -- you say your name is Cliff Leeman, and most families that I know of, especially black families, of which I am from -- we had more than one -- two names. My name is Milton John Hinton, my grandmother's name was Heddy Liddy Carter Robinson, and I noticed that you only -- and most musicians I have talked to had more than one or two names. Now there is no middle name for you?
Oh, yes; I have a middle name -- Spencer.
Oh yeah? Well, you didn't give it to me. That's the reason I ask.
Well, I never liked it so I never used it. I was named for Clifford Spencer -- was after my grandfather.
Well, for the record now, we know that you did have a middle name.
Yes, it's Spencer.
Uh huh. And you were raised by your grandparents. Your mother separated from your father and then your grandparents took over, right?

Well, my father worked in the trucking business as a subsidiary of my grandfather. Well, he did very well; he got his own job in a wholesale trucking business. My grandfather had his own business. Now when

they separated, my father went into the war and my mother pursuing her career, thought that rather than take me with her, because she went to Boston with the Conservatory, one of the org & 16, the big console? She thought I would be better off, she thought, with my grandfolks who were set up. They were just middle down the road people, you know.
Did we mention your grandparents' name?
No. My grandfather's name was John Gilmore.
Your grandfather? How about your grandmother?
My grandmother's name was Annie -- I think she used the name Annie, and I forget her middle name.
Now which grandparents were they? Were they your mother's or your father's?
These were my father's.
Your father's parents. And what about your mother's parents?
My mother's parents -- my great grandfather, no it would be my grandfather on my mother's side -- her mother's husband was lost at sea, he was a sea captain. He was a Webb.
Oh, that was his name? Webb?
Yes, That's where my mother got the name Webb.
Oh, I see.

And he was lost at sea. Then her mother married a very colorful person -- where I got the name Spencer, and his name was -- oh, I have it all, but it's an awful lot to recall at once. But he laid telephone wires out through the Middle West.
Who was that that laid the telephone wires out to the Middle West?
My grandfather, I guess what you would call my step-grandfather. My grandmother's on my mother's side, second husband.
Uh huh. How did he get out to the midwest? He was from Portland, Maine.
His name was Charles Weaver.
Charles Weaver was his name?
Yes, and he laid the telephone wires in the wild and wooly west during the 1800's.
You know, that's a long way from Portland, Maine. Do you have any idea how he got out there?

He went out with the telephone company. Now how he went there as a young man to make his reputation with the company, I suppose. But he became an executive after he returned. I know, becase that's what got me into guns -- he left me a revolver that he carried to the west, and that's what started me collecting.
Oh, we'll get into that.
We'll get into it later on. But that was his background.
Now you mentioned -- did you have any brothers or sisters?
I had a half sister from my father's second marriage, and she died several years ago, at the very young age of 45.
And her name was?

Her name was Pauline Francis. And I was named after my uncle, who was my father's brother, who was Clifford Francis Leeman. He had a very decisive background, too. He graduated from the New England Conservatory of Music in 1915, and I have the original Owen Bauer Book, a hard cover, which is a collector's item now for drummers, and he studied personally under Mr. Owen Bauer.
And he played one Fall season with the Boston Symphony Orchestra which was either 1915 or going into 1916.

Yes, and he met a girl whom he married, and she had a higher design for him in the business world, so he went to Boston University, never played again except for his own amusement -- and after that beautiful background as a drummer, and he became an insurance executive and came back to my home town. Now he tried to teach me once, but it didn't help much. You know how it's very hard to teach your own family?
Uh huh.
But I developed my love for drums through him and through my mother.
Through who? Who was this now? How did you develop your love for drums?
That was my uncle, my father's brother.
Had you established the fact that he played drums?
Yes. He finished, he graduated from the New England Conservatory. The Bauer system is one of the foundations of all drumming systems, and he studied in person with Harry Bauer.
I see. Harry Bauer.
And I have the book -- that's the book, and that's a collector's item now.
How do you spell that -- B-a-u-e-r?
B-o-w-e-r.
Oh, Bower.
He played a date for the edification of some of the musicians, the drummers that might be interested in this thing that we're doing, we could put this like a postscript.
Sure. Say whatever you want to about it. What would you want to say about it?
Well, he was a great musician, and of
course, I got a bit from that, which I took from my mother, too. Sure, that was the musical reward I got.

What other musical background did you have? You tell me about your music background and your schooling, your young days. Now you were with your grandparents, where we are right now, before we got to Harry Bower -- you were with your grandparents, and you had a half-sister, is that right?
That's later on. My father got married in 1920 -- I just went through the family Bible. He remarried in '20 and '21.
Well, were you living with him then?
No, I was still living with my grandparents, but it was an unusual setup because all this time, my father's business was going on, and my grandfather's was going on.
What was your father's business?
Trucking business.
I see.

And he finally -- we bought a farm which was only 4 or 5 miles from Portland, Maine, and my father built a house there. He was doing fairly well, and he was so close -- I was only 10 minutes away, but it seemed to be convenient at the time, with another new marriage, and I continued my schooling in the heart of Portland -- I went
through all the grade schools there and through Portland High School. So convenience sake, rather than live with my father, I lived with my grandfolks.
Uh huh.
And it seemed to be a convenient way all around, except I don't want to get into childhood ...
Well ...
I was a very fortunate person.

Well, we should because this is the history of your life -- don't you think we should get into your childhood? I think maybe the young people might like to know how you came about -- if there were mistakes, if there were misfortunes, perhaps we can sidestep them.

As a child, I missed a mother's love, living with older people, my grandfolks, but I was treated beautifully and I had good schooling. I was never hungry. And my aunt took an interest -- she's still living, she's 91, she's an old maid.
And what's her name?
Her name is Marion Ader.
I've met this lady, I'm proud to say.

Yeah, she's 91 and very alert. And she took an interest in me in the family, living there with my grandfolks. She started me on piano when I was 6 or 7 for about 2 years -- she was a wonderful teacher. And I
didn't go very far from there, but I did it. I did gain some musical knowledge by fooling around myself.

As I went through high school, I knew the keyboard and so forth -- I couldn't play any recital piano. Of course, I had my heart set on drums, because there was a pad around the house that my uncle had made at the Conservatory and in those days you made -- he made his own xylophone, and he was a thoroughly schooled drummer, he was a beautiful drummer, and to give up a career like that was unheard of. My aunt helped him through, that was her brother who helped him through college. But then he went to the Boston University and graduated and became an insurance executive -- and he had a very -- well, shall we say lucrative; he had a good life, and did some very good things with himself.
Some of the jazz magazines say that you started playing drums around 13 with some bands around there -- is that right?

Before studying drums, I studied xylophone with my teacher, and he was a Bower pupil, too. His name was Richard Shaw, Dick Shaw -- Howard Shaw, H-o-w-a-r-d. But we called him Dick. And he was also a Bower pupil and came to Portland to live, and he played in the pit there. Well, he was the best teacher around, and my uncle was busy with his insurance business, but used to come up once or twice a week to give me a little lesson, and have dinner
with my grandmother, and he didn't have the patience with me, so they sent me to a teacher.

Well, I was taught all the rudiments -- but I never really exerted myself to the point of studying like one would today. I was taught all the proper rudiments, but never practiced that much; I didn't have the interest to practice. I would take what was taught to me like the Bower system, and I wouldn't put the time and effort into it that somebody should today. This came later when I found out what I needed, but I had the basics under my finger, being taught by this teacher, Howard Shaw.

He taught me -- I knew a little bit of the keyboard, so the xylophone was in the book, too, so they taught me the xylophone, and I got into practicing at home, but I lost interest in that, too, because of the upper registers of the violin key notes, you know, and I didn't put enough time in, and I was out all the time. But I did like popular music, which was coming along about 1928 or '29, like showboat songs and so on and so forth, and so I would buy sheet music and apply it to the four mallets of the xylophone.

Well, there was a gentleman in my home town -- who Johnny Smith often speaks of, and I don't know whether he's alive or not, his name was Tom Robbins, and he was a kind of, well, erratic sort of person, but he had a basic -- he used to write strange tales, among other things. But he played the x the guitarist
banjo -- he wrote a lot of banjo, he was in all those things in the twenties, he was a banjo virtuoso, and he was also a very strange person.

So we built a base banjo. In those days, they made them to your specifications. And he organized, he gave banjo lessons, among other things, locally, and he took some of his pupils and he organized a banjo band, but he implemented it with the marimba -- he had a big marimba, so as a kid, I was 13 going on 14.
Now what was this man's name again?
Tom Robbins. And for a rundown on him, you could contact Johnnie Smith -- he was a great, he studied with him a bit. Johnnie Smith is from my home town, too.
That's interesting. Great guitarist, just wonderful.
So I went out on the road, we went out for a very short while when I was 14 years old. I was forced to go back to high school, and we went out and did a few what they called the Pantages Theatres?
Right. The Pantages.
We did a few things, and I have pictures of that, of me playing in a clown uniforms -- we all used clown uniforms.
What is that?
Tom Robbins on marimba.
What kind of uniforms did you say you wore?
Clown.
Oh, clown! I see.

Right, and I have pictures of that which are priceless. They had drums, marimba, base banjo, which was a base -- it was strung with bass strings. And all the different -- now I know nothing of plectrum and so forth, but the different sized banjos, and we played popular music with a girl singer.

Well, my father came and got me -- in Dover, New Hampshire, we were playing at the theatre and he said, 'You're going back to school!' -- maybe a little stronger than that, and I went back to high school.
So that's how I started.
Uh huh.

Let's go back to me having a foundation from a good teacher. I tended to read through the Bower method book rather than practice -- I had that in the back of my mind. That's how later on, as I got into music and transgressing with bands, or progressing with bands, I should say, I can explain how my musical ability progressed -- that's the only reason I'm saying that.
And also my Uncle Clifford's drum set and xylophone

was stored in my house -- that hand made xylophone, and I could experiment with it, that's how I, rather than study with my teacher -- I had the foundation, but I would fool around at home to better myself with the basic knowledge.
Now we're in high school now. I'm sorry, I got way ahead of myself.
No problem, Cliff. whatever you want to say.
I just want to do it chronilogically right.
Okay.

I played through school with a local band like everybody does. But I was very, very fortunate during my high school days from 1928 on, in my home town -- in the state of Maine, all the colleges had big bands in those days, and the old Archer Pier which is a beach near my home, with the Shrimlin Brothers -- they played every name band, and I had the opportunity from age 14 thru 18 when I got through high school to go and hear all these bands. When I was only 14 or 15 years old, I heard McKinney's Cotton Pickers in a place called Fry's Hall in my home town. That's just for beginners -- I was only 14 years old.
But I had the chance to watch these people, and Don Redman was leading the band then, and I saw Bennie Pollack's band with the original band with Ray Bauduc on drums at the
Pier -- I had the chance to watch these people in action.
Do you have any idea what year that was, Cliff?

About '28 and '29 and the thirties, through school. From '28 I heard the original Claude Hopkins band, they used to play at the old Archer Pier, it was a very famous spot to play all the big name bands.

And of course, they all played the colleges - they'd be split up, you know, and I would be playing the colleges, too, the local bands, so I had a chance to hear these people in person. Nowadays, a boy goes to school, he goes to college, and he gets the charts, he gets Woody Herman's charts. But I had a chance to be there in person and watch these people. That was my musical training.

Among others, I saw Paul Whiteman's band, the Rythm Boys back in those days, and Bing Crosby, and Jack and Charlie Teagarden were in the band playing that old Archer Pier. And Roy Bargy, Bix Beiderbecke, the Casaloma Band started there about 1932 -- oh, that was a big band in those days, organized and became a very big thing.
So I had a chance to see these people in person.
Did you get a chance to meet any of these people?
Oh, yes. I'd go up, just like ...
Well, who impressed you? Tell about that.
Well ...
I mean, who did you meet?
Well, mostly I was watching. It's the same thing as one nighters today. If somebody is busy, they don't have much time for you.

Well, who had time for you? The reason I'm asking this is because I can remember when I was your age, and there is only a few years difference between you and I, and I'm on the senior side, but I remember going up and meeting Wellman Braud and just hoping that he would drop his rosin so I could hand it to him, behind his bow -- and I did get to meet him backstage. And I had some conversation. I want to hear about some of your conversations -- some of these wonderful people that you're telling me about, I want to know ...

Well, I was a little shy about approaching people. My eyes would open wide, but rather than -- which I should have done, but I didn't have that kind of a background. It happened a year or so later after I got out of my home town. After I got out of my home town, I went out in '33 -- Dan Murphy's Musical Skippers came to my home town and they needed a drummer -- this is all behind my back now -- a local bass player was collecting tacks.
Remember what his name was?
Well, we called him Tubie. Tubie Stervenson. Don't ask me how to spell it!
No, that's all right.

And he found out that they needed a drummer, so he recommended me. So they called me at the house, and after the job, Dan Murphy and his Skippers (that's the name of his band) were eating in an all night restaurant, and they called my house to come down and meet him.
Meet who?
Dan Murphy.
What did he play?
He was a drummer previously.
I see.

But he didn't play any more. He stood in front of it. He had a little waxed moustache and to us, he was old. But we were all young kids. He was a territory band leader, and he had done -- before I joined the band, he had had such luminaries as Nick Kaspian was with him.
What did Nick play?
A trumpet player.
We want these young people or the people in the future know what these people that you're talking about played.
George Bassman was playing piano just before I joined the band, and he had another new band, but that was the type of musician he had.
Nick Kasbian was a ...
Trumpet player who was with the first arranger, composer of 'I'm Getting Sentimental Over You' and arr. of 'Let's Dance'.

Benny Goodman swing orchestra, several years off and on with him. And George Bassman was a great arranger, a piano player. But they weren't there when I was there, when I came in -- there were no names that were famous.
Well, did you meet any of the guys? Who was in the band with you?

Well, when I joined -- this is '33 when we went on the road -- Jimmy Blake, and he's passed away since then, he used to be with Tommy Dorsey; a fine trumpet player. He was about 17 or 18 years old, and Ray Conniff was on trombone. Now he never had a long pair of pants, and we used to wear naval uniforms -- we were the skippers, and we bought them in Charleston, Boston -- Charlestown in Boston, and they had the regular uniforms, we had the white starched uniforms that they still use at the naval academy with the epaulets, and that was our uniform.
And Ray Conniff never had a long pair of pants. He was only about 15 or 16 -- I may be off a year or two here, but he was about 15 or 16. [Pause]

A little more elaboration on the Dan Murphy days -- as I remember, we were all young boys, naturally, it was the first territorial bands they used to have, and when I joined the band, that was a big thing; we talked it over at home and my father said I could go. I think I went at $25 a week, which in those days was a lot of money, and if I sent my
grandmother $8 or $10 home, well, that was in the days when you could get steaks -- in Kansas City you could get a steak dinner for 20 or 25¢.
But what town were you in -- you mentioned Kansas City now.
Well, I joined in Boston.
Oh, Boston? Dan Murphy -- did you work in Kansas City with them?
Well, I joined in Boston, he hired me in Boston.
But did you go to Kansas City with them?
Yes.
Oh, good.
I got on the car -- they had a truck for the instruments, and two cars.
What year was this?
Uh huh.

And we left Boston, and I don't know what time of year it was. I would say it was around the Spring, and the first stop we made was a few minutes in Buffalo -- this was by car in the old days; we stopped at Buffalo to have our pictures taken -- put on the uniforms, which they used for publicity, and I'll show them to you

sometime, and take the uniforms off and get back in the car -- and we haven't checked in anyplace yet. And from Buffalo, the next stop we made was Sioux City, Iowa. Now that's a lot of traveling -- that was two or three days in those days by auto. And I never slept a wink; I was never so thrilled in my life. I was traveling and watching the countryside -- I'd never seen corn and hogs on the way.

Sioux City. Now we worked -- the agency used to be Tom Archer, and I still think he might be alive or some of his relatives -- Tom Archer. He used to hire the territorial bands, and he used to have a whole string of ballrooms, some of them were out in the prairie; Sioux City, Iowa, Sioux Falls, Pipestone, Minnesota and Kansas City, which I'll get to -- we haven't got there yet -- and Lincoln, Nebraska, we had to play in a sandstorm.

This Tom Archer -- his ace in the whole was a six-piece orchestra and was called Lawrence Welk, doing one nighters -- 7 one nighters a week, and they made hundreds and hundreds of thousands of dollars; they were sold out playing polkas, and we would follow them with our appetizing 13 or 14-piece hokum band, they used to call them in those days.
Now what year is this? We just mentioned Boston in 1933 -- is this still ...
Lawrence Welk had a band in 1933?

Oh, yes. Yes. He was the biggest thing -- it was his ace in the hole out there. I remember it was '33 or '34. I went back the next year, they had those long trailers and he was the first person to put thousands of dollars in a big trailer, and they lived in it -- his six-piece orchestra, and they would do seven days a week all over the midwest, for this Tom Archer. And I remember we were flabbergasted, they had showers in there, they had bunks -- and I heard at that time that he paid his men $75 a week, and that was unheard of in those days. I think you have some ideas of your own about what pay was in those days.
Oh, I agree. I was in California in 1933.
So that was the band that we went down to Kansas City with, which was the biggest thing that could have happened to me in life.
[Pause]
Cliff, you were saying that going to Kansas City was the biggest thing that happened to you in life just before the phone rang. So you tell me, what year was it that you were in Kansas City?
Going into the Spring of 1934, I think. We had already played --
When you say 'we', who all were you?
Now I'm still with Dan Murphy. I'm just about to break ... we had played in Denver at Elliche's

Gardens -- and we followed a band in there that was called Benny Moten's Orchestra. Now I remember following them in, and I only bring this up because Bennie Moten, shortly after that was operated on, I think, for a tonsil, and had died, and we hit Kansas City and Count Basie had taken a band into the Reno Club -- he took the nucleus of some of Bennie Moten's orchestra.
But I have to put this in perspective. The Depression was heavy around the country, as you know, in '34, still.
I was here!

Yeah, and the prospects for out of work musicians were bleak -- and we were in the streets of Kansas City. We were there on a Sunday, and I'm getting a little ahead of myself in telling about Basie. I knew little about what was happening there except a cab driver or somebody told me -- I had only a couple of dollars in my pocket -- told me it was Sunday and nothing was opened until Monday, they had the blue laws there -- why I don't know. But crime was rampant along with jazz.
Well, I was walking down the street on a Sunday night, and I met a girl who asked me what I was looking for and I said, 'music'.
Really?
That's what I was looking for!
Okay.
Well, this girl turned out to be -- her name was Boots Castle Dine. C-a-s-t-l-e D-i-n-e.
Uh huh.

But she went by the name Boots Castle. I'm getting ahead of myself here. And discovering that it was music, she guided me to the Reno Club and said after 12 o'clock the band starts, it was Monday morning, and little did I know, that they had what they called a breakfast dance.
Where was this Reno Club? Do you remember the street?
It was on 12th Street.
On 12th Street?
Sure I remember, it was 12th Street.
Was this black place or a white place, because you know in those days, in the 30's there were white and black places.
This was a little club -- it was a white place where ranchers would come in, but all they served was beer and chile.
To white folks?
Yes.
Of course.
But they had an all-black show.
Yeah, but black people couldn't come in.

I heard this band, and for a 15¢ beer, and almost fell on the floor. Now this was the first band that I heard, it was Basie, Joe Keys on trumpet, Oran "Lips" Page and a fellow called Rabbit who I heard with Fletcher Henderson, commited suicide, on trombone, and some people know his name, but I can't remember it, but they had a bass player with a Sousaphone, who wore a cap, it was a round shell, you know, with a big thing down there that said 'feed the kitty'.

But I heard this music, and they had a drummer whose name -- Buster Smith played first saxophone, and wrote the arrangements; Jackie Washington was playing saxophone -- he had three saxophones. And then they played the show; Jimmy Rushing was part of the show. Other names I have later on.
But I heard the music, and I couldn't believe it.
Could you talk a little bit about Oran "Lips" Page.

They were going to open in a half hour over across the street, the Reno Club, but here I saw somebody coming down the street, and she said, "I want you to meet a boy that is a musician from back east" and this man turned out to be Lips Page.
Was this lady white or black?
She was white.
I see. In Kansas City -- and she introduced you to Lips Page.

That's how it happened. The Reno was across the street, and I hadn't entered it yet because it hadn't opened yet, and this was the first time I saw him -- he had a horn under his arm and a velvet case that somebody had made him, this little case. And that's the first time I had ever seen anybody with a horn case like that.
Well, tell me -- what kind of dude was he?
He was just beautiful, he was most gracious and he was nice to me, I thought I was talking to Louis Armstrong, who I had heard on records, but I had never met anybody like that.
My wife says the same thing about him.
He was the most beautiful man, among other beautiful people, he is the epitome.
Who was the other trumpet player? You mentioned ... there was another one.
Joe Keys.
Joe Keys. What about Joe?
He came back with the band back east later on.
But what about him? What kind of guy was he?
Benny Goodman brought him back.
What kind of guy was he, though?
He was a beautiful man -- he played out of tune, but he was very forceful, and that's what Basie wanted.
How did he compare to other black musicians?
He was most forceful, he led that section.
Was he first or second trumpet?
Oh, he was a first trumpet player.
Well, most black musicians didn't read well in those days. But Joe Key's was supposed to be one of the epitome of readers.
Oh, he was.
Yeah, that's what I'm trying to find out about him.
Basie had a little book.
He came to Cab Calloway's band, that's the reason I wanted to know. I'm trying to find ...

Well, he and Lips were my friends, and when I'd go up -- and Basie eventually asked me to sit in, I was scared to death, but I played a little. He wasn't too happy with his drummer. I'll give you his name later on, I can't think of it now. It's not Jo Jones, though.
This drummer you were speaking of -- you say it wasn't Jo Jones.
He didn't get the style of the band.
Uh huh. We can't recall his name.

And Basie, some night there, he would start, and he'd ask me "Do you want to play?" because I had played brushes one night, I didn't even pick up a stick. So I played brushes with him and he thought it was swing enough, he was very happy. That I could keep some time with him.
There's no question about that.
Well, this was when I was learning now. And we all became friends.
And this is 1934, right?
Right.
So you played with Basie for awhile then, in '34?
Well, when Jo came with the band -- see, Jo came in the band five or six months later, I came back, and I walked in one night and Basie was building the band.

We're not talking about when Jo came in -- we're talking about this drummer, whose name we can't recall -- you set in at first. Did you ever work with him regularly, with Basie -- did you come in and play regular?
Afterwards. I'll get to that. I have to tell you about Jo Jones, after Jo Jones came in.
But if it's going to be chronological,
we have to go from the time that this other guy whose name we can't recall --
I don't remember his name, no.
Well, who were you working with?
I was with Dan Murphy, and we were on a panic, as they used to call it. We were out of work for two days.
Just sat in with the band.

Yes, and I'd spend every minute of my time there, and Lips would take me to a club called the Sunset, which is a black club, now. They had race laws then. They didn't allow any white in the Sunset Club where Joe Turner was working and Pete Brown.
Pete Brown, what did he play?
Saxophone.
Right.
Alto saxophone.
What kind of saxophone player was he? How'd you like him?
Oh, nothing like I never heard before.
Same here, I agree with you.
This is how I was digesting -- I was listening.
Okay, I wish you'd tell about these guys.
Well, Duke Ellington came into town, and ...
Well, what about Pete Brown?

I would go up after work, which would be six o'clock in the morning, on Monday mornings, which would be ten o'clock in the morning, we'd all got to Sunset, which went to twelve o'clock, and Pete Brown, and the piano player was the other. Pete ... oh, what was his name.
Pete Johnson?

Yes, Pete Johnson. And then everybody would get off from work. Basie had a set with the police department up there -- there were some very big cats with clubs, and no white was allowed, but I was allowed.
Well, tell about that.
I guess I was passing.
Yeah, you were passing because you were a musician, and most musicians ...

When I would get there, they would have sessions for an hour-and-a-half or two hours -- I was there when Rex [Stewart] came from Duke Ellington's band, and in those days everybody would say he won't do it -- but he did. Lips Page challenged him.
Challenged who?
Rex.
Were you the only white musician there?
That's right, ever -- in that club.
Uh huh.
And I've seen people go crazy, the music was so great, what with Joe Turner singing the blues and ...
Well, before we leave, I'd like to have you mention something about Pete Brown. What kind of a player was he? Mention some of these and describe some of these great musicians that you played with.
Well, as I digested the music and the new music later on, I recorded with Pete and with these people.
But what kind of player was he, Cliff?
He was wonderful. I'm trying to explain -- I couldn't put my finger on it then, but all those musicians were great, and he was one outstanding among many -- but how am I going to compare him?
I'm not asking you to compare him, I just wondered how he sounded.

He was wonderful. Everybody up there was wonderful, everybody on the stand at these clubs. Everybody from the theatre would come by and they'd jam -- they'd do one and two hour sets, the drum men would wear out. So every once in awhile, someone would say to come and fill in, so I got to know everybody that way, a little bit, and I'm still
learning.
Who were some of the drummers, Cliff? Do you remember?

No. Some of the people I did not know their names. The piano player, Jay McShann could tell you -- he knew everybody. I didn't get to know him that good, but he was forming bands in those days. I can't put my finger on them, though -- my memory isn't all that good.
Well, you tell it your way.
Well of course, Jo Jones would be there, and then this other drummer whose name ...
Was Jonathan Jones there? What year was this when Jo was there?

Well, you see, I left -- this is '34 going on '35 -- I left after my first induction into the Reno Club, and this wonderful music, this wonderful band; when I came back six months later, I came back with all intentions, I'm improving as a kid and as a musician, and I'm still with Dan Murphy's Musical Skippers, going in on '35. I came back with all intentions of sitting down with this band, and really with my improved drumming, making a display of myself.

Well, I walked into the Reno Club one night and sat down, and the band came slowly on the stand, and all of a sudden, I heard the God damnest sounds that I ever heard in my life. This band, as everybody who was

around Kansas City at the time will tell you, it's impossible to tell people how awe inspiring it was. Jo Jones will tell you and those people that are fortunate enough to still be alive -- the music was just too much, it was too much to absorb.

And [Ray Benner], garbled Basit, said you're coming up to play some brushes on the next set, and I said, never -- you know, I had just heard Jo Jones and I didn't know anything existed like this. Now I never told that to many people.
Jo has always said so many beautiful things about you. It's nice to hear you say all of this.
Well ...
Can you remember what year this was? Because ...

That's the Fall of '34 and the Spring of '35. I was there the night that John Hammond and Benny Goodman called from Chicago, and asked Basie if he wanted to leave and go to to the Grand Terrace -- I was there that night. I saw them flip; I was around there that Spring of '35, again, when they were building the band.
I was there the night that Lester (Young) joined the band -- he'd already added guitar, and he had added -- he added Lester, whom I didn't know but I met him; he added ...
What did he play? Oh, the saxophone player -- oh, I'll recall his name in a second, but go on while I think -- he was a great saxophone player. [Hershel Evans]

Well, he had added Freddie Greene and I was there the night Lips called me over, and there was a little men's toilet with a little ratchet on the door and he said to come on in here, that he wanted me to meet somebody, and he said, 'This is Lester Young' -- and there weren't any extra beers around, so he said to send one up -- it was just 15¢ and I had to scrounge around for 15¢, and I saw the band growing.
Oh yes, and he added Walter Page who he brought up from St. Louis -- not the Cotton Club, but ...
The Moten band? The way history has it is that Benny Moton had a band and Walter Page took over the Blue Devils.

The Blue Devils. Well, he got Walter Page on bass, he changed from the bass horn, and so he was forming the nucleus of the original band that was going up to the Grand Terrace, and I watched them come in night by night.

Jo Jones, you asked me about -- Jo Jones always played at home with his family, he was very happy; he had children, or that was the story -- and he always used to come in an hour and a half to two hours late nights while I was in town, which was for two or three weeks, and he would depend upon Basie -- this is before the first show -- he would depend on me being in there, being on a panic and
this was probably guitarist Claude 'Fiddler' Williams; Green joined in 1937 in New York.
and still having no money to go anywhere -- that I would be there at the beginning of the evening, so I was the unhired regular drummer in the band until Jo got there, whatever time that might be.
That sounds like Jo Jones!

So at his disposal, I would be there playing, and so that's the extent -- I'd either play brushes, or ... and Basie insisted that I play. I didn't want to get on that stand, and I had written my father asking if I could go back and go in with him on his trucking business, I was disillusioned that I would ever be able to play like Jo Jones. I shall never repeat this again, so you've got it on tape.

Basie forced me to go up on the stand and keep brushes, and he'd smile and he'd play and play -- at that time, I didn't know any of those things; Basie played little piano solos then, you know. I think Buster Smith made arrangements of some of those things, so he'd play -- another one was "Maple Street Rag" -- I remember they had it featuring Basie with this band background.
The saxophone player you were trying to remember was Hershel Evans.
Hershel Evans, that's right.
And so I sat in with the band. Then finally after Boots, who became my girlfriend while I was there -- she took care of
me; she took me to all these places, and late eating places, she took me over to Fairland Park.
What was that? What kind of place was that?
That's where Andy Kirk was playing; that was a big amusement park, and that was a great band, another great band in Kansas City.
"Twelve Clouds of Joy".
Yes, "Twelve Clouds of Joy" and MaryLou Williams played piano.
Right, and John Williams was on that -- remember what he played?
That's right.
Do you remember what John Williams played, her husband? He was a baritone saxophone player.

Uh huh, that's right. And a wonderful guy that died -- on tenor saxophone, he was very good; Benny Thigpen, the original, senior, played drums -- but I wasn't ready to sit in with all those people. I thought they were just being nice to me, you know?

I used to go out and hang out with MaryLou Williams, and Boots used to -- Boots was a great singer, by the way, and about that Fall, Benny Goodman came by there at the theatre, and Teddy Wilson had his own record date, and then ...
In Kansas City?
* Dick Wilson.
Yes.
: But what year was this?
He had a record date in Kansas City.
: When was this? 1935, wasn't it?
Do you remember if Teddy played on that date? Did you do it with him?
Yes. Teddy took some of the guys from Benny's band, because they were there, and there was Harry James on trumpet, Gene Krupa on drums, and Teddy Wilson.
: This is 1935, huh?
Yes, Teddy Wilson's orchestra. And it featured Boots Castle, and who else was on that -- I think Harry Goodman was on base.
: Oh yeah, Harry was Benny's brother.
And I know one of the songs she sang, 'The Hour of Parting' -- it was a double -- a single record, double size.
: This is before Teddy joined Benny?
No, he's with Benny.
: Oh, he's with Benny now.
Yeah. I might be a month off, it might have been January of '36.
: Oh now, I couldn't dispute that.
He made the record, because I have it at home.
And you made the record, you were on the record?
No, I didn't make the record.
Oh, I see.
She made the record. This is Boots.
Oh, Boots.
And she sang beautifully.
Oh, I see.
But she took me to all these wonderful things -- to breakfasts from seven to ten o'clock in the morning with hot biscuits and all that, with Lips.
What town are you in now?
Kansas City, still.
Kansas City.
Roll around the Reno.
Yeah, the place where the black people ate, the restaurant there.
I never went to that restaurant.
Oh, I see.

Just a private home. And at sunset, there was a little place we'd play in the garden, and MaryLou used to come and play and I used to carry a pair of brushes with me and play a piece of cardboard. So I wasn't thrown out, nobody said no. So that's how I progressed, but I listened to that -- I heard things in Kansas City, and everybody that was
there says the same thing. There aren't enough superlatives to tell you how intense the music was.
But there were a few people there, few who witnessed this like you did -- this is why the Smithsonian would like to have it in your own voice.

Well, Jo Jones -- if we were in a club or something, Jo just looks at me and if there are any other people around, he says, "Kansas City?" and he shakes his head, and I shake my head -- no sense in talking about it because nobody would know what we were talking about.

But it's important that somebody should know. Now we have Jo on record and we have you on record, and these things coincide, which is just beautiful. All your years are exactly the same years that Jo talks about, and about the Kansas City -- and of course, I was there at that same period, and I have been through that, too.
Were you with Blanche?
No, I was with Cab Calloway. And all of these things coincide, and it's so very important that, for posterity that these things be recorded.

Then there are other people who I heard that I couldn't digest, because I didn't remember until later years, like Johnson was there -- oh, it's just impossible, you have to go through the archives of jazz to find out who was living there and playing there then.

(UNINTELLIGIBLE) and they came over to Chicago; I can tell you the years that they came to Chicago from Kansas City, because the whole migration was south and the middle west, and Chicago, which was the hot bed of jazz, even before New York.
Some people think that jazz started in New Orleans. But we won't get into that controversial thing.
No, not at all.

But the middle west, Kansas City -- it was just alive, it was like a hot bed -- all these great musicians that came out of there in that era, and God was wonderful to me that He took me there, and I believe that He said, 'This is it' and He just wanted me to be there, and it's like anything else. I was there at the right time, at the right place at the right time.

Well, you were there, and besides that in all the annals of history, you are without a doubt the only white drummer that came up, because you knew all of these people that you have been involved with because of the association -- how you got from this town in the New England states to Kansas City is a miracle, through Dan Murphy in Boston, which is as different as night and day. And here you are, in all of the annals of drumming, all the great drummers of the jazz era -- you, Cliff Leeman, have bridged the biggest gap, and in a society in which jazz is

considered a black art, you have been around longer and before most of them have been involved with most black artists and most black performers, and you have been involved with Basie, in Kansas City with Dave Tough, Jo Jones, Gene Austin Jim Krupa, with Baby Dodds, Buddy Rich and Cubie? -- Sid Catlett these are -- and Big . So here you are -- your name ranks high among all the other drummers that I just named, and I'm certain that there are more that you can tell me about, because I can't tell you about your profession -- but your name ranks high in there and here is a record as proof of where you came in, before Jo Jones in Kansas City.
Can I interject something?
Yes sir.

MR. LEEMAN: I don't want anybody to get the wrong idea of how I put this together. As I said before, I had no background with racial disturbance, and when I went to Kansas City and made all these beautiful friends and all these wonderful people who took me with open arms and under their wing, musically -- and I wondered why, I couldn't figure out whether or not I was a very fortunate person that they accepted me musically. So I had no racial problems with it.
I had a feeling in my heart, was all, as a lot of people do have, predominantly among the swing players there
seemed to be more blacks.

When I was on the road, I used to buy records, my one love was Duke Ellington's band, that was before Basie came back into recording. And that was the epitome to me, and of course, Basie became my idol. Those were the two, really, because when he came back, he started recording.
And these people taking me under their wing -- that's why over the years I ended up playing with 2 and so forth, and I'm not getting ahead of myself.
But I had no qualms and I had no antagonistic racial feelings, which God was very good to me.
Well, what about the bands you played in -- you were of Irish descent, right? Leeman is not an Irish name, is it?
No, no.
Then, what?
It's German, English and Indian.
But I haven't asked you that. What is your ethnic background?
My grandfather, or my great grandfather was one of five brothers who came from Germany. I've been tracing this for two or three years now, my family tree.
Uh huh.

And my grandfather was born up near the Canadian border, and I have the names, I can give you later. In Maine, northern Maine, he came down and met my grandmother who was born in Portland, Maine, she was a tailor. And it's a most interesting background, which I'll go over with you sometime.
Well, how about your relationship with the bands that you played in? You played in a lot of bands where there weren't any black musicians in them at all.
That's right, but I was also with Charlie Barnet when we had a third of the band was black.
But before you get to the black bands, the ones you played in that were all white, what were your feelings?
When the band broke up that spring when I came out of Kansas City --
What band?

The Dan Murphy's Musical Skipper's. For a very short while, I was with Hank [Viogrin] -- now he was another old man, but he had a little better musical talents, and a lot of men came out of there like John Best --
Oh, the trumpet player. Lives in California now.
This is how this happened. John Best --

Just name them and characterize them so the people will know who he is. John Best is a trumpet player, and you mentioned that he lived in California, and he has a farm out there, doesn't he? An avocado farm. Good, now go on to it.
And he's still very active.
Very active, and a fine trumpet player.
Oh, beautiful. We play with him every year. And we had Les Robinson on saxophone.
Now what about Les? I don't know too much about him. Can you explain him to the public that's gonna be listening to these tapes?
Yes.
Who was Les Robinson?
Les Robinson was beautiful. His background, I don't know where he came from, but he was the most beautiful alto saxophone player, but he wasn't fully developed.
Now what town was he from?
I don't know.
Well, when did you work with him -- in whose band?
We were with Hank Biagini and we came to New York, I was only with him a couple of months.
And who was this Hank Biagmini Veogene?
He worked in that Detroit ballroom in that band. (Casa Loma Band's predecessor - a Jean Goldkette unit called 'The Orange Blossoms'.)
The Grey Stone?
The Grey Stone Ballroom. And he conducted. He was a --
Is this before --
He was a non-competitive trumpet player, but a leader.
Was he before Glen Gray?
Oh yes.
Before?

Yes. A haphazard name for having a steppingstone, as Joe Haymes' orchestra was later on -- it was a steppingstone for good musicians. Anyway, on a Sunday afternoon, somebody said, 'Somebody here wants to talk to you' and we were at the Roseland doing a matinee, the old Roseland on Broadway. The other band across from us was Woody Herman, his first three weeks that he broke up with Isham Jones, and were forming a new orchestra. I was with Hank Biagmini Viagmini.
Hank Biagmini Viagmini, right.
And we were performing in the afternoon, a Sunday matinee, and somebody said that Artie Shaw would like to meet me, if you've ever heard of him.
Well, I hadn't really heard of him, but I went out --
Who was Artie Shaw?
He was a studio musician who had a band.
He played what?
He played clarinet. A great clarinetist.

And he wanted to see me and John Best and Les Robinson, and he wanted to know if we were interested in joining his orchestra -- he had just broken up a small group that he had with George Wetling and four strings at the Meadowbrook, and he was gonna form a new band.
Had he ever played with any other big bands before this? Artie Shaw?
He was a big studio musician. It was between he and Benny Goodman in the studios.
Oh, I see.

Because Benny Goodman had already come out and started his band, and Artie was on the same trail. So we went and rehearsed, we said yes. We rehearsed in New York on 49th Street, the original studio -- his old studio was upstairs, and we went in --
(Inaudible) studio?
I don't know.
Who was there?
Well, there was Les --
Les who?
Les Robinson.
And what'd he play?
Alto saxophone. And John Best --
John Best was on trumpet, and Artie Shaw was a clarinet player.
And we met one of his -- Artie Shaw's old friends, Tony Pastor, who was the one who played the saxophone, and let's see if there are any other names I can remember ...
How many pieces were with you in the band?

14 pieces. Let's see, three trumpets, two trombones -- oh, George Harris on trombone, from Detroit, and I'm trying to remember the names of consequence that I can place my finger on now -- we rehearsed a bunch of orchestrations, because we all said we'd go with them. They offered me $65 a week, and I never heard of such money. So we all said yes, naturally. We were getting $25 or $30 with Hank Vogini, which was on scale. And who should walk in but a few arrangements -- we had stock orchestrations we were cutting up to fit Shaw's style so we could get started as a band. Fletcher Henderson was enough to make us shake in our boots, as kids, you know. He was friendly with --
Now let's let people know who
Fletcher Henderson was.
Well, he was a great band leader in his time, and a great arranger.
And he had a band.
Oh yes. The nucleus of his arrangements were done to form the Benny Goodman orchestra.
Later.
Yes.
At this time, he hadn't formed the Benny Goodman orchestra though.
Oh, yes. Benny Goodman was in production then.
Then he had a band of his own.
I see.
So he brought in to help Artie, who was a friend of his -- and that's how we got started with the Artie Shaw orchestra.
Oh, Benny Goodman was already established.
Yes. Benny was on his way with the Let's Dance Show.
And hadn't you made some arrangements for him already?
Yes.
'Stealin' Apples' and all that stuff
he/ you did for Benny Goodman?
Right, yes.
I see. Well, this is important that we know.
That was the formation of the Artie Shaw orchestra, and then we went to Boston.
And you were the drummer.

That was '36 and I was the drummer. That was 1936, and I can go on from there what we accomplished. We were in ballrooms in Boston; we did all over New England in the schools, and getting back to Les Robinson, like you asked me -- Artie Shaw was a great alto man, and he --
Artie Shaw was?

A great alto man, along with his clarinet. He played in the studios, he played first. And he taught Les Robinson the way he wanted him to play -- he taught Les Robinson the art of playing lead alto saxophone. He never put anything in his mouth but an alto saxophone. He never played a clarinet or anything like the Glenn Miller Band and all used to double.
And Artie tried to find a style for about a year -- '36, we're in Boston.
Artie Shaw, this is?
Artie Shaw. And we did our one
nighters in Boston. We finally came around and we were a ballroom band and we played and he kept on developing it, and changing musicians and arrangements. Then he had Jerry Gray on his side.
Who was Jerry Gray?
Jerry Gray scored the original "Begin the Beguine," and Artie used to give him a chart to go by, and how to style it, and then Jerry Gray would arrange.
Oh, so he was in there doing the arranging then.
Yeah, with "Begin the Beguine," and we did --
He's an arranger, then.
Yes.
That's what we're trying to find out.
Okay.
And he was on staff with Artie Shaw -- he wrote a lot of those things, until '37.

You see, drumnistically, I was forming in my mind the routines that we were playing, but I still had Jo Jones instilled in the back of my mind and the Basie band, and that's the kind of music I like, along with my records of Duke Ellington.
And Shaw's band was an entirely different thing -- he was trying to find a style, and I had gathered a few little

things. I wanted to play in the Basie vein, but it didn't work out with what Artie Shaw had in mind, and I would mention Basie's band in Kansas City, and nobody knew what I was talking about, because they hadn't quite come back east yet.

Now, Sy Schribman had something to do with Basie's band on the road, and Billie Holiday was signing with the band for a short while, but I don't think she liked the one nighters with Basie, so anyway, somehow Schribman wanted Billie Holiday to come with us to see how it worked out with Artie Shaw and his white orchestra. This was in New England, now.

And Artie Shaw insisted on what he wanted in life, and he wanted Billie Holiday who was just as great then as the day she died. In order to come with our band, and we were doing ballrooms, Sy Schribman had the idea that Billie should come on as a single and they should have a white vocalist that sat on the bandstand, and perform with the band. And Billie would come on as a single and perform her bit.

My first wife -- her name was Selma Cord; Artie hired her as a singer, she had sung around the clubs in Boston, and she was very young but she had a good voice, [and her] and Pete gave her the name Nita Bradley. Now we were married, we were on the road with Artie Shaw, but
* Boston-based Ballroom owner and band leader.

she sang on the bandstand and she roomed with Billie, and our past discussions about the racial question, one night in New England of all places, they didn't want to let us in the hotel because we were playing a college town, so Artie Shaw did not check in a hotel unless the whole band checked in, and she roomed -- my first wife, with Billie. They were roommates.

So we went through several scenes that way. Then we went down on a southern tour and Billie rode with Sid Weiss, the bass player, and I rode with him, and I forget who -- either Al Avola, the guitarist or a trombone player called Rogers -- the five of us rode together down south because things were very rough.
Excuse me. When you say rode together, you weren't in the bus with the band?
No, we didn't have busses; we had autos.
Yeah, I want to make that clear.
Yeah, we had individual cars.
I see.
And a truck. And anybody that wanted to pay for their own car would get a new car through Artie Shaw and pay off out of their --
Now explain who rode together in what cars?
I rode with Billy and Sid Weiss, down
through the south, and we wouldn't -- they wouldn't let Billie eat in the diner or the restaurants unless she went and sat in the kitchen. So we all sat in the kitchen with her.
This was you and Sid Weiss?

Yeah, and a trombonist called Rogers, and I can't elaborate on that -- that's just the way conditions were in those days. In some places, they wouldn't even let Billie sing. The one college they wouldn't let her sing, it was up in New England, it escapes me, the name of the college. It was a girls' school, they wouldn't let Billie perform because she was black. Well, those were the only racial tensions that I was under until later.
What years were these? Around --
That was the last of '36 -- '37 was when Billie joined us, when she left Basie's band.
Oh, so she left Basie to join you?
Yes.
I see.
She was with Basie a very short while. Billie didn't like one nighters, and of course she came with us and did one nighters.
I was trying to develop my style of drumming, but I had to coincide with the type of music that we
played, with the type of band that we were developing -- so it was a little rough with Artie Shaw's temperament, and you wait here and I'll explain. But stop it for a minute.
(PAUSE)

: I'm in the same vintage as you, and you are considered during the big band era, the epitome of jazz, of a big band jazz drummer. The things that you set were the standards which Buddy Rich followed, which Dave Tough followed, which Cozy Cole followed, which all of the great big band jazz drummers followed. Now you were going to tell me -- you said that when you were with Charlie Barnet, you were trying to establish your own style, so continue with that.

Let's stay with Shaw. I was grateful to Shaw for the opportunities he gave me, as a kid learning. The rhythm section was a struggle for me -- I never came out in any of the records we made, they were all hits, they did such great things, but it was a struggle for me. Sid Weiss was a good bass player, and Al Avola worked real well with me -- he was the guitar player. The band was really swinging, and I was trying to get them to swing like Basie, and it didn't work out. I had a little problem with the piano player keeping time. But those are the things that you overcome.
A drummer might be interested in this, because one reason I wanted to play on the top cymbal [with Artie] on clarinet, I
always felt that way, you know? And Artie Shaw wanted -- the tom toms came in to prominence with Benny Goodman when he made that 'Sing, Sing, Sing'.
Right.

So Shaw thought that he would keep the tom tom idea behind his chorus, but he wanted it behind all his choruses -- and all these great records we made, you listen. So I had a special little tom tom, a little Chinese tom tom, and I worked it and I stuffed it up with bandaids; God knows what else.
Name some of these great records you made with Artie Shaw. Some of them.
Well, I'm getting to that -- we're coming right in to it next.
What were some of these records, Cliff? 'Begin the Beguine,' did you say?
Yeah, 'Back Bay Shuffle,' 'Indian Love Call' -- all in the same day.
The same day, huh? What year was that?
1938, in the Spring.
Great.
And we left town, he was thinking of dissolving the band, but he had a commitment in a hotel in St. Louis and he couldn't take Billie Holiday down there,

so he hired a new singer called Helen Forrest. And we went to St. Louis, and in the middle of the engagement, after a week or two in St. Louis, he got a call one day from RCA Victor -- this is only two months later -- from RCA Victor, from Leonard Joy who was a big man there, saying to come back. He was already gonna dissolve the band, now. But Begin the Beguine and the record date is a sensation, it is sweeping the nation.
Well, as a bunch of kids, you don't know how thrilled we were. So we booked one date, we had a battle of music with some band, the house band, at the Savoy in Chicago.
The Savoy in Chicago -- do you remember, was it Erskine Tate?
One night on the way back -- I can't recall.
Okay.
And then, they had us booked in to the Lincoln Hotel, because they reopened. We reopened the Lincoln Hotel.
When was this?
Oh, it must have been May or June.
But what town? Lincoln Hotel where?
New York City.
Okay.

And we were a sensation. That's when they came in with all the contracts and so forth. During that time, we made the one movie I made, which was a short subject at their studios, and for the jazz archives -- we did 'Begin the Beguine' in a Warner Brothers short subject.
Well, while we're on that movie thing, you and I did a movie together.
Yes, we did.
With different bands.
Yeah, and I wish we had known each other more.
Oh yeah, do you remember that? The Sensations of 1900 or something.

1945. Eleanor Powell and W.C. Fields, Dorothy Donnegan -- and you were with Woody Herman's band and I was in Cab Calloway's band, and Chubby Jackson was your base player, and I was playing the base with Cab Calloway, and we used to go backstage and have us a nice taste out of our bottles, because we had to bring our bottles.
There was a drummer that I always loved --
William Randolph Coles?
No. J.C. Herd.
Was J.C. there? Oh yeah, I remember that.
He sure was, he was a dear friend of mine.

Uh huh.

Frank --

Yes.
