Yeah, pneumonia, and they didn't realize it.
Oh, it was a great tragedy, and we all felt so sadly about it because you were away.
Especially him coming into his own at the time, but of course, he lived a full life ...
That was your first marriage. Now you had a second marriage, right? You did have a second marriage.
Oh yes, with Mae. Irene.
The latest is with you now, this lovely lady which we all know, and is almost as popular in the music business as you are.
We had our 28th anniversay last week.
Beautiful.
And we had three children. We have Chris who is 26, and my daughter Nancy is 21. And we lost, 7 years ago, we lost a daughter.
We sadly remember that, yes.
She was 17 at the time.
Right, and we sadly remember that.
The reason I'm here with you is because of our close relationship, and our deep respect for each other and knowing what

family life is like. I mean, I've been married to my dear wife, Mona, a couple hundred years now! And we have close friends, and we know what it is to be family. That's one of the reasons that perhaps you and I can relate -- we are of the same era in music and jazz which we have been involved in, and our wives -- your lady and my lady -- have been so beautiful in enhancing our lives and making it so very comfortable for us, and I think that your lady deserves all the allocades we can say about her.

We're of the same fabric -- everybody isn't coming from a family, if it was broken up at times when I was young. I always wanted a family life, and all those years that I put my dues in, years we haven't even gotten into yet, with the bas$ drum falling off the car in the middle of a blizzard in Iowa, and those things that we haven't delved in yet -- I always wanted a family life, and I've had it. And I have it now.

And we do have it now, and we're enjoying it, and we will digress back to that -- I think that you and I can honestly sit here and say that if it weren't for our wives, things wouldn't be as nice for us now as they are. Do you agree with that?
They get better all the time.
Right. Now let's digress to the bad days. Whatever you'd like to say about them.

Oh, there were so many. I don't know where to start. But when you're young, and you love what you're doing, that's how much music meant. And you're idealistic -- it was just wonderful to travel and go through all those hard knocks and everything.

Can you give us some experiences, any time you had a big problem on the road, as a drummer, what you had to do to set up the drums, and did you ever get to some place where it was snowing and everything was just ...
Oh, Jesus, we played in Waterloo, Iowa in 19 -- oh, one of the years, 33 or 34.
That's what I want to hear.

Those were the two years with Dan Murphy, and we played Waterloo, Iowa, and we went to work, and I know that in my memory because it was the home town, that great trombone player that started with Artie Shaw 8 years later -- what was his name? He died so young. One of the great ...
Cheffry ...
Yea, and anyway, that is his home town, Waterloo, Iowa; and we went to work and it was cold.
Jack Jenny!
Jack Jenny, right. And we played a ballroom there. And in those days, they used to heat the
ballrooms with pot belly stoves. I'm not kidding -- and these were big ballrooms, you know, where a lot of people could dance.
Right.
And we got through, with those uniforms on, those things were just starched linen, and they just got -- and we were out there, and it was 36° below zero --
Boy, I'm freezing now!

We got to go out and unpack this truck, and they already had about two or three feet of snow in the four or five hours. That's a blizzard -- that we were playing that job. But my father had sent me a bear skin coat, because he knew I was on the road and he knew I was gonna be cold traveling, sitting in those cars, and the radiators, the heat didn't always work then. You'd go four or 500 miles sitting up in a car, and that thing saved my life. But the only thing is that I was picked to pack the God damn truck because I had the warmest coat! And it's 36° below zero.

Yeah? I think people who are gonna listen to these in the future, and even young people today, and the older people today, don't really realize I'm glad that you're a drummer and I am a bass player -- we are what we call partners in time, we are the guys who really pay the dues -- everybody else gets through and puts their instrument away -- it takes quite a time to get a bass fiddle
in a bag and get all of those things packed up.
Yeah, you're packing up drums and everybody's saying "Come on ..." And you ain't put the snare drum away.
Sure. And I can remember playing with Cab Calloway, and it wasn't a matter of black and white --
And didn't you have band boys, and what they called ...
We had band boys, but they had nothing to do with us playing in a cold tobacco warehouse. A band boy didn't play on the bandstand. So we had to play.
That's when we were well off.
Yeah, but what about when we played in these places -- and everybody in the band was cold.
We played drums with mittens on. I've seen saxophone players with earmuffs on. And nobody in the ballroom.

Yeah? I've seen Chu Berry play with gloves on, and I played bass with gloves on in a tobacco warehouse in West Virginia, and it was cold -- and the bus drove right into the warehouse, and we had big drums with -- what do you call those big gasoline drums and what not was filled up with -- to try to keep us warm, and there was no way.
By the same token, I have played with Tommy Dorsey at a tobacco warehouse, because we did the

Raleigh show, and they brought us down there, and I played there in the summer time at night when there were ten warehouses, and they put up a bandstand for us to play, and it was 110 or 115° on that stand. Skeletons on a hot tin roof.
This is what I want you to explain to young people -- about the differences and the difficulties under which we worked. I want you to tell that; I want people to realize the dues we paid.
When we were younger, it was a lot easier.
Oh, of course, and young people today don't have to do that.

It was the inspiration that you're going to arrive some day someplace, I hope, and then if you have a lot of luck along with your good talent, and a lot of people that never did get there, and a lot of people not as fortunate as you and I -- and I can say wholeheartedly -- lots of talent never got recognition.
Absolutely -- no question about that.
And that's why I'm naming some of these people.
We want to show what the reasons were, and what we went through that it wasn't all easy for you.
Oh no, it's no such thing as easy. It was a thrill trying to get there.
You mentioned a couple of films -- we mentioned one film, was there anything you wanted to mention about the era, I want you to talk about your eras.

I did a little picture with Charlie Barnet once where they gave me a little acting part, which was nothing. I think they wiped that off the face of the earth, they don't play it -- it was called "Juke Box Jennie". I had about three or four minutes in that one.
That was 1945.
Yeah, the Sensations of '45, but we made it in '44.
Yes, we did.
And that's where I was taken, and the draft was on in Hollywood -- Ernie Caceres, he and I went together, we were roommates.
Ernie Caceres was what kind of player?
He was a saxophone player.
Thank you.

And never did get any recognition for being the great clarinetist that he was. He was mostly known for his baritone playing, all the records he made with Bobby Hackett and in that era. I got him -- what we needed, we lost the first saxophone player, and I mentioned him to Woody, and he hired him. He was never so happy in his life; nobody had any idea that he could play lead. Now he had been in the
Glenn Miller band.
He was of Mexican-American descent, wasn't he?
Yes.
I think we should mention that.

Yes, and he had a brother, he had two brothers -- Emilio, who was a great jazz violinist, but he never got out of that Texas era. He got back to New York years before I had met Ernie, but the whole family were artistes, and they used to have a little Mexican band within the family, and they used to go around ...
He decided to call it the Mexican-American Wetbacks at that time.
Well, that word came later on to me. I never associated it with that -- and they still call them that.
Right.
They still do that in Texas; they say the wetbacks are coming, and you know, there's that little bristle that goes up and down my spine. Just another part of the racial thing.
So what was that era now?
What year?
Yeah.
It was in '44. And he went into the draft, he went to Fort Dix, and I was deferred. He was just
before me.
When did you go into Eddie Condon's?
Did you want to go into that era, or do you want to talk about something else?

No, it was the turning point. In the first place, when I left Woody, I was looking for a job, and I was walking down the street and I saw Cozy Cole, and he said Raymond Scott needs a drummer. And this was only a couple of days after I was without a job. So I went up and tried out for the job -- he tried everybody in New York City.
What job were you trying out for?
Raymond Scott had a 15-minute CBS coast to coast radio show.
But how did you know that he needed a drummer?
Because Cozy Cole had just quit him.
Oh, I see.
He was a very hard man to get along with.
Oh, this is where I want the story to begin.

When I went in that band, this was my first association with Ben Webster -- this gets to the nubbing. In that band, Raymond Scott and Webster had black and white -- they had Charlie Shavers playing trumpet, this is '45 now, or '44 -- and he had Ben Webster on tenor,
and Milt Yaner, you remember him --
Yes, a great trumpet player.
And he was white.
Excuse me, was Milt Yaner a saxophone player?
Yes.
Oh, I thought you said trumpet.
No.
Shall we check that to see if it was the trumpet or not?
Who?
Milt Yaser
Milt Yaner was the first saxophone player.
Okay.

Definitely. And we had Ben Webster, as I mentioned -- Israel Crosby was the first week or two, he was changing all the time. Maybe he came from Fletcher Henderson's band in Chicago, a great black bassist. A great one.
Right, one of the truly great ones.
But Raymond was changing -- every other day or so, he'd try somebody else because he got away with the union because he could give them a week's notice, a five-day notice, a day-to-day notice.
Who was responsible for that conversion from the CBS which had no black musicians at all -- do you remember who was responsible for that?
Well, Raymond Scott must have had with this band, a great deal to do with it. We had Tommy Young, as I mentioned, for awhile there.
That was CBS. Do you think CBS might have had something to do with that?
Yes, and to coincide with that, who was in the office there -- oh, he had something to do with it. Lou ShooBe. He was the contractor, but he had a great deal to do with it.

I'm sure it was John Hammond, because I was supposed to go in there, and I know that John had come to Cab Calloway's band, and Cozi Cole had been taken from Cab Calloway's band to join them, and John Hammond had been responsible for that.
Oh yes? Well, then we'll give him all the credit, because at that time, I never questioned who ...
I see.

All I know is we worked together and he was a hard drinking man and a hard playing band, and this same period of time -- I don't know how many weeks it was -- just a few weeks -- we're on the air at 4:45 to 5:00 -- and we would run over to the old Charlie's Tavern, and we tipped the
elevator boy to wait for us, and we'd run over and he'd have the bar set up before we went on the air, because Raymond was a stickler for ...

That was 7th Avenue, right? And Charlie's Tavern was -- just to explain to the people that might not know, this is 7th Avenue between 50th Street and 51st Street, and 799 7th Avenue was on the right hand side going south, and Charlie's Tavern was on the left hand side.
It was on 7th Avenue.
Right, it was 7th Avenue.
In the Roseland building. The old Roseland building, and downstairs on the 51st Street side, I guess was the original Basin Street West. But we'll get to that afterwards. Now where were we?
We want the people to know a few years later, exactly where these places are.
You know, I think that office building is still there.
It is there.
For awhile, it was A&R.

Well, no, the office building -- it's now the City Squire, which is turned into the Sheraton Hotel now, where that same place was. It's now the Sheraton there, Roseland and the Roosevelt was upstairs, and ...

During this period of time, Charlie Shavers who apparently -- we had just worked together for the first time, and Ben and I got along so well, Charlie said John Kirby is going to reorganize. Would you like another gig? Now we were off the air at five o'clock -- we rehearsed from like twelve o'clock noon and we were off the air at five, and he said -- and remember, this was the thick of the warfare around the world -- World War II.
And there was a place called The Aquarium.
That was on 7th Avenue, between 47th Street and 8th Street.
Right. And he said would you be interested and I said sure. And I had heard lots of records then, and I knew how important Charlie was in that band.
Charlie who?
Charlie Shavers.
Okay, because we were talking about Charlie Barnet and we've been talking about Charlie Webster, Shavers, and we want to know which Charlie you're talking about.

Oh, I can tell them about John Kirby's name is that they'll have to use research, because I can't get in -- John Kirby was a big hit at the time, 52nd Street, the old Congress Hotel, and I remember he had Buster Bailey, Russell Procope -- Buster Bailey was a great clarinetist that used to be with the original Fletcher Henderson band from Chicago -- among others. Russell Procope, a great alto saxophonist, was still in the driver's seat around New York, and --
And the only living ex-member of the John Kirby band.
Of the original band.
Only living member.
Well, I'm a living member of -- we were the next band.
Oh, I'm sorry -- were you in the original band?
I went to work with them.
Well, you said they were going to reorganize. I thought ...
They had reorganized; they had broken up.
Well, weren't you in the original band?
No.
Okay, I'm saying that Russell was a member of the original one.
Right.
Yeah, that's what I'm saying.
And Billy Kyle.
Billie Kyle?
Billy Kyle was in the army, and Russell Procope was down in Georgia someplace in the army.
Uh huh.

So I went with the band, and they added Ben Webster, and Ben had done just the same thing with the arrangements that he did with Duke Ellington's band when he first joined him. He had no parts; he made his own. He made his own parts. Until they could write him some part. And you'd never know it, that's how people don't know the greatness of Ben Webster, how deeply he knew music, to sing with four saxophones and make a fifth part -- you don't do things like that.
Well, he did the same thing with John Kirby's band, and it was a fly book.
He was in that reorganized band -- Ben Webster?
Uh huh. And we had intended to take Billy Kyle's place, who was down in the South Pacific, and we got Ram. on piano -- Kirby got Ram Ramirez. He was a fine piano player.
Composer of 'Lover Man'.
Yes. And by the way, my first wife, Nita -- he was with Barnet for a while when we were in theatres, and he was stuck for ...
Beautiful.
That was on the way, that's just a side remark. George Johnson was a great saxophone player.
George James?
George Johnson.
George Johnson? I don't know George Johnson.
He was a very light-skinned boy, a great musician -- he was in the studios for awhile.
And you're sure it wasn't George James?
No, George Johnson -- and I think he just died this last year. I think. I don't like to say things like that unless I'm sure.
Sure ...

But I think he's among other friends that I lost along the way -- we added, or he added Ben Webster, played his own parts, and we went to work through thick and thin. Now we did that show -- I'm coming up with a scary one -- we did a 12 o'1 rehearsal into five o'clock and came off the air. And then I had a few hours to relax a little bit and go down from nine to four in the morning, or nine-thirty to four in the morning with John Kirby's band.
Yeah, who's was this show?
Now this is a double job, we're doubling now.
Yeah, but what was the show?
We had no show; well, I was on the CBS show.
Well, what did you do with John Kirby?
We played his book.
Where?
On the bandstand.
The bandstand in what club?
We went into the Aquarium.
Okay. The Aquarium. And can you tell me who the musicians were? John Kirby revised band -- not the O'Neal Spencer, not the Billy Kyle. Not the original band, this was the revised band.
Uh huh, yes.
And Cliff Leeman on drums, and Billy Kyle on piano?
No, Billy was in the army. Ramirez on piano.
Ram Ramirez, and there's John Kirby's the bass player and leader, and Buster Bailey -- was Buster Bailey there?
Right.
Is he?
Yes.
Okay, Buster Bailey is there. And Charlie Shavers ...
Charlie Shavers and Ben Webster, and George Johnson playing alto.
So we didn't have -- Russell Precape wasn't there?
No, he was in Georgia, in the army.
So you added a man, then. A tenor player.
Added a tenor man, and ...
It was a bigger band than the original John Kirby band.
One man more.
All right, okay. Thank you -- this is what I'm trying to find out.

And in the interim, we went in there for about a month or two. Raymond Scott booked the Roxy Theatre and said we'll coincide our rehearsals and our CBS show, because the Roxy Theatre was right next door to ...
At 49th and 7th Avenue.

Right next door to where we did the CBS show. Now he's not figuring us with Kirby, that's the last thing in his mind, but he figured we could run from the theatre, we could run from the air show over to the theatre and do our shows.
It was on 50th and 7th Avenue.
That's right, one half block.
From 50th to 51st street. And the
CBS show was what we now call A&R recording studios -- 799 7th Avenue.

Right. So we did four -- three, no, four shows a day and five on Saturdays and Sundays at the Roxy Theatre. We were five days across the board. Weekdays we did the air show across the country, the radio show, and when I would come off from the Roxy Theatre -- the three of us -- Ben, Charlie and myself, we would walk down the street three blocks and go to work with John Kirby until four o'clock in the morning.
Where was that?
The Aquarium.
Oh yes, that's right.
Let me tell you, we were doubling three jobs. This is really for the boobie hatch.
That's right.
Yes sir; get my white coat ready!
Now, Cliff, just for the record, what kind of bread -- I mean money -- for the people of any other area, we call it bread ...
Well, it was during war time, and the money was good.
But I mean price wise -- I was -- I remember, I was with Cab Calloway in 1936, and I was making $100 a week, and Cab Calloway was paying very high money. Now
what kind of money were you making then?
Well, this is late '44-'45, this was during the thick of the war and money was very loose, nobody was keeping too many records -- except CBS.
Uh huh.

And I got paid $150 -- this was the first big money I had ever seen, I was paid good by Woody Herman, the biggest -- up until then. I'll give you -- but this is way behond proportions today, this was a fabulous amount of money at that time.
Oh, it was unbelievable.
I mean, $150 was for doing the radio show.
That's like $1,000 now. Easy.
I know -- and $175 for doing the Roxy Theatre, was scale. Now that was $325, and John Kirby was giving me $175 out of his pocket, ripping off these big bills ...
Oh, man ...
The organized --
And the best hotel in town cost you $90 a week.
The organized people that owned clubs at the time, owned the Aquarium, you know, and wrote that thing off.
Sure.
So that was a fabulous amount of money, and I didn't cap that for several more years to come.
Oh yeah, that was easily a tremendous amount of money. Your musicians ...
I couldn't go on very long, I was only getting 3 or 4 hours sleep a day, and this was an impossibility.

You were a premier musician. But I can't think of any better musicians than you were playing with. John Kirby and all these gentlemen that you've named -- these were the epitome. John Kirby had been the greatest bass player.

Oh yeah, and I didn't mention him as a bassist, too. We had a friendship -- it was a friendship organization. Charlie Shavers - whatever Charlie said to Kirby -- was just getting himself straightened out, Kirby would go along with, you know. Charlie, he listened to Charlie, because he did a lot of wrong things business wise.
Yes.
And he needed reorganization.
Right.
However --
Is this at a time when he were still married to Maxine Sullivan?
No, he had been divorced. He had been married two or three times by then.
He'd been divorced?
Two or three times by then, yes.
Because he was once married -- John Kirby was once married to --
I know, that's when they first hit. And she made 'Loch Lemond' And the band had white tails, they wore, and ..
Yeah, they had been the biggest little band in the world.
Very close -- the biggest little band in the world, was the way they were billed, the way they were written up, and classed. [PAUSE]
Right.

We was just talking about John Kirby and that fantastic band -- and I don't think any other small band has ever come up to that reputation, the biggest little band in the land, John Kirby, with that fabulous group, of which you had at one time been a member of one of the groups -- maybe one or two of the groups, with Cliff Leeman, which you had once been a member.
Will you continue?

Before me, the band was comprised of impeccable musicians, Buster Bailey's thoroughly -- because Charlie Shavers wrote a book that was pretty rough to play, and they played impeccably. Every member. By the same token, Billy Kyle fed that band, and I played against them with Charlie Barnet, doing the Worlds Fair in '39, and
they almost cut us a brand new one, and I had never seen their drummer.
O'Niel Spencer?

O'Niel Spencer -- who fed them double time -- the thing with the fast wrists, and he and Charlie Shaver, they almost blew Charlie Barnet 's 16 pieces -- we had four trombones, and four or five trumpets then, and you should have heard them out swing us at certain points.
Uh huh.

Now, getting back to me while I was in the band, just one thing to end this up, this era in the Aquarium -- that was when we were talking before, and I don't know whether it's on tape, about Charlie Shavers, he got the offer then to go with Tommy Dorsey, and he left John after helping him out as many days as he could -- he went and joined Tommy Dorsey; I don't know whether he was at the Pennsylvania Hotel or not, and he had seen that John got straightened out and gotten on his feet, so he sent Dizzy in, if you pardon me -- I had worked with Dizzy. He had come to Barnet 's band, we had ever black or white trumpet player that ever lived -- we had Peanuts Halland with us. Well, anyway, Dizzy had come from that little altercation that he had with --
My boss, Cab Calloway!
Yeah, Cab, down in Hartford, Connecticut.
Hartford, Connecticut, right.
A State Theater, I'll tell you about that later.
You can't tell me -- I was there! (Laughter)
He came straight from the State dinner in Hartford and ran into Barnett's fold, so I knew Diz. Well, Diz came on the band and he was still pursuing his beat all, 'Salt Peanuts.'

And he came in and he was having a little trouble with Charlie Shavers' book. Now I don't care how great a musician you are, but Diz is one of the greatest musicians alive, but there is no trumpet player that could have an easy time with Charlie Shavers' keys.
Oh, I agree with you. No question about it.
Trumpet keys. He wrote for what he had learned.
Well, he had been the guitarist.

Yeah, he wrote the book for himself. Never thinking another trumpet player would have to do it. Anyway, Diz would sit there and every time Ben would take -- they played extended solos, you know, we'd extend the arrangements for short, you know, and we'd send the solos, so there'd be some jazz to play. And Ben would be going, and I got to do this -- it's got to be on tape -- and Diz would

be sitting there very nonchalant -- and he'd be going, they'd come to an end of a phrase and Ben's playing a solo, you know, and Diz is going, 'salt peanuts, set peanuts,' he's developing this thing, he's doing it all along the street -- and I wish he were here now, God bless him!
Sure ...
But Ben didn't like that -- and I'm not gonna tell any tales out of school, but Ben sat down and pulled one of his old-time tricks that he used to pull with Duke once in awhile, he took out a shiv.
A shiv? We want the people to know what that is.
Now he's one of my dearest friends in life, and he started cleaning his nails.
Oh, it was a knife.

But there was another purpose for that knife, I've got it in my hand, and he'd look over and argue, 'Well, Dizzy, don't ever do that!' and Dizzy would look out, you know, at all the people, I'm shaking my head and fast around, looking around at all the people with the eye exposure, and Dizzy would ignore him and smile.

But Ben would dress it -- and that's just a little aside here. So Dizzy figured he wasn't gonna scuffle with that book, there wasn't that much worthwhile, because he was working on the street here and there with Charlie Parker and all the

guys, you know, and that's when he was going through his little salt peanuts -- he was developing that routine, it was just about that era. So they didn't know who to get and Charlie Shavers got Emmett Berry, God bless him.
Uh huh.
Well, he and I had been friends over the years.
Emmett Berry played what?
Trumpet -- a great trumpet player, and he didn't get enough to play with Basie to become -- I think he took Buck's place, Buck Clayton's place at one time.
On trumpet.

On trumpet, yes, in the Basie band. When the Basie band was developed, after they were well known. But Emmett could read more than anybody would give him credit for, along with being a swinging trumpet player -- and a charming, beautiful, wonderful man.
Right.
And I have to keep saying this, because some people were just so close to me.
Now what band was this --
This is still Kirby's band. Dizzy didn't want any part of it.
And Emmett Berry played better than Dizzy?
Well, I would have to say so, because
he read --
I want you to tell the story.
Well, he read the book, and I'm not comparing the prowess of the musicians. But he had a prowess -- he read the book better than Dizzy did; Dizzy didn't want to be bothered with that.
Well, Dizzy probably wanted to be more creative.
He wanted to have his own thing.
Yeah.
But you weren't about to turn that book down; you had to read the ... you had to play the book.
Because Charlie Shavers had written -- Edward Greig's music -- and you had to play these things first.
And just about that time, somebody brought in 'Coney's Special' to us. That's a feeding son of a gun arrangement -- did you ever hear Coney's Special?
I don't remember.

And I did a few of those things. The only recording I did at the time with John Kirby was I did a couple of Musak things and I've never heard them. I saw one listed that I made once, and it didn't have my name on it. Who was the drummer ... a little short fellow --
Uh ...
* Bill Beason

He got credit for one of those Muzak things. Because when Kirby went back, he played against Duke Ellington, and I had gone home - that's when I went home. That gig was over, and I went for a very short time on the road with Jimmy Dorsey, which was a bad experience, because he was sick and I just mentioned that I went with Jimmy Dorsey three or four months.
And then around -- what year did you go into --
I had gone back home then, I went back because my father died-- that was 1945, just before the D-Day.
Uh huh. And you played with Dorsey until '45 -- that's when you left.
Yes.
Uh huh.
And I went back home; I had a little piece of land that my father had left there, that my aunt gave me.
Two years you stayed away.
Yeah. I built a house.
Uh huh.
But I never figured that -- I had a little insurance money that I put together with the land that I got -- we had a 35-acre farm. And my aunt gave me a piece

of property there, an acre and a half or two acres, and I built a house; I thought maybe that would do it. And I designed the house, I did the architecture myself, I got the money from the insurance, the local musicians -- contractors, and designed it, I got some stone masons there, they were 80 and 82 years old -- and built a lovely home, but I didn't figure that I needed money to make a living. I had the home, and no money.
And, John Kirby called me to come back and go to the Aquarium. So the house was just finished, it wasn't even painted inside, and I came back, and that must have been in '47.
That was 1947, and you came in with Glen Gray, right?
Well, I came into work with Kirby, but he'd already hired this other drummer.
What was his name?
Going back in the Aquarium with him. I can't think of his name. (Beason)
Yeah, well, that's okay. Then you worked with Glen Gray, is that right?
He came along, hanging around Charlies Tavern.
Dorsey, and then you went to Nick's.
Yeah.
Now I want you to tell it -- you tell
it because these are just facts that I've read and heard about you.
Bobby Hackett got me in Gray's band, and they went on the road, and then we went out of Texas, and I quit and went back to New York. And Bobby Hackett went into Nicks-
A great trumpet player, Bobby Hackett.
First -- oh, I'm sorry ...
But that's who you're talking about, Bobby Hackett -- the great trumpet player.
Yes, yes.
Okay.

First, when I came off from the Glen Gray band, Charlie Barnet reorganized in '48 and I was with that new band, and he didn't know who to hire, among other things -- he was groping around for musicians, and I mentioned Stan Kenton's first big band had broken up, and they were well known in all the polls and everything, you know, I had suggested Eddie Sefranski; he got him.
Eddie? Oh, yes.
And he had a couple of the arrangers -- oh, I can't think of their names. Out in Hollywood, he got ...
Ralph Burns and those guys.
Well, Ralph originally was in Louie's Woody's

I'm trying to explain it to you. Right.
I did a couple of schools, and that's what I was there for. We played the jazz concerts.

It's straight up.

Yeah, we took a bus once. Incidentally, I've been very fortunate to be invited to a few of those parties, and I have some pictures of you when you were chef, where you were making grape leaves in the kitchen -- I have some of these great, some of my very precious pictures of you in the kitchen with a whole chef's uniform on.

Well, that was for Mattie. She asked -- I had cooked every year previous to that, and she called me up. He called me for the party and he says you got to cook, and I said, 'Yeah? What do you want?' and he said, 'Mattie, what do you want Cliff to cook?' -- because I always got a big bang out of chefi ng. So she said how about some stuffed grape leaves, and I said, ah, come on, I'm used to cooking spaghetti and all that, and I had cooked some dinners out there, and I said what's with the grape leaves?

So I said okay, and these were my dear friends -- so I went across the street, and there was a camera man from CBS who lives across the street from me, he's Greek and his wife really cooks. So I say do you know anything about stuffing grape leaves? And she told me what to do, where to buy them, etc.
So that was a new ...
Well, some day I want you to see these pictures, because you are a mess in that kitchen.
Well, I used to carry my chef's outfit around -- but that was really in the great days during my really drinking days. Of course, I started drinking when I was 14 years old.
We ought to mention that.
And I never had a problem until the last few years.
What were the last few years, Cliff?
Well, it was catching up with me.
Well, what do you consider the last few years?

I been 7 years without it -- no, 8 years, no, 7 years without a drink. So all of a sudden, God was wonderful and I saw the light, and in fact, I don't take too much credit, because I was dying. So I gave up drinking and thought it never could be done, I had tried many times, but I didn't think you could go up on a stand and play. I was always of a nervous nature, and a lot of my drinking was because I was a nervous person.
Well, you should be congratulated to be able to do these things.
Well, it was cold turkey, and it took me six months to eight months to get over it.
But you should also give credit to people who helped you through these things.

Oh yes, well, this is my wife. And to make a comeback -- Ralph Sutton helped me after I got over this terrible seige, he, Ralph Sutton and hiw wife Sonny who owned their own club in Aspen -- we worked there together -- insisted that I come up and I said I don't think I'm ready yet, I don't think I can play without drinking. Well, I found out I could. But it took me years.

So I found out that you don't need any stimulant. I can get very high on black coffee. I can get extremely high, because I'm a fairly nervous person. And it took me a lot of years to learn something. I used to think that I got warmed up by drinking, I guess kids still do today. But my warming up period -- I'd get there an hour to two hours ahead of time on any job that I do, even if my drums are all set up, like with a steady job or a concert hall -- and I spent two hours there warming my hands up. I have wrist exercises that I do to get the blood circulating, and warming my feet up and I do calisthenics. And I was ready to play without any booze, and I finally got so that I wasn't in a panic in front of a bunch of people after all these years.
Now that's just 58 years minus 14 years, is 44 years of continuous playing in front of people, and I always

figured there was no way to make it without the booze, and God has been good to me. It's a better world since I stopped drinking, and I did myself some good, too, and Dick -- Richard Gibson stepped in there and helped me get over that, so all these things came -- nobody had any qualms about hiring me again. I might have told a few people off along the way when I was in nightclubs.
You admit that?
Oh, certainly.
Well, Cliff --

But I never fell down on the job. That's why I kept continuing until I was destroying myself. You don't need that. It's an illusion. I drank because I was a nervous guy all my life, and there were times when I thought I was doing better because I had -- I was half ...
But what did you say, it wasn't going to help the music?
It wasn't going to help the music. Studying and practicing is what furthers your music.
I can't think of a better way to end on this point, that it's not gonna help your music.

I warm up without anything but caffeine. And that's coffee -- and I get there two hours early, and all the concerts I do across the country, I am whipped if I don't and, we'd get into towns, and we'd get off the plane with the World's Greatest Jazz Band, and I go and I have it

all set up, somebody check me in, I'm going over to the hall, four o'clock in the afternoon, we're there from the plane, the concert is from 8 to 10 and I'm over there at 4 o'clock with my own coffee pot I travel with and my change of clothes, and I sit down backstage and I practice, and I warm up, rather, is the word. I don't practice, I don't do any of those things. I never touch a drum; I have a set of exercises, and I'd be happy to show anybody that was interested.

And I could warm my hands and my feet, you know, because more than any other instrument, playing drums is a great deal of athletics. You never saw an Olympic field, they don't get there early before they do their hurdles, they warm up, and if they want to swim, they're gonna warm up. No matter what you do that's athletic, you got to warm up those muscles, you got to pull something.
And that's what I have to do. Play the drums without any stimulants, any false stimulants.
Uh huh.
So I'm getting wound up in this thing, but that's it. You asked me a question, and I don't need any stimulants.
Sounds beautiful. We can end this for now. (CUT)
This is a continuation of the Cliff Leeman

interview and recording. As Cliff will tell you on here, after a long session we had the other night, he went home and had some sort of chance to relax, and here he sort of explains himself and recollects. Here are some of his fine recollections -- and Cliff, thank you for this little note telling me what happened.

Dear friend Milt Hinton, this is Sunday, the 25th of February. Yesterday you interviewed me for the first time for my musical and personal history for five solid hours of tapes. It was like breaking the ice in Chesapeake Bay frozen over by the Coast Guard. I'm exhausted today.

We did accomplish so much, and I learned a lot from your interrogations as to the value of explaining names and places -- so they would be understood to those studying the tapes. You see, I drop names to you as a friend, who understands and I expect the uninitiated to understand, also, which they won't without further research on their part.
So, in the future interviews, I will be more explicit.

Just play that back for a balance, and found out I had a frog in my throat, upon commenting on the frozen over Chesapeake Bay and the ice should have been with a Coast Guard cutter. You must admit we worked pretty hard for our
first session, but it was so fruitful.

Before continuing with our work and thoughts at large, I want to say that I am greatly honored and deeply grateful to the Smithsonian Institute and those responsible for including me on their prestigous list of persons to be entered into the archives of jazz. I feel I have contributed much musically over a period of some 50 odd years that may be of importance to the uninformed and the interested -- student or researcher.

So I am most excited to get on with the work ahead of us. To continue, each band that we discussed on the tapes previously, that I played with was sort of a private story, an episode in my life, and I have kept scrap books and articles, writeups and ads since high school days. As I said, each band as I progressed, and have categorized with complete pictures of personnel, towns that we played and cities, ballrooms, theatres, the players within it, within them -- each band is separated individually in scrap books which I have, and there are many stories and episodes connected with each scrap book separately. It's impossible as we discuss the overall picture of what I've done, to allign all these categorically as we talk on tape.
Well, missing incidents covering the era and my transitions from one band to another up to the present day, without going back over the data which we have, and

letting me reminisce about the different bands and musicians at leisure, I have referral notes from a great many of those incidents, and we can discuss them -- but they cannot be reinserted on the tape. Like you can in written manuscripts. You see, you can go over them and come back, and reinsert.

But tapes are a little rough in that matter, and I may miss things. I think the interest is all there, if they are added to the finished overall tapes under the heading of "Thoughts at Random", omissions and corrections and summing up of my favorite musicians I've worked with, how they enriched me musically and helped me attain the best out of my drumming, to reach peaks in my playing ability.

I have these notes to refer to, notes only, mind you -- because I might miss something very important; I might miss some very important things to me, while relating and reminiscing on tape. So if nobody has any objection, I would just love to work with you, Milt Hinton, in that manner.
As I say, I have the notes only -- I do not have a retentive memory, and I have to recall things, and the notes help me to be correct.
As I sit here and reminisce and look over some of my notes, I find myself becoming interested in how I got into jazz so deeply as a young man. But during 1928 to '30 when

I was in high school, I had a next door neighbor -- a young lady, her name I remember her name vividly, her name was Pat Bolen, Patricia Bolen -- and in the summer, I would practice in my room with an open window, and I would hear this music, and she had every Top Five, Louis Armstrong Top Five record to date at that time -- and this was '28 and '29, and of course back in New England, that was unusual to hear that kind of music.

And I had that coming in my ears day and night. She used to help her mother in the kitchen; she used to have an old crank phonograph and she used to play everything -- and I would hear 'Sleepy Time Down South' and 'Cornet Chop Suey' and a whole array of all the songs that Louie first made, and that was my first intro to jazz along with the bands that I heard, which we already discussed -- at the old Beach and the playing of the colleges in my home town.
But I had a fairer knowledge of Louie, God bless his soul, through the courtesy of Pat Bolen.

Thank you very much, Cliff, for that, and I'm sure that any kind of way that you want to do this is gonna be just fine. The most important thing is to get your history down about what you have done and I'm sure we can file it in such a way that this will be most interesting to anyone that wants to hear it.
So if you can recollect these things this way, by all means, let's do it, so if you'd like to go on talking
about the Charlie Barnet band, please do so.

There is much that we hadn't gone into about the Charlie Barnet band in the forties and '41 and '42. But one of the incidents -- I gave title to, that I thought might be interesting, which I named the Casa Mañana Affair, or, a disaster for us -- when the (bleep) hit the fan for the Charlie Barnet band, and it was some titles of our idols and heroes and how they turn on us, and it goes like this --

We were working at the Casa Mañana Ballroom, or club, it used to be the original Cotton Club when Louie Armstrong worked there, in California, outside of Hollywood. And Duke Ellington's band was playing in the show, Jump for Joy, at a theatre in LA, and Barnet and he got together and talked, as they were so dear friends, and the band and the musicians, that possibly it'd be nice when they finished the theatre on closing night that they had an old fashioned battle of music. It was planned.

And we worked at the Casa Mañana, -- so Barnet, we were all very nervous about the whole thing, because they were our idols, the Ellington band, Duke -- so Barnet came up with a very bright idea. He said pick your own man and find out what his favorite bottle is, what kind of favorite booze he drinks, and let it go from there. We were supposed to supply them with booze and get them stoned, I guess.

So we were considered one of the biggest hard drinking boozing bands in the business - the Barnet band. However, no one pointed out that Duke's band was undisputed number one in that category. They drank all of our booze, they drank all their own booze, they drank all of the bar's booze, too. There was no contest, musically.

I think we managed to play "Pompton Turnpike" and that was about it for us. Some day I hope you'll reminisce with Sonny Greer, I'm sure he'll remember about that. That was in 1940, to put it in the proper perspective.
I can also add that we had a lovely time socially listening to our heroes.

In our previous session, interview session, Milt, we went to great lengths on Jo Jones and his impact on my drum, his impact on me drumnistically. But there are other very important things that affected my plan and eventually help me to adopt my own style of playing and expression.

Next to Jo Jones, I would say Sidney Catlett, then possible Zutty Singleton along the way. I'll get to each one eventually. There was Davie Tough, all 110 pounds of him ringing wet! He was a great swinger. And equally as powerful. I have had some people compare my approach to his in a certain period in my life. His was not to predominate the soloist, but to feed them. His big band work with

Woody Herman showed how exciting he could feed without getting in the way of the soloist and the arrangements. I was -- to hear over the years, Baby Dodds, who like Zutty Singleton, came north to Chicago out of New Orleans via the riverboats. Their's was a pulsating, four four beat of the traditional Orleans style. Baby Dodds played with the original Three Deuces in 1939 when I had the chance to hear him and to study his approach.

He worked at the bar with the Deuces with -- did I mention 1939? Yes. He worked with at that time Louie Armstrong on piano and the fabulous -- to me, fabulous -- Lonnie Johnson on guitar, a truly great blues guitarist, blues vocalist. I've been hearing what used to be called race records then, I used to get a hold of everything I could get my hands on, and in that idiom, and I guess that meant predominantly black artists, the race record title that is, because some blue, racy, or possibly offensive material was on them in those days, and most of them were found in juke boxes around the south and the midwest and in bars and so forth.

Anyway, Baby Dodds had a roll and snare drum, so artistically smooth it was referred to as smooth as silk or satin. He played, as did Zutty Singleton, with the open tone of the base drum. They tuned the base drum, but no padding in the heads and vibrating free. Baby Dodds employed all kinds of little tricks in his solos, using

tom toms and bass drums, the butt end of the sticks, etc. on the bass drum, making a tom tom sound. And with the wood blocks and the rims of the bass drum, one heavy cymbal, his breaks were like Zutty -- the same approach on drums, but they were most amusing, very amusing.

Zutty and I were close and dear friends. I knew him from 1936 until his death in the '70's, which his work rubbed off on me and it influenced my work in that particular era, and it was especially predominant in the Artie Shaw record which was Blues A and Blues B, a collector's item now -- it was double sided, 78, and I think it was a Columbia recording, but I'm not sure. But I think you will hear all of their influences in my playing on these sides -- at that time, before I had changed to what was my present day style, and in addition, my employing on that record 'A and B Blues', the giant 25-inch Chinese cymbal that I started using frequently throughout which caused an influx on sold out Chinese cymbals at Bill Mather's Drum Shop in New York -- the interested jazz buffs and drummers bought them.

George Wettling, another great Chicago drummer, with superb taste, he got a musical sound in tuning his drums, he was well studied in drum instruction, and a most exciting soloist -- his solos also had a great deal of humor in them, technique -- and we were wonderful friends, and I lean towards

many of his musical approaches as my own career continued. George and I first knew, after I followed him in Shaw's first big band, and I would find him at Nick's in the Village, in 1936, and he was with Bunny Berigan's first band, and one-nighters through New England, we had battles of music with them, and a battle of music in those days was two bands that was promoted by the ballroom, and the bookers, two bands in the same ballroom taking alternative sets, and let the people decide which band they liked best. I don't know what it proved, but it was interesting.

George also was with a large band featuring Red's first wife, Mildred Bailey. More battles of music in New England. I've saved Sidney Catlett until now, a prince among fellows. But a king on the drummer's throne - that was what we called and still do, a folding drum seat. A drum throne. Sidney, considered by many drummers, historians and critics, as the greatest jazz drummer. He was very close to being that. I always had reservations about calling anyone the 'greatest' anything. Because each individual has some wonderful attributes that another great doesn't have. Thank God everybody can do a little something different than somebody else can. An exception to the rule for me is the fact that Buddy Rich is the greatest drum soloist of all time -- to me. No holds barred, and I don't believe he will ever be capped. He's one of a kind, period, and I call him a close friend.

We were playing a Command Performance for the Queen of England, and at the reception afterward, the Queen of England came up and said, "Mr. Rich, that was a wonderful performance -- how do you do it?" And Buddy, whose ego is not lacking, as we all know, at a loss for words, replied, "Just lucky I guess!"

Well, back to Sidney Catlett. I first met him when he was with Louis Armstrong's big band, had our association during his days with Louie's small band. And he was playing on 52nd Street also during the heydays when I was with Don Bias of the Three Deuces, he would be with Don at other times when I was possibly with Ben Webster, and later when I was with Ben Webster at the Famous Door, Sidney Catlett was with Don Bias. And when I was at the Famous Door with Ben Webster -- I must remember later on to tell you this, it's really a funny story.

So we became fast friends, Sidney and I, and I mentioned with whom and where he played so you can understand I had a long time and many chances to observe this man. A large man, well over six feet -- long arms, and extraordinary large hands. When he sat down at the drums, the drumsticks looked like toothpicks in his hand. You expected to hear a thunderous eruption from the drums. Instead, well, a soft, fluid flow of assorted sounds emanated.
Whatever the music called for -- let's put it that
way -- he listened, and that to me is the most important part of drumming, the listening; listening the soloist. Listen to what they're playing.

Sidney's timing was impeccable, his execution in taste predominated, and he had excellent training, basically, I'm sure, but we never discussed it. He played a swinging, awe inspiring show. He loved to play behind great tap dancers, lines of girls dancing -- and shows in general. He enjoyed playing them, as much as he did jazz runs. And some of that rubbed off on me, thank goodness, because with Barnett's band, I had to play many, many shows; theatres. The Apollo Theatre, Washington's Howard Theatre -- these are all black theatres, and we had black and white revues with Charlie Barnet , and there was a whole string of theatres that we played.

And all the greatest at that time, and we had the original Cotton Club boys and girls -- wonderful dancers, and we had comedians, Pigmeat Markum and Avis and Estraledis, stepbrothers, and to me the greatest of all dancers was Baby Lawrence, the greatest jazz dancer. I don't think anybody could disprove that. And Bunny Briggs, too -- Bunny Briggs was with us for a long time, stumping for some of the acts. There were some of the acts, among many.
And I enjoyed playing them. A good drummer could make an act really more exciting. I enjoyed that, I

know Sidney did, too. I admired and idolized his work, it was impeccable. You can't say enough or much more. He shaded his lows as the music demanded with such intense intuitiveness, it was almost uncanny. The drummer's drummer.

As I told you before, knowing and listening to Chick Webb play helped me to model some of my ideas. He tuned his drums. Sidney Catlett, too, about the same way, with opened and dampened heads, and got a high sound. Chick Webb's was predominantly on the soloist's side, and it was just so wonderful, you had to hear them. There weren't enough recordings of his, and of course, they were very technical -- I mean, they were full of technique, is what I should say, swinging technically.

And I adapted to tuning my drums along those lines, and still adhere to those sounds today. I can't stand a deep snare drum's tone. That's why I use a three and a half, or at the most, a four-inch deep snare. I like the four-inch by 13-inch in diameter, the so-called piccolo snare drum in my work -- I've been using it for a long time for a crisp sound.

I'll save my dear friend Gene Krupa for later. His part in the drumming world is a legend in itself -- not only as a playing artist, but in the breaking down of old traditions and the drum's importance in bands. The huge growth of drum equipment and sales is an outgrowth of

his association with Benny Goodman. Benny Goodman's entrance into the jazz picture from '35 on, I only mention this -- not to deviate from my personal story, but because all of us drummers in the jazz era were affected in some way of another by his predominance. A legend in his time, without peer.

I mention Ray McKinley, a great drummer, whom I heard with the Dorsey brothers around '32 or '33. I heard him a couple of times in person on one nighters, and in Massachusetts and then back in my home town on the radio from Glen Island Casino -- I loved the sound of his drums, Ray McKinley. Here is tuning again -- his intense, but loose swinging beat and taste behind soloists. He's one of the masters of his time and through the years, a veteran swinger. He and I were also friends. I'm beginning to sound like Sammy Davis, but nevertheless, we were dear friends. I worked with his orchestra for a short while. When he hit the Fin egan book, and he asked me to go out on the road with him -- I went out for five or six weeks, and he said he'd split the book with me.

Well, it turned out that I did all the vocalists; Ray directed and did the vocalists, but when it came time to clear the swinging drum parts, Ray used to come back and say I've got it, Cliff. But however, he's a dear friend, and we shall remain that way.
I had mentioned an awful lot of names and people

along the way up to this point. But I would like that you understand the opportunities I had to listen and hear and be among the great artists of my time, and to adopt some of their approaches and to my way of playing.

The student today, they have music schools which are just wonderful -- wonderful bands they have, they play all the big charts, they have wonderful instructors, but they don't have the opportunities that I have had in the past. We had to find out the hard way by listening and applying ourselves and learning from others which the present day student doesn't have. He just applies it in school, and then he's on his own. Of course, there aren't those opportunities today, of jazz bands and so forth. I wonder how they're applying it to rock and so forth. However, there are many schools that are trying to keep the old jazz and the big band feeling alive, and the only way they can do that is by listening and research -- and maybe this will help somebody along the way in that line.

Thank you very much, Cliff. I'm sure that it's gonna help a great deal, the young people and people who are listening, to become a little more acquainted with these great jazz drummers that you've mentioned, and as you know, you and I both have had the opportunity to play with many of them, and I know your great respect and your great love, like mine, for them.
So thank you very much for that, and we will continue.

I would like to inject a remembrance that occurs to me that I forgot to mention when we were on the Tommy Dorsey subject. When I was with that band at the Pennsylvania Roof, we were the first band to fly to anybody's knowledge -- we were the first band to fly in an airplane as a group. And they flew us to Toronto, Canada, where from Newark Airport, for the Canadian Exposition -- I think that was the first year of the Canadian Exposition, 1939, in the Fall.

Continuing with the Tommy Dorsey orchestra, flying to the Canadian Exposition -- when we arrived in Newark to leave, we were all a little bit nervous, nobody ever flew before, and of course it was a chartered plane, with a Rolls Royce engine and twin props. Flying today is so common with everybody, I don't think you can appreciate what this was like.

It took us about two and a half to three hours to fly to Toronto from Newark, which is usually about a 40 minute trip today. And going over the mountains, they flew at pretty low altitudes then, into Buffalo and into Toronto, the air currents are pretty bad. However, it was quite an experience, and I remember at the Exposition, we played in a tent then, and I believe that they built

buildings now where it's a yearly annual thing. And we played in a huge tent, and it was a young crippled lady in a wheelchair that came back and asked us if we would play a demo, asked Carmen Masfrjen and myself, the guitar player, Carmen Masfrjen, if we'd see if Tommy would play this demo.

Well, when we returned to New York, we tried for about a week or two to get Tom, between sets, to go into a back room that we had up at the Pennsylvania Roof and listen to this record. And we couldn't get him to do it, but eventually he came in and listened to it, and that song turned out to be 'I'll Never Smile Again,' which after I left in a few months, Frank recorded, and I guess that's the story of that.

Another incident you might enjoy, Milt Hinton, I don't know whether you can use it in our biography -- however, while we were at the Pennsylvania Roof, that summer of 1939, we doubled for a couple of weeks at the World's Fair, that was the beginning, the 1939-1940 World's Fair in Flushing Meadows, and we doubled afternoons. They had a band show there, and the people would roam around and then come up to hear the bands of the era, and we were there for two weeks.

And while we were there, a set up of that band shell was across from the Frank Buck display; he was there, he was alive then, with some animals. And we had in the band a wonderful trumpet player, whom I know you worked with, just

a great lead trumpet player. He was with Tommy's band, his name was Andy Peretti, he was well known for his griping, he was an artist at griping, and he was also very beloved by all musicians as a great artist, and they sent Frank Buck over at one of our short intermissions; we were still sitting on the Bandstand, and he came over to get the crowds around and they used to advertise; they'd take times like this to advertise because they had a big crowd listening to our band. So Frank Buck came, however, with a pith helmet and all his array, the jungle suit, the whole works -- with an ape, or a monkey, as you will.
And, he set the monkey on a chair and started to do his spiel about come on over and I'll explain and I'll show you some of our animals and explain some of my expeditions into Africa.

Well, Andy Peretti, who didn't like the looks of the ape -- the ape turned around and stared at him. So Andy stuck out his tongue at him, and the ape didn't like that a bit, and he bit him. Not enough to draw too much blood, but he did bite him. Which broke the band up -- we thought it was very funny. And I don't know -- one of the great things about Andy is that he lisped badly, and he said, 'That thon of a bitch bit me!' Well, that was a laugh in itself, but I don't know whether it was coincidence or what when Frank Buck led the ape off the stand, the ape got sick, which broke the
band up, and of course, we had to take a long intermission to get over that.

I would like to get along to my association with Don Byas, another legend in his time, in our time, rather. And Ben Webster. First I'll take Don, because it follows in sequence that late '44, I played several weeks, maybe two months with Don Byas, our trio, with Clyde Hart on piano and I think, if memory doesn't fail me it was Teddy Sturgis on bass.
Of course in this band with Ted Sturgis on bass, you playing drums; of course Don Byas was a great tenor saxophone player, like Ben Webster -- also a great tenor saxophone player, huh, Cliff?

However, the other band with a young new piano player from Pittsburgh -- was Errol Garner and Slam Stewart was the leader, and wonderfully talented Harold West on drums. He did lovely brush work, and utilized a new sound to me by accenting the heavy part with the stick and the bell with a large cymbal. A little of that rubbed off on me along the way.

With Slam, he injected great humor in our style, and of course Errol Garner was contributing his great new piano style, and Clyde Hart on piano with us, was a great underrated musician, also. Billie Holiday used him on some of her records and Don Byas, another one of a kind tenor
player, with such intense feeling and tone, was a thrill to me to be picked to play in his company and to be picked as a side man.

At this period, the war in Europe was building to a climax, and the major cities blacked out after 11 P.M. hey were -- the Germans were sending the bomb into England at that time, and they were afraid it might reach into the United States in some of our big cities. So anyway, New York was blacked out, and it was an eerie feeling to go to work on 52nd Street at four o'clock in the afternoon with the sunshine blinding us, we had to rearrange our drinking habits and our bar appointments with the bartenders at the White Rose, on 6th Avenue and 52nd Street to get in shape for the playing ahead of us.

One incident of note -- I had an arrangement with Harold West, an excellent soul food cook -- that was his hobby, as well as mine. I have been cooking since I was a kid. I started actually cooking on the road because I loved my grandmother's food, and as a kid on the road, I missed that New England home cooking, so I had to cook it myself to remind me of home.

However, back to the Deuces -- Harold West and I came to -- had an arrangement where he played some of my sets on one Sunday while I cooked, and I'd reciprocate and cover him on his sets the following Sunday while he cooked.

They didn't serve food in the Deuces, because they couldn't afford a regular cook, a chef. So I had a beautiful kitchen all to myself for the first time in my life -- with huge ranges, 10, 15 and 20 gallon pots. Just shining, steel pots -- the works, and I was thrilled.

I paid -- I went shopping on Sunday morning, and I got at the club at 10 AM, I had gone down to the Italian section, which was open on Sundays, and this is the first Sunday I cooked, and I made 10 to 15 gallons of Slum Gullion* Now this was something I developed over the years, which is elbow macaroni with bits of ground beef and steak and Italian sausages and peppers, cheese and what have you, and with a light tomato and garlic sauce (Gee, and I'm getting hungry now!) mixed in all together, and I put it in the warmer, the steamer, and made another huge mixed salad. I made a huge mixed salad in a ten pound container, and several loaves of French Italian bread, and I left a dish and a sign on the kitchen table, reading, "Wash your own pets and dishes and don't forget to feed the kitty."

All day long the kitchen got busy, and as word passed around the street, Charlie Parker ducked in, Dizzy Gillespie, Ben Webster, countless musicians of the era that were developing their styles, especially Dizzy with his "salted peanuts," he was still working on them.
And only a few of my patrons -- I think Charlie

Parker came in for threesies. So just for the record, when you left that little thing in the kitchen that said feed the kitty, you didn't mean for them to take the food and give it to the cat -- you meant for them to lay some change when they got through eating and cleaned up their dishes, to leave a little money so you could be reimbursed for the food.
So now on to your great friend and mine, Ben Webster, the great saxophone player -- tenor sax.

However, I have to say first, as we went to the rehearsal, he hadn't hired Kenny yet, and we rehearsed first without Kenny and somebody suggested that Monk --Thelonius Monk -- was at Minton's and he was out for awhile and he could use a job.

So, after the rehearsal, Eddie Barefield suggested that we try Kenny Kersey, which worked out beautiful. So we opened at the club, and Ben opened with a couple of traditional arrangements. He kind of weakened on the second set, and demanded only an arrangement of 'Muskrat Ramble', and by the third set, he collected the arrangements and carefully put them under the piano and we never saw them again. It was the night they collected Dixieland, and we were all delighted to just play jazz. We used to have an expression, 'natural born jazz' with Ben feeding some of his Duke backgrounds behind the superb Buck Clayton and Eddie Barefield on clarinet, he was just a wonderful musician.

About then, things were slowing down on the street financially for the owners of clubs, and we closed The Famous Door; it was closing after many years. And the management came up and told us, 'Look, we're closing, we can't afford to keep open and so I thought I'd tip you off

before we foreclose. If you want anything in the kitchen or anything in the club, when we close Saturday night, take whatever you can get out without anybody noticing, and you're most welcome to take it, because this thing is going into a receivership."

And that's all I had to hear, because if they had another kitchen like the Three Deuces, it would thrill me to pieces. And I couldn't see how I could -- a couple of ten gallon pots I could get in my bass drum case, and I had my eye on something that I always wanted, which was a meat cleaver. And I've got it here in the kitchen sitting beside me right now. I've used it over the years.

However, the story -- while we were on the stand in the last couple of sets, Kenny Kersey who, after a few beers or so, was more or less of a prankster, and the piano was going out of tune, and they didn't care, of course, because they were closing -- and he had long legs, and he had a way where he could lift the piano up with his legs and his feet, and let it down suddenly and make a thump.

Well, he did this a couple of times, and Ben Webster was busy playing and turned around and glared at me a couple of times, good friends as we were. He was just about to get pretty ornery, and Kenny did it a couple more times, so I screamed at Kenny and I said, "Don't do that, dammit, don't do that. I'm getting blamed for this" I was thinking, and

Kenny thought that was funny. So one or two more clumbs, and Ben looked at me. So when the set was over, I screamed at Kenny, and the guys in the band didn't quite know what was going on, but they knew that we were having an argument.

So when the set was over, we were done, the place was closing, and I had it all prearranged for myself to get a couple of those beautiful pots in to my bass drum case, and then I ran before it was too late -- I was gonna put them in my snare drum case -- I ran for the meat cleaver.

Well, I hope you find it as funny as I think is is, because it really was -- the band, Ben Webster, who was always known to be quite capable of throwing his weight around, and Eddie Barefield, especially, who has been in training for what, I don't know, for some 60 years, they grabbed me. Everybody was positively sure that I was after Kenny Kersey with a meat cleaver! Maybe the way I've told it doesn't strike you as being funny, but I had taken a lot of explaining so I could get that meat cleaver in the drum case!

I think you explained that beautifully, Cliff. That must have been quite some scene; I can just see all those dudes grabbing you, thinking, well, okay, here goes a piano player. That was quite funny -- and I'm glad you still have that meat cleaver.
I know you'd be interested to know, Milt,

My association with Ben Webster was a musical romance. I use that expression to show my admiration and love for many of the great instrumentalists I worked with. But this one was special, very special. And I had a great love for Ben Webster as a person. He was unbelievably heavy in his drinking towards the latter years, and it just utterly destroyed him. Many people talked of his mean disposition when drunk. Well, to me, he was beautiful, and as the saying implies, seeing and believing is in the eyes of the beholder.

You will appreciate knowing this information, and my final episode in his quartet. I was instrumental in Ben's seeing and joining a new set of values in recreation. Number one, we were heavy drinkers, or we had a drinking problem, as well as mutual admirers of musical taste. Second, he couldn't get over the fact that I had a beautiful pair of hand made western boots, cowboy heels, and a beautiful Stetson and rancher's twilled pants that I carried on the road with him, anyway, a huge Mexican goat skinned and hand-tooled show saddle. A bridle and breast plate, all with silver spangles. He was a farm boy, originally
and he said he used to ride as a kid. I told him I rode some and broke some ponies that my father had as a hobby for show purposes at county fairs, in Maine.

We had so much in common that we damn near self destructed. So on with the Ben Gazi incident. About the last of '47 or early '48, Ben asked me if I wanted to go to Washington, he was going to the Ben Gazi nightclub, it was a black club in the black district in Washington, D.C. The band was Sonny Wright on piano -- and oh, he was a lovely piano player, he made so many records that Teddy Wilson got credit for behind Billie Holiday, they sounded a great deal alike -- and Teddy Sturgis on bass.

And I took the saddle with me, as I discussed, and he checked us into the Dunbar Hotel, it was an all black clientele, and I was told at that time that it was the largest hotel in the world, up to that time. And I was the only white person to stay there -- there were hundreds of blacks. And Ben told the management and anyone concerned that I was to be looked out for, not to have anyone bother me, and he was looking out for my safety. And this was a reversal of the racial difficulties blacks suffered.

After checking in the hotel -- and they were a gang of lovely people in Washington, D.C., so many, and of course, the black society was in Washington, D.C. for one thing, and Ben's first wife came from there. And he was wined and dined
by all the professors at the university; a great deal of them lived there, and ...

I would just like to interject here and mention -- excuse me, Cliff -- that the university to be mentioned is Howard University, which is a very prestigous, was then and still is a very prestigous black university. So that's just for the record.
Hey, we didn't mention, also, that Ben's wife was from Washington, D.C. -- she was a lawyer, an attorney, which really put him into the black society of Washington, D.C. Now please carry on.

They just adored Ben Webster. And we went over and rehearsed and it was a day ahead of opening, and we rehearsed for awhile, and Ben called the rehearsal off and took me with him, he couldn't stand it any more, because we had to go to a sporting goods store and look all over for someplace that carried western gear. And we found him a beautiful pair of black boots. He never had them off in the 8 to 10 weeks that we were down there. He made quite a sight going to work, and he got a Stetson, a beautiful Stetson western hat, and it was western hat, and at that time Ben was into carrying hand-tooled silver canes, and walking sticks. He loved walking sticks, and he had a dog at the pound around there -- Ben couldn't stand to see anything destroyed, so he went over and got himself an old dog,

a scraggly old thing, and Ben had him all washed and he would walk down the street going to work with his horn under one arm, his walking stick in the other hand, and his Stetson, as I said, and his cowboy boots, and a beautiful $300 hand-tailored suit, and with the dog in tow. And it was quite an entourage. Frank Sinatra would be very proud of that one. On our way to work ...

And Ben set this whole thing up to be the play period in his life. Music wasn't incidental because we were all serious about our playing nights, but he had us all set up, we'd go to bed at one, two, two thirty in the morning, or rather we'd stay out late drinking and got through at that time, and he had a six o'clock appointment for the next 8 to 10 weeks that we were there, with a stables, and it happened to be a stable in Rock Creek Park.

And we'd get up at six or seven o'clock in the morning with very little sleep, and still stoned, and go riding. And we did this morning after morning and day in and day out. And then he would set up with some of the lovely people he knew there, and he liked my cooking, and I had to cook every day. Ben would buy the groceries, and we'd go to somebody else's house every day. And I'd cook the meal.

Midway in the engagement, our saddle sores healing, we got very daring in our riding. Now if you know anything about jumping horses, you will know that you don't do it with a western form and a Mexican saddle.

So I lost my balance on a four ft. high hurdle, pulled on the horse's mouth, the horse responded beautifully, he stopped in mid air, but I didn't stop in mid-air, but continued on to the cinder bed. I was most fortunate -- just five broken ribs, three front and two back. So back to the hotel, X rays, and one of our doctor friends and an admirer of Ben's taped my rib cage from waist to armpits, and I played the rest of the engagement that way.

I couldn't bend to pick up a drop sticks, if any, and the management planted a waitress to keep an eye on the situation to pick up the sticks. I'd drop them only because of my unnatural position with all the tape around me and pain.

I finished the engagement through the courtesy of Gilby's gin and some codeine for the pain at night. Oh yes, just about then, Ben bought a beautiful 30-30 Winchester 94, and kept it off with a fine bow and quiver of arrows. Ben was sighting his rifle while cleaning it out of the fourth floor apartment in Harlem, in New York, and somebody noticed him and called the police, and they took Ben to Bellevue for evaluation. Sidney Catlett, Ben's dear friend, went down to get him out. The psychiatrist, a lady -- the psychiatrist was a lady, and she was buttered up by Sidney, telling her it was all a big mistake, and all about Ben's virtues. She called Ben in and asked him what in the world he was doing in the city with his sporting equipment, and Ben replied, 'I was just trying my bow and arrows out!'

It took more sweetness on Catlett's part to get him released in his custody. So you see, whoever may study these tapes to further his career, must understand a musician can have his recreation and create beautiful sounds at the same time. I miss the sounds of and the playing with Ben Webster, may God watch over his merry soul in heaven, and to cap off the Ben Cassy saga, I would say that as we ride off BENGAZI
