On 52nd Street, I worked the other side of the coin, as they say. I went into the so-called Dixieland oriented club of Jimmy Ryan's across the street from the Three Deuces. I hadn't known Sidney previously, I believe Jimmy Ryan himself asked me or recommended me to Sidney, and Sidney asked if I'd go in with him with a quartet, the wonderful Kenny Kersey on piano and Vic Dickenson on trombone, and myself.
I consider myself lucky to have the ability to go from a Webster oriented group to work with and please a traditional New Orleans legend.

Sidney Bechet was very strict with drummers, he had that reputation, I'd heard that from Zutty, and the time had to go exactly his way. He was rather gruff and rather hard to get close to. But once Kenny Kersey and I got the feel of the thing, he seemed pleased and I never had any serious words with him. He seemed very pleased with what we did for him. There was a Bechet album issued in France the last few years -- 2 or 3 years ago, and it's a long playing album, three playing sides, three long playing records, I mean -- let me get this straight now -- an LP,

and I find it very hard, I'm trying to find out, I'm looking at the album now, it says 'recorded in the Rendezvous Club during his visit to the states" in '49 or '50. And he lived in France then and he visited here. The band was Vic Dickson, Kenny Kersey and myself, and the Rendezvous Club, it says here on the album, they recorded a whole night of music in Philadelphia in that club.

Wow. That must have been something for you guys to be playing with the great Sidney Bechet. I've got to find that album, Cliff, and have you loan it to me so I can make some tapes from it. Because that should be a masterpiece.
Let's see, that's Kenny Kersey on piano, Cliff Leeman on drums, Vic Dickson on trombone and Sidney Bechet on his soprano saxophone - is that it, just four pieces?

I have faint recollections of appearing at the club with him, but Kenny Davern bought this album for me in Paris as a gift, and I'm listening to it, and I imagine the way I played then to accompany Bechet, and his innovations and style which originally stem from his native New Orleans roots. Ryan's roots.

For a drummer studying these tapes for my style of drumming, changing through the years to adapt to a more modern technique, as the swing era progressed, you, too, as I was, will be for want of a better word, amazed at my adapting to Bechet's playing.

Of course I did it his way. The ideas of backing Sidney were lots of snare drums, and press rolls, and general New Orleans background. By the way, before continuing, Vic Dickson played some of the nicest things that were ever put on tape, or that he ever had on tape, and they were a joy - and if anybody can find this record, or if it's still produced, and I know it's a collector's item, I might not have sounded that adequate had it not been for the wonderful Kenny Kersey on piano and one of a kind virtuoso, Vic Dickson. I don't know where the album can be found, it's stamped stereo, Universelle, with a French accent -- stereo Universelle -- they must mean Universal, but in French, 1973, disque number seven, France. It's an amazing study of the master of the soprano saxophone. I never was paid for the album, by the way -- it was bootlegged.
Working with Sidney, to me, became another feather in my cap, and I cherish the memories of working with him, it was a wonderful experience.

There's been an urgent prodding in the base of my mind or in the back of my mind, I should say, to get this off my chest. The black and white issue, or -- if you wish, the problems involved in my career racially.
So many have asked how come I worked with so many great black musicians and groups, and my answer -- they liked my playing first, and then me personally, I suppose. As I did them.

God has been kind to me, to bestow me with a sense and feeling of love for all people -- and enough talent for them to accept me as a participating fellow musician. It brings to mind an observation -- and I believe that it was writer /critic Dan Morganstern in his evaluation of Eddie Condon. He said Eddie Condon ignored the racial issue as if it didn't exist. And them is my sentiments.
Of course you realize it's there, and it does exist to too many people.

To me, in the first place, Louis Armstrong was the great forefather -- he was to me, and the great swinging big bands of the era were black -- Fletcher Henderson, for instance, and Kenny's Cottonpickers, Claude Hopkins in the early thirties, large band - they all were to me, great swing groups before publicity and Benny Goodman capitalized on the term 'swing'.

And of course, Ellington was in there, too. The black and white bands swung, and the name 'swing' became the standard accepted logo, and the great soloists in those groups -- my love and inspiration musically, and my getting to play with a great many of those greats later on when I progressed with talent, as a drummer. And I was to be accepted by them. An impossible dream come true for me, during the forties and fifties, that is why I lean toward blacks in my playing -- some or many of my super musical heroes were
black, and I felt I was always accepted by them as an equal -- not just a pretty good white drummer.

And oh yes, by the same token, I've worked with some black musicians with big reputations, who didn't have time and music in his bones, a statement I make with tongue in cheek -- some didn't swing worth a bleep, and played unmercifully out of tune and with bad taste, and on the other hand, some of the great white musicians I played with could never be surpassed for greatness -- black, blue, green or otherwise. Jack Teagarden, Lou McGarity, Billy Butterfield, Venus Huckie, Joe Vanuti, Dave McKenner, Bob Haggard on base, Bobbie Hackett on trumpet, Hank Lawson on trumpet. I'm going to stop here -- I mean, there were so many. Color has no priority to great musicians. Nor to their talent. And God only knows that I've worked with hoards of whites with good reputations of being great swingers, and I will take the liberty of being a little cruel here. There were many who were really freeloading with the union cards, black and white.
I'll sum up by saying it about evens out. To me, God passed out the talent in this world in a dimly lit room.
I have to add this. My wife just heard this tape back so far, especially on the race conversations, and she reminds me that when my son Chris was two and a half years

old (he's now 26) but when he was two and a half years old, he was riding on a bus with her, and he noticed a black woman on the bus and he said to my wife, as children will, about the color and why and so forth. That's a beautiful story, Cliff.

To get back to the Condon band, when I went in with Eddie in '51, that band was the most charging band, the most exciting -- I don't believe they ever had a bad night. I can't remember a bad night there. That was with Wild Bill -- Wild Bill Davison, Edmund Hall, Cutty Cutshall, Schroeder Gene Shrader -- Shrader Shroder -- take your pick.

I got Walter Page, I recommended Walter Page for the job, and Ralph Sutton, Lou McGerrity, and -- in those days, the place was jammed. I've seen them hang from the -- there was a railing around the top there, there was an upper part, and they'd come down from West Point, the Army-Navy games and so forth. And we played with that band, all the traditional Dixieland songs, because they were requested. They were references -- it was a Dixie style orchestra, which it was not. With Wild Bill and Eddie, and the manner in which we played could be referred to as the Chicago jazz style, it was just straight jazz down the middle.

And as I say, never a bad night. And it was also -- we used to play medleys, and there were some beautiful things; Cutty Cutshall on trombone would play something, everybody took turns with the medleys, and I had an association with Edmund

Hall, who was wonderful. He asked me to do a couple of recordings with him, and we went up to Decca and recorded -- "Big 'n' a" with him, we Ralph Sutton was on piano, and he took Walter Page up, and we made one or two recordings or albums -- I forget which; there was a transition then from 78's into LP's, and I never received those recordings. Somebody played them for me at a hall once, and I asked them who was playing brushes, who the drummer was -- I didn't even recognize my own playing. I felt very embarrassed admiring the drummer, and it turned out to be me.

However -- at this time, I was in to the Hit Parade, which I did on weekends, and my reputation was growing there. I was fortunate to be able to read and cut a few parts, and I was hired by contractors, I had a reputation of working on the Hit Parade, which was a great show in those days -- I was hired, I ws what you'd call on the 'outside'. A freelance artist. But I was still working nights until four o'clock in the morning, which was killing at times.

And from the Hit Parade show, I would sub on the Perry Como Show and I did the Jack Benny Show -- these were all outside things -- the Jimmy Durante Show, these were all the beginning of television; television was just coming in strong then, and I was in on the ground floor. I did the Telephone Hour with Red Nichols, and I also did the Telephone Hour as a musician -- they hired me to keep time with several

of the modern features they did on those shows. I did the Steve Allen Tonight Show, and I did a great show that featured Louis Armstrong on CBS -- You Are There Show, and one of the titles was The Closing of Storyville, and that was a great feather in my bonnet. Louis Armstrong, Bobby Hackett -- I was with the Lawson-Haggard Band, and we emulated the original Dixieland -- the Original Dixieland Jazz Band was the name of it.

That You Are There Show as done by the great Walter Cronkite, and also -- I don't know whether I mentioned Jack Teagarden, but he was in that. I did thousands of commercial jingles and free lance pop records, with all the top stars of the era. Thirty-one jazz albums with the Lawson-Haggard band, which I will get to as a separate piece, because that was one of the highlights of my life.

And I did a series of Billy Butterfield albums -- and we'll list these later on if anybody's interested, I can't get into the research now. Bob Crosby albums, especially South Pacific and Porgy and Bess -- those are collector's items now, and I'd recommend anybody that wants to hear a powerful type of music.

I made an all time record that's considered an all time jazz collector's item with Joe Turner Sings the Blues on Atlantic Records. Now that's a thing that we'll have to get to, and I'll have to explain that because that's a great part of my life, just making it in two days and recording it
with all the stars I had known back in the old days. I was the only white person on those dates, and -- well, we'll get to that later.

I made some recordings that were great sellers, but you know, they were in the commercial vein, too, like being on staff at Decca Records, I recorded "Lover" with Peggy Lee, and I made a Paul Whitman album with Paul in attendance, and we featured Tom and Jimmie Dorsey -- his life -- that's what Whitman was setting up in the album. And I appeared with Bob Crosby's Bobcats at the Rainbow Grill in Manhattan and the Riviera in Las Vegas -- that was my first time in Vegas. That was a beautiful experience. In the late sixties, I was at Condon's, and this is all working -- all these outside things were done while I was working nights, so I could get to play jazz and get that out of my system, and be on call by the contractors. I was just fortunate in being able to do the many exciting dates on the outside that I can't -- hadn't even gotten to and hadn't mentioned yet.

Now we get to the Lawson-Haggart band, and my expression comes to the forefront, my expression -- a musical romance. Well, it certainly was. Yank Lawson, who I knew, had associated with -- in Tommy Dorsey's, he was in that great band along with Pee Wee Irwin in '39. Now, just as I was finishing up in Nick's, Hank came in one night and said he was doing a Show of Shows, and he was on the outside, to make some money. He was doing the Show of Shows, and he said
Bob Haggart and I had done so many things that Bob Crosby got credit for, that we want to get together and organize a group. And was I interested.

And I naturally said yes, but I took it with a grain of salt because somebody's always saying, "Well, we're gonna do this and we're gonna do that". However, we were rehearsing at Lou St. 's house, and the nucleus was that ank Lawson and Bob Haggart, naturally, and they were at a loss for a piano player, and we went over to Lou Stein's house -- somebody suggested Lou, I did for one. He was a great player; I had been recording with Lou, and they didn't know if his style would fit in the group of what they had in mind, of the music they had in mind.
Well, it did. And if you're acquainted with any of the great albums Lou made, God only knows I don't know who would have covered the situation any better.
We had on trombone at the time Cutty Cutshall, and I've got to research this for a moment. That's right, it was Cutty, and Bill Stegmeyer on clarinet, who I wasn't that ...
Stegmeyer.

Even if you weren't too familiar with him, because he was truly one of the great musicians of our era, and our era really covers a lot, you know? We're talking about the early thirties and twenties, to today -- '79.
Billy Stegmeyer, over the years,

afterwards, became a wonderfully close friend, and his contribution to the band was an amazing thing because Billy was an arranger -- he was arranging all over New York, with the big shows, the Hit Parade and other shows at that time, record dates and so forth -- and he was busy arranging. And it was always on the tip of all musician's tongues that they could never understand how Billy sounded and played so great, because to anybody's knowledge, he was never playing around at any jazz joints, where his lip came from and his articulation.
But he was one of the mainstays of that Lawson-Haggard band, for sure.

That night over at Lou Stein's house, we made a demo, and I went back to my job, and heard nothing -- I went for a few weeks, but we had a nice night, we had a lovely time. We had a very good social night, too. But we were recording five or six songs, and apparently in the meantime, Yank and Bob Haggard had gone to Decca Records, and approached Milt Galber. Now Milt was well known as a musician's friend and so forth -- he had the original Commodore Record Company, which was, did nothing but jazz research for years. Anyway, he was hired to do part music and jazz, or in charge of jazz at Decca, and Yank came down to see me at work and said we were going to record, that they had signed us up for a series of albums, or for a first album, and that was that.

To sum it up better, that was the begining of a beautiful thing --' recording wise and friendship wise, and a series of albums, running between 20 and 30. We made in the middle twenties, amoung of albums.

We got to the first date at Decca on 57th Street, and did our first album, and they're talking about mutual admiration societies -- ank and Haggard -- Haggard did some arrangements first, I can't remember what was on the first date, but of course that's another research project. We did so many albums. On that first date, there was "Jump for Joy" and "Kisses and Jubilation", and the playbacks were just way beyond what we expected. Of course, Milt Galber was more pleased than he expected, and that was the beginning, as I say, the long series of albums.

Now, as we progress with the albums, Haggard wished to increase the personnel on the records for some of the arrangements that he was doing. They wanted us to -- I've been associated with Bob Haggard and Yank Lawson, and the Lawson-Haggard Band. Since then, and those were the early boys, up until now -- up until the present time. Up until the last few years, I've been doing concerts -- they've done concerts all over the world, and I've done a great deal of them with them. Once in awhile, I would be busy on other projects, and they'd use other drummers. They've done that twice in Europe because I was busy with my Switzerland

International Jazz Concert in Bern.
However, we've kept the mutual admiration society alive, and we're still open for concerts. I do tours, I've done several this past year, and the reason we're not doing concerts now probably is because Bob Haggart has bought a home in Mexico, and that late in the Fall, he goes to Mexico to his home, which leaves the Lawson-Haggart band hanging. We don't want to do any concerts without Hag.
And then I'm expecting any time now, this is February -- in another month or so, Haggart will be coming back from Mexico, trotting back, as it may be -- and the Mexican Foxtrot is implied there, and we will be doing more this year -- concerts, that is.
There was a while in the late sixties, Richard Gibson decided to form a band and he took Bob Haggart and Yank Lawson, and used their arrangements, and that was the nucleus of what he found was the World's Greatest Jazz Band. At the time they formed, I was ill, and the now departed, and great drummer, Morey Feld, was used -- and he, once he was in the World's Greatest Jazz Band, we've all gotten to dislike that name -- the world's 'greatest' -- it reminds me of Mrs. Astor on the Titanic, when it struck the iceberg, and she said, "I rang for ice, but this is ridiculous!"
However, that's pertaining to the title, 'the world's greatest'. They were close! And in that period until they

broke up, until they broke away from Richard Gibson, he sold the band to an agent in Arizona, and his name -- he still is the bassist for the World's Greatest Jazz Band, of Yank Lawson and Bob Haggard. His name is Bark Hickox, and anybody who'd ever like to hear the World's Greatest Jazz Band in person -- we're open for engagements. His address is 4350 East Camelback Road, Phoenix, Arizona 85108.

Among other credits in the World's Greatest Jazz Band, and one of the things that I am most proud of, I just went in my living room and brought back a plaque, and the plaque was sent from the White House in Washington, D.C. I must read what it says: It says, "Dear Mr. Leeman, Mrs. Ford and I were delighted that our guests had such an enjoyable evening in the White House Rose Garden, on July 20th. A Salute To American Music was certainly enthusiastically applauded by everyone present, and the World's Greatest Jazz Band made a splendid contribution to the program. As one of the talented members of this outstanding group, your participation added a great deal to our pleasure on this occasion. You have our warm thanks and very best wishes, sincerely ..." and it is signed by hand, it says Jerry Ford and Betty Ford.
That stemmed from a command performance. We were asked at the White House, and it was for a Centennial of American Music, which also pertains to these archives at the Rose Garden, 1976.
When I say 'pertaining' to the archives, I meant that
I was told that our performance was recorded at this time in the Rose Garden, and was to be included in the archives of -- the Presidential archives.

I have to add that Ella Fitzgerald was on that bill with us, and above the plaque that I just mentioned, there was a picture sent from President Ford, and was taken of he and his wife, Betty, with the Lawson-Haggard band, and it's rather humorous because everybody comments on it, everybody was in tuxedos and the President was in full tails, except myself, and the reason for that is after our performance, not knowing we were to be photographed with the President, I changed my clothes; I was wringing wet as usual, and to the uninitiated, I wore western clothes, and for reasons which I'll get to later on -- I have for years, and I had a very flamboyant western sports suit, it was light tan in color, my pride and joy, llama boots, yellow with a very pointed toe. The picture is in color.

And, with my western shirt and pearl buttons, I did -- when they told us we were having pictures taken, I put on a black bow tie. I really wish since -- it turned out so ridiculous that I wished I had a ten-gallon hat to go with it, for the picture. However, the picture is for posterity, and here it is, as it was taken.
Oh yes -- my predominant huge silver belt buckle with my Odessa sherrif's department badge rounded out the picture. I think I looked pretty good!
When the wonderful, great piano player, Ralph Sutton, visited my house, he looked at the picture and commented, "Where were your sixguns, Cliff?" and I said "Security wouldn't allow me".

And I need an insertion here. That was the Bicentennial that we were playing -- I left out the word 'bi', which was of course, nationwide -- rather, our nation's great celebration. I noticed that in playing this back, that I had talked into this machine, this fool machine here for 10 or 15 minutes about the Lawson-Haggard band, and upon our recording with a larger group, and I forgot to push all the proper buttons. So it was deleted. However, Bob Haggard and Lawson in doing the arrangements, wanted to enlarge upon the band, certain things that Decca picked for us to do, they wanted a bigger sound -- we augmented the band, so we had two Lawson-Haggard bands. We had the original which I mentioned, and then some dates he would add Billy Butterfield on trumpet and Peanut Hucko on clarinet or tenor, and he used Bud Freeman on tenor, and the most wonderful, one of my greatest musical loves in life, Lou McGerrity on trombone.
And of course we added George Burns, who was working at that time on the Hit Parade. So I hope this might be inserted -- it's of importance to me.
I went through great detail, and that was left out, the freedom that Bob Haggard and Yank gave us -- he said to

just go ahead and play and if you want anything, let us know, if you want to change anything, let us know, if you want to go back and redo the thing, it was just a happy relationship, everybody must be pleased, or we wouldn't continue.

We made things with -- so fast, that were excellent, there was very little going over the tapes. I don't think I go to where tapes were coming in then. Instead of tapes, and it was easy to insert, it was becoming easy to insert, or we'd do introductions and endings without doing the whole thing over again. But we didn't do too much of that. I remember we brought in an arrangement of 'Tiger Rag' in a modern vein, and we ran it down once -- this was by sight -- everybody happened to be not only a jazz artist, but a schooled musician in that group. And we ran it down once, and said well, now we'll try it out. We just sight read it.

Well, we tried a couple of times, and the tapes kind of fouled up, and Yank said, 'Let me hear that first one'. And we played back the first tape, and that's the one they took. Now this is a phenomenon in reading something down and have it swing, and the jazz solo, of course, is another thing, too, but everything was just a beautiful, swinging feeling, and so they took the first tape. And I just mention this as an -- such an unusual organization in its field.

Bob Haggart told me to play any way you want to, if it's too loud, we'll call it down in the control room, do whatever you want, just use your own feeling and your own taste -- then he told me what to do. Now, it's seldom in this world, unless you're the leader and you're the drummer, like Buddy Rich -- and there are only one or two of those around, possibly Louie Belson, that anybody that has the opportunity to work with their own natural feeling without somebody standing over them with a baseball bat.
I can still Yank Lawson's voice saying; 'be happy, Cliff, do whatever you want.'1)

To go back to the drummers that I mentioned, I find out upon reviewing that I left out one -- Cozie Cole's name, for one. When I was first with, I first knew him, when I went with Artie Shaw in '36, and we were in New York, he took me over and he says, I want you to hear a drummer -- because I had a lot to learn, and Artie knew this, and he wanted me to hear some of the things that he liked.

And he took me over to the Three Deuces at the Onyx Club -- I guess maybe it was the Onyx Club, and being featured there was Stuff Smith and his orchestra; they had come out of Buffalo, New York, and this was the swingingest, damnest band I heard, and the walls almost came down with the pulsing beat, and that was Cozy Cole with his dancing slippers on, playing drums, Stuff Smith, I'm not sure of the
rest of the orchestra, but it was a small six piece band, and it was the damnest thing. You have to do your own research on that.

So I got to know Cozy Cole, and we became dear friends over the years. He was a wonderfully well schooled drummer, and he -- at that time. used a most pulsating roll on the snare drum. He had so much technique from good studying, which he applied to his swinging and that roll was put on in my mind with an afterbeat, and he got that thing going, he got the whole place rocking.

He continued his studies on drums, and along the way, after he went with Louis Armstrong -- he went all over the world with Louie Armstrong, and was such an outstanding soloist, and to this day, he's such a beautiful man, and he's still in the picture, I don't dare estimate what his age is -- I know it's around 70, and he's all over the world with Cootie Williams' orchestra, a small group, and they cover concerts all over the world, and they do some of the nicest work, and Cozy is still in there pitching. He is one of a kind; he is one of my favorite comedians. There is only one Cozy Cole.

I must mention -- I did the first year of the Newport Festivals were starting, with Eddie Condon, for George Wein, Schroeder he was the promoter. We had Peanuts Hucko, Jack Lesberg, Gene Shrader, and Cutty Cutshall among others. And it rained

and it poured, and this great outdoor auditorium, and if you know anything about Eddie Condon, instead of playing the guitar, he took it upon himself to conduct the six pieces, and because of the rain which didn't cover the back, or the front of the show, where he announced, he had an umbrella over his head -- and it made quite a picture.

Since then, I've done many of the Newport Festivals, especially when they moved down to New York, and they call them now the New York Newport Festivals. I've done them with the World's Greatest Jazz Band, and I've done them especially with Eddie Condon. And the last couple of years, they've had a subsidiary that is part of the Newport Festival down in New Jersey. Sponsored by the New Jersey Jazz Society in connection with -- or I should say the New Jersey Jazz Society working hand in hand with George Wein. And presenting the New Jersey-New York Waterloo concerts at Waterloo Village. It's a 200 year old or more restored village that goes back to George Washington's time, that would be 1700 -- at Waterloo Village, New Jersey, and it's a beautiful background to jazz concerts.

There will be much more later of what the New Jersey Jazz Society is doing for jazz, and the promotion and preservation of it, and doing very well along the concert lines every year, and we musicians are greatly indebted to them, and we'll get to that another time. But I must
give credit where it's due.
Hey, that's nice, Cliff; thank you very much. I tell you, we were gonna talk about Bobby Hackett. Now tell me something about your relationship with Bobby and when you first met him.

I first became acquainted with Bobby Hackett in 1934 and '5, possibly 1935, when I was with the Dan Murphy band back in Boston. And I used to go down to an after hours club which was called The Theatrical Club, in Boston -- and Bobby had a little jazz band; Bobby had been playing for only a little over a year on trumpet. He had been playing guitar for several years; he had been working with around Boston, a lot of club dates, I guess with society club dates on the guitar. He was from Providence, Rhode Island.

And for a fast resume, he worked at the Theatrical Club, as I say, and it might be a little bit comical, but Bobby was a stickler and he had started to play trumpet, as I say, only a short time previous. He was wearing tails and white tie, with his little -- let's see, a five-piece jazz band. They used no base. Every once in awhile, somebody would come charging through the club with a base over their shoulder to help out. But in that band was Brad Gowens, and I was going to do some more research on somebody else. He was older than Bobby, and Bobby learning on the clarinet -- Brad Gowens was on lots and lots of old records in the beginning -- from all the early records. And he was teaching
Bobby a lot of things that he didn't know about players and so on and so forth. He was helping Bobby along, and he made arrangements for this band.

And that's -- primarily to get to the point, that's how I met Bobby Hackett. And it wasn't long before the word got out all over the country about this little cornet player down in Boston that sounded so much like Bix, and that's before Bix's big image across the country was on a few elite privileged people who knew about Bix, and his playing and had the records.

So Brad Gowans talked to Bobby about this, and it wasn't long before the whole country was hearing about this wonderful clarinet player, as I said, that sounded like Bix. So that was my first association listening to him, and then we became close friends, and next worked together in New York. Of course, there's a span of time there. This was, as I said, in 1934-5, and Bobby came to New York and went into the original Nick's in New York on 7th Avenue and 11th Street.

And he played there for four or five years, and we did several jazz concerts here and there, but my first long association with Bobby was when he took me into Nick's which we talked about before -- he took me in there in late '39, and our association musically went on from there.
I misplaced ten easy years, Bobby didn't take me

and I was out with the big bands, and when I returned to New York, Bobby didn't take me into Nicks in the Village, which had then moved over to 10th Street and 7th Avenue, he didn't take me in there until '49 and the first of '50. Not '39-'40.

If this is confusing to you, you're right. It's also confusing me, but I have to get my dates straightened out here. After that, we used to have Tuesday night jam sessions at Eddie Condon's, and that was one of the features of the club, and Lips Page used to be one of his regulars, and Bobby Hackett, too. So we kept in touch. Bobby Hackett used to play there every once in awhile, and he was great.

We played a good many private parties for Jackie Gleason. Jackie Gleason just loved Bobby Hackett, and we used to play quite a few of those at Toots Shoor's. Bobby was always a regular at the Gibson parties, and we kept in constant contact. We did lots of record dates together. Bobby worked at the time in that era, he worked at ABC Radio and TV. He also worked with the Whiteman group -- Whiteman kept the radio band at ABC, a couple of times a week.

And Bobby would ask me to be on the programs a couple of times -- Paul Whiteman had Jack Teagarden back with Bobby Hackett, and he loved it. And Bobby would always ask for me to play drums; he didn't care for the staff drummer behind him, and so we had some pleasant moments then.
We did so many countless numbers of things over the

years, that I just can't put my finger on many of them without research. Until we came to the point of Dick Gibson, and his World's Greatest Jazz Band, and he opened into the Roosevelt Grill in New York, and had a music policy there. That's another one of his wonderful promotions for jazz music.

I worked there with Jack Lesberg. He and I -- he was bass drummer and I was the house drummer, and we worked there with such groups as Joe Venuti as a leader for awhile, and Buck Clayton a couple of times, and we had Peanuts Hucko for a leader -- we were what you called the intermission band, I guess. While the World's Greatest Jazz Band took time off.

I'll get to the time that I was there with Bobby Hackett because we made five or six albums while playing live from there. One of the greatest albums I ever made in my own personal taste, was the last album. The sound and the soloist and he fours that I took, and so forth, were to me, the best -- the epitome of my playing, if I may say -- for my liking, the band was Dave McKenna on piano, Jack Lesberg on bass, Bobby Hackett and he made it a co-feature with Bobby Hackett, featuring Vic Dickenson.
I'll try to research and find the name of that record. It's one of my loves. I think it would sound better if I said it as one of my better accomplishments. Please, for
my sake, try this album for sound. This LP album is available; it's called Bobby Hackett featuring Vic Dickenson at the Roosevelt Grill.
Now I find this rather hard to pronounce; always have -- it says 1977 Chiaroscuro Records, a division of Audio-Fidelity Enterprises, 221 West 57th Street, New York 10019.

We made four or five albums at this time. This particular album has a picture of a steaming trumpet on it, or a clarinet, rather, and the steam coming out of the spit valve, and there's an old fashioned fireman on the ladder blowing one of those old fish horns. That's just to identify this particular record.

Now the songs, just to make sure, are Fidgety Feet, 'Baby Won't You Please Come Home,' 'Wait on the New Orleans,' 'Tin Blues,' 'Sweet Georgia Brown,' 'After You've Gone,' New Orleans, 'Struttin' at the Barbecue,' 'Basin Street Blues' and 'Wolverine Blues.'

And there are some most interesting notes here, that Hank O'Neal who recorded and produced it wrote down. It starts off -- and I'm only going to take a couple of them here -- "I hate Dixieland jazz, at least I hate the kind of rubbish people play." In '77, they called it Dixieland.
Later on, he goes on to say "Why am I putting out an album with all these Dixieland tunes on it?" A good question, and an easy answer. It isn't Dixieland. Thank
God. When Bobby first made these recordings in '70, I programmed two albums, and I bought one and kept the other.

In 1970, we recorded ten nights, and produced a gigantic pile of tapes. There was an awful lot of material there, when the albums were programmed, because in my preconceived notion of the truth, I rejected all of the tunes with Dixieland titles, except one -- I never listened to them.

Listening to them now, however, I was surprised to find they were not Dixieland at all, but just good, swinging songs with Bobby, Vic, Dave, Jack and Cliff. Being as tasty as they could be -- a real revelation. I kept listening carefully, and in most instances, the selections are not only spirited, but played flawlessly. And being somewhat easy to play 'Sweet Georgia Brown' than a difficult ballad. These were just good songs being played sensibly. What a relief.

Later the guys who played these tunes the same way every time and every night in 1961 at Ryan's and other places, should give these tunes a listen, and realize what time and tone and taste can do for a song. A tune, rather.

I want to stress that I'm not trying to sell albums, but for the student who might be interested in my progression as a drummer and my different expressions in playing, might find this as an example of what I tried to bring forth before -- and not the epitome of my playing, but I
enjoyed the sound, the different sounds that I got on the drum solos, and I would like to convey this and pass it along to somebody who may be interested.

That's a good idea, Cliff, and I know those records; I have some of them myself. And that one is a special one; I remember playing at the Roosevelt Grill down there, I was in one of the bands, also, so it was my good fortune to listen to you guys every night and to hear such good music that Dick Gibson was putting together in the Roosevelt Grill in those days -- and it is a good idea to make the suggestion that, for posterity, some of these records should be kept around, and reissued -- especially for the great playing of you and the magnificent Bobby Hackett and the very great Vic Dickson.

I'm going to add that Bobby Hackett proposed me for Masonary which was another beautiful thing in my life, and Paul Whiteman signed the papers, and I was a brother of Bobby Hackett's in more ways than one. When Bobby Hackett died a few years later on, I participated in a few jazz sessions across the country with Bobby, and when he died, the music business lost a great, great trumpet player, and I lost a most dear friend.
I might add that while I'm thinking of it, that in 1977, I played the inauguration ball for President Carter in Washington, D.C. with the World's Greatest Jazz Band.

And that was my sixth Presidential Ball, beginning with FDR Roosevelt's in 1940, I believe that was the first one I did with Charlie Barnet , and I did one after that, another, which of course was Roosevelt, with Charlie Barnet , which was a repeat inaugural, and I made them all with the exception, I guess, of -- I did make them all with the exception of Lyndon Johnson, who of course, had no inaugural ball because he was sworn in upon the death of President Jack Kennedy.

I played another Presidential ball, which is a story we must cover if we ever have time, but right now I'll just mention it was the inaugural ball for Richard Nixon, with Eddie Condon's six-piece jazz orchestra, and we had Wild Bill Davison on trumpet and Lou Stein on piano, and Jack Lesberg on bass, and I must tell the story at some other point, it was a motley crew -- please believe me.

It was white tie and tails, for one thing, and we had business suits on, which all in all, was casual. In the second place, we're standing there and Condon said, "When he comes out, do we play ruffles and flourishes?" and Wild Bill took a drink and says, "I don't know" and there came a soft voice behind Eddie Condon, and the head of the Marine Presidential greeting trumpets said, "No, we'll play that!"
After taping days, and nights when I try to relax, I think of some of the things that we covered, and every once

in awhile, I jot something down, and I'll say, "Gee, I forgot to mention this or that". I wanted to say about Ben Webster. I didn't bring it up that -- you see, nobody mentioned Ben Webster's great sense of humor. If you talked to anybody that knew him, that's one of the first things they'll mention, along with his playing, and the fact that he was a champion among storytellers.

A great many true humorous incidents of musicians and a great many fabricated incidents were a part of his storytelling. He would taken an extraordinary amount of time building a tale, never losing its interest along the way, to an extraordinary climax and a burst of hilarious emotional outlets. And in passing along this information, which people should know, I sometimes think his playing was a great deal patterned in that vein -- possibly he was unaware of it.

In remembering my thoughts last night, I remembered I have a plaque here, a bronze plaque, it's 20 by 30 inches, and it was given to me by the New Jersey Jazz Society, because I mentioned them yesterday and the wonderful things they did to continue the preservation of jazz.

Anyway, the plaque reads "New Jersey Jazz Society to Cliff Leeman, a musician among drummers, his playing has enriched the jazz heritage immensely, providing a standard by which others must be judged. The award is presented by

the New Jersey Jazz Society, February 12, 1978."
Up until that date, I was the fourth musician so honored. The others, I believe -- if I recall, were Vic Dickenson, Joe Venuti, Jess Stacey, Milt Gabler and John S. Wilson, eminent music critic of the New York Times, was on the nominating committee, and I am grateful to them.
To me, that's my Oscar. I started to say, also, this year Wild Bill Davison had been so honored, and he will be over here from Europe -- he lives in Denmark -- Copenhagen, and I will be in concert with him in a couple places, especially for nostalgia, back at Eddie Condon's club for a week, around June. And he's been so honored, and since I'm starting my day with an ego trip, I might as well describe another plaque received last year. That's hanging below the aforementioned Jersey Jazz bronze. This is another bronze plaque, and it reads "To Cliff Leeman, the world's greatest drummer par excellence, from Local 364 AF of M, Portland, Maine, March 23, 1978."
They may have been a bit carried away with the inscription, as that's my hometown local, but nevertheless, it was presented to me in March in concert with the -- well, I was in concert at the auditorium in Portland, Maine, with the World's Greatest Jazz Band, but it was cancelled out because of snow. And so they held it until they could bring me back last December, for a jazz concert in my home town, and

I was the guest instrumentalist. I should say guest performer with a local group which was just wonderful, and I had a wonderful day reminiscing with a gang of old friends whom I hadn't seen for 40 or 50 years.

That gave me the opportunity to go by, they drove me by where I was born and the house I grew up in, it's still there, O'Neal Street in Portland, and they drove me out to Cape Elizabeth, Maine, where the house I had built originally, the one I designed, is still there and in beautiful condition, which sits on the 35 acres that my grandfather and father had as a 35 acre farm originally, and my father's home next door is still there -- beautifully preserved. So I just reminisced and was with all the guys that I went to school with -- and it was a wonderful experience.

Those are enough accolades for the present, and now I will get on with some more notes. I'd like to do a fast resume of the Richard Gibson, the Dick Gibson parties that he started in '62 in Aspen. We covered some of that, and the first band which was his favorite -- Condon band, and with Teddy Wilson's trio.

Well, the following year, you know, all his parties have been private subscription -- his guest lists, as they were originally, the party for Mattie Gibson. So the second year, he wanted to elaborate on the party. His guest list, people heard about it, and they heard about it
in Denver, and so many people were asked to be on the list, he kept it down to a minimum. But it was more than he could accommodate in the hotel.
It comes to me now, Milt, because we couldn't recall before -- but the name of the hotel was the Jerome Hotel, and it's a picturesque hotel that goes back to the Gold Rush days.

Now, as I said, the guest list was growing, so how he ever managed -- Dick Gibson talked to management into letting him tear down the partition from the room, the dining room that we were playing in, he tore down the whole wall leading into the lobby of the hotel, so that people could -- he could put more chairs in and the people could be seated properly to see the music.

He asked me the second year -- how can we elaborate and maybe have a few more musicians, because we have a guest list, and it's growing, and I don't want to make any money on this. And I suggested -- he would confide in me quite often, and I suggested the Lawson-Haggard Band whom I had been recording with, it was a great jazz band, according to his likes and tastes and so forth, and so it came to be that second year, he added them to the roster.
And the third year in Aspen, he asked me and Jack Lesberg, and I suggested a bunch of names that possibly he might add, the musicians, so the groups got larger. So he got

a whole bunch of musicians from the coast, and some beautiful people like Eddie Miller and -- well, I shant go into the names because there were so many, as the parties grew, and I have every set -- Richard used to write out the sets of all the musicians who would be following each other on the bandstand, and I have every one from back in '62. I rather think that I'm the only person who has preserved all those things.

But we don't have time on these tapes to go through all the personnel. The fourth year or so, he decided for a change of scenery, and the guest list was growing larger and larger, and in fact, the parties were, as I say, the guest list was larger, and the party gained prominence around the country by heresay, and everybody was clam pring to get on that guest list, and Dick had to screen whoever he wanted, and he was allowing the real jazz bands that could afford to make the trip and come out, he was adding them to his list. And as a change of pace and scenery, he decided to get out of them and developed -- it had just been accepted as a corporation, was Vail, Colorado. Now that was undeveloped then. In the middle sixties. And of course now, it is a reknown place. I think former President Ford has fallen down on the slopes a few times there.
Anyway, we had two years there, and the guest list kept growing, and the bands kept getting larger and larger.

Then he decided to go back to Aspen for a couple of years, and he employed two or three places to present the music as the list of band musicians were growing larger, and he would have one session in the afternoon at the Jerome Hotel, and then up the street there was a nightclub, and he would employ that because it could seat enough people.

Then eventually, after six or seven years, he tried the Broadmore Hotel, we went down there in Colorado Springs - and I do believe that hotel accomodated the guest list fine, it had a big, enormous dining room. Of course the hotel is one of the world's most famous -- still is -- and we had the last few years, oh, I should say eight approximately, and I don't want to stop and research that, but 8 or 9 years we had been at the Broadmore Hotel in Colorado Springs.

And to give you an idea of how this whole thing snowballed, I believe we had between 7 to a thousand people on the guest list last year, and he had 67 musicians, performing musicians on his guest musical list.

If it may be pertinent for these tapes, for the Institute, Smithsonian, if they care to elaborate -- I was saying if the Smithsonian would care to elaborate, I would be only too happy to furnish 16 years of written sheets of the sets, the musical sets that Richard Gibson put together and how they followed each other at each different party.

This would be an invaluable amount of information for a student to scan over these sheets and -- like the last year, and see how Gibson formed 67 different musicians into groups, and how they all formed together. There is no set group, all the different stylized musicians working in assorted groups together, and that's the way Richard Gibson liked it. That's jazz at its height, I believe, inasmuch as it's spontaneous, and each musician applying himself to the other musicians' styles and so forth and so on.

I failed to say that these wouldn't only be invaluable to a student, but they would also be most valuable to a researcher with some initiative -- how a whole gang of musicians with different styles can put it all together. And for the drummer, especially, if they could study those lists and those sets and conceive the different musicians I was with and the sets that I did over 16 years, an unbelievable array of different styles that I had to back, and play with -- beyond comprehension. Let's say one drummer could be a stylist to fit in with all these different groups of players.

Milt Hinton, I want to straighten one thing out about the Tommy Dorsey issue because in the first place, when we first discussed him, I believe that I had worked with Charlie Shavers and Tommy, but after I left Tommy in 1939, there was an interval -- of course, Buddy Rich was with him

for several years, and I didn't work with Tom -- I worked with him off and on for 15 years or more, but I didn't work with Tom -- the names of the bands leading up to '44 and '45 before I went with the small bands, and Charlie Shavers went with him in 1944.

Well, Buddy Rich was with Tom for many years, and every time they'd have a fight -- which was often -- Tom was always on the phone calling me. We had -- well, let's just be frank and say he liked my playing immensely and I'd be the first person he'd call whenever he'd have trouble with Buddy -- which is a different thing; he just liked the way I subtley played time in his band, and he would skip the the drummistics and great showmanship of Buddy Rich for awhile. However, I couldn't always go with him. But in '47 when I went back to New York after being in my home in Maine, he found out - I was looking for a job in New York, and Tommy Dorsey got in contact with me, he had a fight with Buddy on the coast and he was opening -- he always opened for several years, many years -- not at the Paramount, but at the Capitol Hotel on Broadway, I think it's at 53rd Street. It was, anyway.

And he did the Christmas show for three or four weeks, contacted me and asked me if I'd go in. And Charlie Shavers was with him then, of course, and there were a couple of friendly incidents at that time. However, I did that three weeks. Well, I might as well mention -- in the

first place, we opened Christmas Day, and my Christmas present, Charlie picked me up at the dressing room which we shared, and informed me that my wife, my first wife, had taken my son and left me. She was in Maine, living in my home, which I love so dearly, and had built -- and she cleaned the house out and took everything -- all the furniture and was gone. But she left a sofa, I guess it had something to do with the law, you had to leave something for someone to lay down on, to be within the law. So she left me a sectional divan and my two shotguns in front of the fireplace, and that's all she left.

However, to continue -- I was in a pretty bad state of mind, and that's when Charlie Shavers and I became closer and closer friends. Charlie Shavers looked out for me, because I used to come in and get down on my hands and knees to have a water glass full of booze before the first show, to stop the shakes and I could go on. That's just a byline ...

And I must get to New Years Eve, an incident that happened that might be worth reminiscing, and worth a chuckle. Charlie and I did a lot of drinking together, we were both into it pretty good, and between shows, we used to fool around with pranks here and there and so forth, and up in the dressing room, someplace in one of my travels out west, I used to carry some two-inch salutes - firecrackers. And sitting in the dressing room, I thought it would be
beautiful, this is New Year's Eve -- I opened the window and I told Charlie here we go, and I lit one of these two inch salutes.

Well, it went down -- there was an alleyway and this salute dropped down in the alleyway, and of course that amplified the sound, it was like an echo chamber, and went it went off, it sounded like a cannon. And we're sitting there laughing and all of a sudden, the doors burst open all through with cops and their guns -- and they went through the theatre. But I mean, there was a call out, a cop in distress, and they went into Tommy's room and Tommy dispelled them and said nobody fired a gun up here.

It seems that the police had an alert out for a killer who had escaped from jail, and the policeman that set the alarm off was calling in on the phone, a police phone, and was down in that alley. I imagine he was quite surprised and a bit jumpy.

Anyway, Tommy knew it was a damn prank, so he called the whole band together -- he used to love to do that, bawl us all out and said, "I don't know who's responsible" and I guess I was always a dead giveaway because I blush very easily, and that was the end of that incident.
We were called to task on another incident. By that time, I had interested Charlie Shavers in cheifing -- because I was cheifing for him, too. He used to tell me about down home

pots and soul cooking, which he grew up on. So I used to try to please him by making spare rib stew -- that's a beauty for anybody that's interested in getting in touch with me, and Charlie said, "Well, look, let me cook this pot this time; I want to show you something."

So we went out and bought -- and this is still at the Capitol Theatre between shows -- went out and bought a double burner, an electric burner, and pots and pans, and all the food on 8th Avenue in the Italian shopping district -- this is between shows -- and I don't know, we must have spent fifty, sixty or seventy dollars at that time just getting pots and pans and the cooking utensils, and the food -- we could have eaten very nicely at any of the foremost restaurants in New York and forgotten this hobby.

But we got a one pot burner, Charlie did, and we got three pots burning between shows, and we went on and played our shows, but never realizing that the aromas were just excruciating backstage -- and the air conditioning, or the cooling system wasn't on, but the air conditioning in the hotel circulated these beautiful aromas. And Tommy came back and the manager of the hotel came back and he says, "I know you fellows like to have a good time, and I don't know what the hell you're doing, but I've had about 100,000 complaints from theatre goers here and customers about the aromas from the restaurant next door" which was filtering into the theatre - and after we finished

that pot for the band, call it a day with your cooking! That was the end of our culinary exploits for the present, and Charlie had somebody come in and build a very special crate and box so he could carry the equipment on the road with him, which he did. And he has his own kitchen from then on, and I heard many stories about his efforts as a chef.

To keep These incidents -- in a musical context, I might add that during our show at the Capitol Theatre, I think we were the first jazz band -- I'm quite sure -- to do the Rhapsody in Blue in its entirety, which is quite a feat, and Tommy at that time had made records using large string sections, and to keep this picture and some of the arrangements which we played -- I don't know who talked him into it, but he had 20 girl violinists -- a string section with 20 girls, a complete string ensemble, among other things -- and we did this Rhapsody in Blue, and Tommy hired Walter Gross, a most brave pianist of many accomplishments, to play the piano for us. Now Walter was quite a drinker, and an old friend of Tommy's from way back in the old days before he had a band, in the studios. Walter had a reputation beyond recall.
He -- Tommy, we must say, had been on the wagon for many years, although he was known -- his doctor prescribed a certain tonic which he called it; I think it had a little

alcoholic content, but Tommy didn't drink until later on, which was one of the reasons of his death -- did the Rhapsody in Blue -- Walter tried to straighten himself out enough to play this Rhapsody, which is a feat in itself. It's a musical accomplishment.

And he would introduce Walter, and he would go into the Rhapsody, and the first thing that would happen after the introduction was Walter Gross walked out very artistically, and would sit down at the stool, and Tommy would lay a $20 bill on the piano, and the people aren't in on this inside joke, our story, and Walter Gross would reach in and put a $20 bill on the piano , before we started the Rhapsody.

Being an inside joke, this was a bet between them to see if Walter was able to execute the whole thing without making any mistakes, and I think for the three weeks, it was about -- I think the bets averaged out 50-50.

There was just one night with a full, packed house, and Walter was celebrating a bit, and had a slight difficulty in execution, and as you know, the Rhapsody in Blue builds up to a tremendous climax. Walter played this tremendously beautiful arpeggio and loud pedal on, finished the arpeggio, and when the band was still holding the chord, Walter Gross walked off the stand, bent down, refused to take a bow, and Tom went over to the piano and picked up the
two $20 bills, and waved them at the band and grinned, and stopped the show for about 5 minutes, chuckling at his winning the bet.

After that three weeks with Tom Dorsey, I didn't work with him again, that I can recall, until 1958, and the incidents that happened then -- I was doing the Hit Parade then, and Tom had been having -- had a fight with Louie Belson. Louie Belson left the band, Louie had followed Buddy Rich. Charlie Shavers was still with him, and they were at the Pennsylvania Hotel.

Well, he wanted to sign me to a contract as Louie Belson said he wasn't coming back -- but I couldn't afford, I was doing so well on the outside, and those were the top years for me -- being a musician on the outside and then the studios -- and I couldn't afford it, I had built my new home here in Whitestone, New York, and I didn't want any road travel. I wanted to continue doing what I was doing. So I refused.

However, Frank Sinatra had made a picture in late ;57 -- well, we went in in '58, and the picture was just being released, and it was like a preview. Frank Sinatra was a cowboy, by the way -- the picture was Johnny Concho. So Frank, I believe it was said, hired the Paramount Theatre, and we went in with his picture and the great Frank Sinatra was the star, and he hired Tommy Dorsey as the band on his show. He was in the driver's seat then -- it'd had always been

The office had talked Tommy Dorsey into making up -- their standing feud over the years with his brother Jimmy, and it was then that it was the Dorsey Brothers, and we opened the Paramount Theatre -- great publicity for Frank and his picture.

The engagement was a smash success -- and it was four weeks, a month -- and that was the first time, a first for Joey Bishop. Frank had heard Joey Bishop and liked his work, so that was the comedian that was on the bill, that was the first time for Joey Bishop on Broadway.

Tommy and Jimmy did a medley of all their hits over the years -- the ones that Jimmy did with his band and Tom with his band, and I think we did about 20 minutes. The rest of the show, we played for Frank Sinatra, and he put on a hell of a show, as he always does, and it was his music. So we played 40 to 50 minutes behind Frank Sinatra, and that was plenty of music to play. But we didn't feature the band that much.

In the meantime, Jackie Gleason had a big contract with CBS for the Gleason Show, and The Honeymooners. CBS gave him a summer replacement show -- I'm trying to recall the name of the show -- oh, the American Bandstand, I believe it was. And Gleason with his love for music and

bands, he wanted every week to feature a different band. No, the Bandstand wasn't around -- it would be 15 minutes of one band and 15 minutes of another, and 15 of another. In other words, the hour show was a revolving bandstand with these 15 minute segments of four groups.

Well, he was up there to see Frank all the time and his old friend whom he loved, was Tommy Dorsey. So we opened that show that summer -- the summer replacement show, which was on Saturday nights. While we were at these four weeks at the Paramount Theatre. In other words, we doubled, which was a hell of a job, because on Saturdays and Sundays -- and Fridays -- Frank was doing five shows a day, sometimes six, and we had to arrange the shows so that we could go over -- it was only four or five blocks up to the CBS playhouse, which was on 53rd Street, I think.

We'd have cabs waiting for us, and we'd rush over there with no rehearsals, because we knew the music, and we'd do the show, our fifteen-minute segment. And we're still running back and forth with drums and so forth. I later on played that show with four different bands, after the Dorsey show band, I think Simon or somebody wrote me up in one of the New York newspapers as being the house drummer of Broadway.
Back to the Bandstand show, we did two weeks I'm sure of, and maybe three -- and we followed, we got there

and set up in our section in the back, that hadn't revolved yet, with the long cameras, while we were setting up, we heard this (UNINTELLIGIBLE) of songs, we thought then, of the band ahead of us, the artist ahead of us, which we were to follow as the bandstand revolved, and we were all looking at each other -- the side glances, and asked us what kind of music was that and what's going on and we were set up, and we would do our segment when the bandstand turned, and we'd do our bit.

I want to say that later on we asked who the hell that was, and that was Elvis Presly's first appearance on anything major -- the powers to be arranged with the Gleason office that he was to be presented on that show, and that's the first time he ever appeared on television to my knowledge. And that was the beginning of the great Elvis.

I must remark that back at the theatre, the Paramount Theatre, Charlie Shavers and I confined our culinary efforts to having a standard order with Sardi's, which was next door, and we had a waiter service, and about the biggest thing we cooked was music.

One minute after the last show, we had cabs waiting, and we did -- at the Paramount, a show at the Paramount, we had cabs waiting and we rushed down to Victor Studios on 24th Street and did a four sided record date with Tom Dorsey, and that, I believe was my last association with Tom, and of course, the last recordings with the exception
of the previous -- I mentioned before this doing an album with Paul Whiteman which featured his old players, Tom and Jim Dorsey, and that is the end of my association with Tom.

It wasn't long after that that Tommy Dorsey choked on some food while he was sleeping and died, and it was no more than ayear later that my dear friend, Jimmy, died in I think it was St. Claire Hospital, New York, of cancer.

Not knowing the seriousness of Jimmy Dorsey's illness when he was in the hospital, and I couldn't get in to visit, I sent him a telegram and I heard The Shadow on the radio playing, The Shadow Knows, I love you, and get well, Cliff -- the telegram said. We had been drinking buddies, also, at the time of my association with his orchestra.
Had I known the seriousness of his illness, I wouldn't have sent that. But maybe he got a smile out of it, anyway.

To sum up Tommy Dorsey and my association with him, after so many years of evading integration in his band -- instrumentalists, that is -- Tommy Dorsey grew to love Charlie Shavers as a most beautiful and unusual human being, which he was. To say nothing of his awe of Charlie's vast technique on the trumpet, as well as his wonderful warmth and beauty of his playing that he added to the band. Tommy had those attributes on trombone -- technically and

warmth in his playing. And I, among others, never considered him a jazz player -- his idol was Jack Teagarden. I can't recall working with Charlie Shavers again after that episode, although we were real fond of each other and saw a lot of each other constantly in New York. He only lived 5 minutes away from me in Corona. And two or three blocks from Louis Armstrong.

I'd go into clubs like the Metro in New York to say hello and Charlie had a quartet there, and several other places, and I would listen to him and he would have me over for barbecue occasionally, and we were in close touch until his death. His death was premature. He had had many illness including diabetes, he wouldn't stop drinking or taking doctor's orders. I don't think Charlie was given full evaluation of his warmth and his beauty, because he had intertwined a great deal of technique in his jazz performances, and it might have turned some people off -- I don't know why, possibly they were jealous, because the warmth was there and the swinging was there.

Today one of the greatest trumpet players alive to me is Clark Terry. He's accepted as such, and I don't think critics of musicians put him down for his great technical prowress and swinging. Maybe Charlie didn't live long enough to enjoy the fulfillment and acceptance of his greatness, along his technical lines and
so forth -- as people admire that today, too, along with a person's swinging.

I'm going to attempt to do a couple of like -- I have to skipover so much and not get deeply into the subject, but I want to get into the subject of some of the jazz parties that are spin offs from the Gibson parties, and I'm gonna start, as Milt Hinton will agree with me, I'm sure -- the next big one for us was the Odessa jazz party. So I'll get into that one now.

My thoughts were just interrupted here -- a telephone call from Dick Gibson, from Denver, and he just hired me again, for his 1979 jazz party at the Broadmore Hotel in Colorado Springs this coming Labor Day weekend, and this will be my 17th year. I consider that a pretty good average!
Now for the Odessa party. For the past two years, we've missed the original ingredient for the Odessa party. I'll go on to explain.

The Odessa party was a dream of a gentleman, Dr. O.A. Jim Fulcher, who was an eminent surgeon and a lover of jazz music. After visiting Gibson's parties as a guest, he got together with a few influential citizens in Odessa, Texas, and they formed a committee called the Odessa Jazz Unlimited Incorporation.
They backed the first concerts there. Their first parties were also private parties -- it was a guest list, invitation only -- and they still are. Their list is sold out,
and it's growing every year. This'll be my 13th year there this May.

I believe their first party was in 1966. Their party is a beautiful, intimate and it's six days long, instead of the three day short parties of other people -- that other people hold -- and it is held in the unique Inn of the Golden West Hotel, and our wives, girlfriends, what have you, are always the guests of the committee and the Odessa Committee.

Also, they keep their list of musical artists to only about 20 to 25 players, which makes the party more intimate -- it doesn't get too cluttered up. We play four hours a night -- that's the schedule, but we run over, you know, it's hard to cut off the sets late because the musical excitement reaches tremendous peaks.
Then, we are wined and dined each night by the wealthy sponsors at their homes. They have bank Presidents, famous doctors, surgeons, owners of oil wells -- I'm getting envious -- and what have you.

They don't make the mistake of just saying in Texas -- it is West Texas, by God. They don't associate their higher plateau territory with the lower country of Houston, Dallas, Fort Worth and so on. Everyone has heard of southern hospitality, but if you've never had the Odessa, Midland west Texas treatment, you've never lived! Ask any musician lucky enough to be asked to play there.
Oh, yes, I have those sets of the different jazz stars performing also on file. And I would love to furnish those also to the Institute files for the research and digests.

Just quickly, I have one of the late party programs in front of me. For one week we had -- we had for a week long, but each night you would get to hear George Duvivier, and Jack Lesberg and Milt Hinton on bases -- Pee Wee Irwin, Clark Terry, Wild Bill Davison, John Best, on trumpets -- and one of Dr. Fulcher's great loves on tenor saxophone, and personally, is Flip Phillips. He's one of mine, too. I might mention here.

I've done a bunch of recordings with Flip, appeared with him 6 weeks last year at Michael's Pub in New York -- also jazz concerts around New York, and Milt Hinton was in on some of those. Milt, you were with me in Michael's Pub, weren't you, with Flip, among others?

To continue with the artists at the Odessa party, we also had on that same program, on trombones, one that's always with us, the superb Carl Fontana. We had Lou McGarity until his death. And a wonderful Texas trombonist, Ashley Alexander, Jr. We had Ed Hubl on trombone -- another really great unsung hero musically. Let's see, there's myself on drums, and Duke Hanna, and Mousey Alexander, Bobby Rosengarden - that's a motley crew!
On reeds - clarinet is Johnnie Mince, Peanuts
Hucko, Mattie Matlock, and Mattie Matlock until his death.

We had Buddy Tate on tenor. The piano -- Buddy Tate needs no introduction, of course, he played many years with Basie. On piano we had Ralph Sutton, Dick Wellstood. Lou Stein, and my hero, Dave McKenna.

Aside from all this, just on the aside, all the piano players mentioned here are my heroes, as I put it, without their superb playing with me, I'm nowhere on the drums. Add to that list Teddy Wilson. He was there last year, too. Playing with Teddy Wilson -- gee, I did some work with his trio, quite a lot of it -- he keeps a drummer on his toes, especially using lots of brushes, because of Teddy's tempos -- they were breakneck. He does it so easy. And it's not that easy on drums to play softly applied sticks at those tempos, and yet Teddy, once again, makes it so easy and makes it look so easy.

Now to finish off one party, this one party that I just started, was Red Norvo on vibraphones, and Ducky Pizzarelli on guitar, and Herb Ellis on guitar. This line for a solid week should be awe inspiring for a jazz buff, or a musician.

To bring th is discourse to an end, I spent countless hours with Jim Fulcher on Odessa. Jazz was our interest -- we had several interests, such as bird hunting we discussed that. I never got to accept his invitation to
join him. He owned bird dogs and did much dove and quail hunting.

We had a mutual agreement to stick to bourbon and I to vodka at this time, which was another one of our close interests. He had a tremendous love for Ben Webster, and he had a record collection that was unbelievable of all the greats down through the years. He was a big collector, and when he put this party together, those of us who were still living and so forth, he hired us, and I'm happy to say I was one of his favorite drummers, and when he found out how much I knew Ben Webster -- he didn't realize that. One of the things he had of Ben, I was on.

And of course, Flip Phillips was another of his loves, which I have mentioned. And he knew my love for guns and my interest in hunting, and also on becoming a sheriff -- my father was up to high sheriff in Cumberland County, Portland, Maine when he died -- he died just before attaining the office of high sheriff. I have his badges and also badges and the history of my grandmother's brother, Sam Taylor -- a well known policeman and sheriff in Portland, Maine in the late 1890's and early 1900's. I was always obgessed with police work and law and order -- even if I was for a period of my life a crazy SB, as we would say with tongue in cheek.
I was also deeply into studies of the Old West and

how it was won, and Jim Fulcher knew all these things, and along the way, one of the parties we did, he had the sheriff of Odessa swear me in as an honorary sheriff in front of an audience, during a concert.

And he had a little gold badge for us, and there were two or three guys -- I think Yank Lawson and Cutty Cutshall, and Bud Freeman, I believe, and the guys that were in on that particular party -- and we used to wear those little badges in case we got stopped in Odessa, because we had the swagger, and we are now honorary deputies.

And he presented the whole group at that particular time, with silver western buckels and everybody got a western rancher's dress Stetson hat. I think that particular party we were on, about 15 people -- this little party was going at the time, and I still have the Stetson, and I've put that thing under hot water and I've reshaped it, and around the crown I've got some Mexican silver doodads -- and I still wear it everyplace. The sheriff then was Elwood Hill, and I got my new badge in 1977 and my ID -- no, I got the regular commission from Sheriff Hill and later on, the new sheriff, that lasted two or three years, Sheriff Faught -- and my new badge in '77 and ID is under Sheriff Faught. I'm a little confused here, because I don't know what I gave -- said it as it is, I got a regular commission in the sheriff's department under Elwood Hill, and then as the sheriff's changed, the new badge, the one that I carry with me now, is from Elwood Faught, and of course, the sheriffs change after you have your new ID card.

I also carry and hold a full commission on Jefferson County, Arkansas sheriff's department, and I carry that badge. I ws saying before that I have a commission -- and it's a full commission, but it's all over now because that sheriff is gone -- Bernalillo County in the state of New Mexico, I got a full commission in Jefferson County, as I just said, and I am an honorary citizen of Pine Bluff, Arkansas -- to make that commission binding, and one last aside, and I will finish with the Odessa parties.
