Late sixties, Jim Fulcher's mouth deteriorated, but all the while, though ill, he was foremost in setting the Odessa jazz parties up each year, calling us all personally from his sick bed to hire us, and he wouldn't have it any other way. He wanted to do it personally, and a series of strokes took their toll.

And he came to the sessions with a cane, and he wouldn't miss them for the world; his strength was taxed most of the time, but he'd sit there smiling and make his one announcement each year, telling the people to shut up and listen to the music, that they were making too much damn noise. There were quite a few people that made those parties not solely for the jazz, but to socialize and make it a society event.

The ladies and the gentlemen there would sport their latest creations from Dallas and Fort Worth -- it was party time for them. So Fulcher would tell them to shut up and listen to the music. But still to go on -- he progressively got worse until a massive stroke, and his death two years ago in 1977. End of that part of the story.

But we still go on, and I'll be there this May, and many other musicians he loved will be there, too. I believe that Jim Fulcher will be with us, also. It's a wierd feeling that we can't see him, but we will feel him.

Another insert on the jazz parties, was one of our fans in the Odessa parties was a gentleman called Max Christianson from Midland, Texas -- of course, that's only 30 minutes away, about 30 or 40 miles from Odessa.

So two years ago in '77, he decided that they wanted a session over there in Midland, along the same lines, but with a few different musicians to add a little flavor, around November, which would be -- our parties in Odessa were in May, and that would be mid-year, so that would be six months apart, and he started his jazz sessions, his jazz party with the nucleus of some from the Odessa parties, but adding a few younger, more modern generation musicians to add a different flavor to the music, and I was asked to open that first party.

That has become an extremely successful party, too, and of course, as I said, the six month interval doesn't interfere with the Odessa party. I didn't get to say in the Odessa parties, and the guest lists, and also in the Midland parties for Max Christianson, the guest list included many people from all over the country in all walks of life, so that the clientele was not local in entirety, by any means, and

a lot of those people came after they learned of the parties that were regulars at the Gibson parties. So there is a great movement, jazz wise, as a throwoff on the original Gibson parties. We have the one down in Jersey now, and there is one every year down in Manassas, Virginia, which is sponsored by Fat Cat Johnson McCree - Johnson McCree.
And his parties aren't on such a large scale, but it gives many musicians who aren't quite so famous, along with a few famous ones, a chance to participate, and their list ... (CUT)

This is Saturday, March 3rd, and this is the 8th day that we're under these tapes, Milt Hinton. Milton, it just dawned on me that for many, many years, I've always called you 'Judge' -- that's been your nickname and every musician I know has always called you Judge over the years. I haven't used that expression -- while you've been my interviewer and on these tapes and so forth, and I always took it for granted that when any of us had problems or were in trouble or anything, we always respected your opinion and we asked you as a friend what you thought about our situations, and we always relied upon your answers as very helpful, and your decisions were final, so possibly that's where the expression, 'the judge' came from?
And I think that since you are my interviewer on these tapes, that you should tell the people how come you were named the judge.

Hey, Cliff, it's funny you should ask that, for me to explain how I got the nickname "Judge." But it certainly didn't have anything to do with my judiciary or my tremendous knowledge anymore than any other person. It just so happened that many years ago in the recording studios, when I first broke into the studios, you know how it's necessary to be punctual and on time and everything. I always tried to be on time and be one of the first ones in the studio so I could get my instrument out and tune up and be ready to play.

It reminded me of an old story that my grandmother used to tell about a dear soul brother in Mississippi where my grandmother came from, that was just a beautiful soul. Everybody in town loved him, but he always had a way of getting in his cups, and on weekends, Saturday night he decided that he should get drunk. Everybody loved him. He worked all the week and every Saturday night this fellow got drunk and he's laying out in the streets on the corners and he's very inebriated and very happy, talking a little loud. So, late Saturday night the police would come along and they didn't want him to be seen on the corner laying in the streets when people got ready to go to church Sunday morning. Late Saturday night they used to lock him up and put him in jail for safe-keeping over Sunday---let him sleep it off. And Monday morning when court opened they'd let him out and he was always the first one in court. When he came the judge would be sitting there all clean and everything and he'd say: "Would you please get out of,here!"

And I think I told this story many years ago and in the morning when I walked in a recording studio, when everybody came in I would say, "Good morning, Judge." And that's actually the way the name got started. Not the brilliance of----Naturally, over the years I've become one of the senior citizens of the recording business. Being an older person they'll say, "Well, here comes the Judge and we'll ask him what he thinks about that."

But that's honestly. It's wonderful to hear you tell these stories about these great Gibson parties and the different parties in Odessa and Midland. And you know, Cliff, that I have been on some of these parties, not as many as you have, and I have been the recipient of those sheriff badges, not as many as you, and ten-gallon hat and silver buckle. And I'm very grateful to have them along with you. You've made me responsible for being on those parties and I just want to thank you for that. Will you please continue with your story.

I'm gonna touch lightly upon my associations with some more wonderful musicians, and I'd like to get to Pee Wee Irwin -- I say touch lightly upon them because there are so many people to cover. Right now, I'm running out of tape.

Pee Wee Irwin -- of course, I first knew him when I was with -- when he was with the Tommy Dorsey Band, and in '39 along with Yank Lawson on trumpets and so forth and so on, and I -- when Bobby Hackett left Nick's that first year, I stayed on and this is 1950 -- I stayed on and Pee Wee Irwin became the leader, and I'd done much work and recordings and concerts with Pee Wee over the years. We've been more than friends. I went to Britain with Pee Wee; Scotland, England, London, Edinburgh, Stockholm, Sweden, Germany -- we played the German International Jazz Festival, this was only 3, 4 years ago, we played the International Jazz festival in Hanover, Germany; and we also rehearsed for four days in Iceland -- and I repeat, Iceland -- I don't know who booked that! But the office did when they brought us over to Europe, and I was with the group that Pee Wee was the leader of was called the Kings of Jazz. They named us that over in London -- the office did -- they thought that was apt.

It was some band; there was Bernie Privin, the guy I used to work with in the old Artie Shaw and Charlie Barnet days, and he had been in the studios for years; he's a wonderful trumpet player in the Louis Armstrong vein. Dick

Hyman was on piano with us and Major Holley on base; Ed Hubbie on trombone, Kenny Davern -- he played both the clarinet and primarily the soprano saxophone -- I have a mental block with that word 'soprano'.

However, on with the story. Kenny played that instrument just about as great as anybody alive today, that I know of. And I mentioned before that we had a little trio with Dick Wellstood, but that's beside the point. Johnny Mince played the clarinet -- Johnny had been in that Tommy Dorsey band in '39, too. It's funny that we all reunite after the years and after the many years in between to pursue our pursuits of music.

We played with the same group -- that group that I just mentioned, in concert in the states, too, from the Jersey Jazz Society, they brought us down, and recorded us, but it has never been released yet. I hope it will be someday; it's -- we were in jazz concerts in the states, too; we went down to Arkansas and so forth. And that's another group like the World's Greatest Jazz Band that we put together, and keep together.
I can't say enough about Pee Wee Irvin -- he's a great trumpet player, and we've been in constant contact over the years, and I do many concerts with him, so we're in personal contact at all times.
Now I'd like to get to Wild Bill -- Wild Bill

Davi son, and I'm trying to get to these people one by one to keep in context with my career, but we don't have time, as I have said several times before, to get into the many jobs that we've done together.

So I'll skip over lightly on some of the things the first London years over the years, ever since my first years with Wild Bill Davison -- in 1976, he was instrumental in bringing me to the Swiss International Jazz Festival held in Bern, Switzerland. We also played Geneva and Zurich, Germany, the group the first two years was Ed Hubble on trombone, Peanuts Hucko on clarinet, Bob Wilbur on clarinet and there goes my mental block -- on soprano saxophone, Bob Wilbur Ralph Sutton on piano and with the Swiss bassist.

Wild Bill lives in Copenhagen, Denmark, and I have joined him and Bern for the last three years. Bill and I have great respect for each other, the other's talent, and he is one of a kind, period. He is a driving trumpet player of great reknown, and not even beginning to slow down at 73 years of age.
Over the past years, the bygone years, we were known to raise a few elbows with Eddie Condon, and with Eddie Condon's prowess as a boozer, the three of us took on all comers.
Bill will be back again this year, and I will be doing concerts with him -- I think I mentioned that before, and

Al Lawson will be going and Eddie Condon's number three nightclub, which is owned by Red Balaban - he was a friend of Condon's, and he had permission from Eddie Condon's' wife to use her name in the present club here in New York.

I've got to get to one of the most exciting record dates, and a definite high point in my career. I was called by -- I don't remember whom, to do a record date while I was on the Hit Parade, and I had a record in front of me, and if you wait until I research, I'll give you the year.

Well, there is no date on the album, but I think it was around '55. I was called for a record date at Carnegie Hall rehearsal hall, that's where it took place and they had set up equipment there, and when I walked in, I was flabbergasted the people on the date. In the first place, I walked in - and I always walk in early to set up the drums; there was Walter Pope there, and we said greetings and Joe Newman was there, and we had just begun to know each other, really; and Lawrence Brown on trombone; Pete Brown on alto sax -- now he'd been ill, and they found him. He hadn't played for a couple of years, and Frank Wes$ on tenor saxophone, and Pete Johnson on piano. Now the last time I saw or heard about Pete was at the Sunset Club, which we covered back in Kansas City in 1935, and all these people were in Kansas City in 1935. Freddie Greene was there on guitar, and
I was the only white on the date, and this was -- well, the date was Joe Turner's, and the name of the album, which is a collector's item, is The Boss of the Blues.

I think he had asked for all the musicians that they could reproduce from the old days in Kansas City in that association, and I was there because possibly, Joe Jones or somebody from Kansas City who had played with them, didn't, or couldn't make that date, and it took a lot of hello's and explanations -- nobody remembered that I was that kid in Kansas City, and I didn't get any credit on the album, that I was around at the time, so I fit in on that date, I put that badly. The arrangements were by Ernie Wilkins, and it was like Basie's little nine-piece band, the backgrounds that we played.

And I settled back and did that record date. But I have had hundreds and hundreds of musicians who have asked me what it was like because it is one of their favorite records. Now that record was reviewed two or three years later, in the New York Times, I believe it was, by a panel and a group of jazz critics; some of them prestigous -- and they picked 80, I believe I have the article someplace , we can't research it now, but they picked 80 of the foremost jazz records of all time, beginning way back, all down through the years,and this album was high on the list as a must for anybody's record collection and listening.
One of the outstanding things was on that date was

Lawrence Brown's trombone playing behind the side "Morning Glory" -- behind Joe Turner when he sang; it was -- another two things I'd like to call to attention is the second day, there was a two day date, and we went back and I had set up, and they were still waiting, they were starting late on the date -- they were waiting for a trumpet player. There might have been a mixup, but Joe Newman wasn't there, and they didn't know what to do.

Well, I had just finished a Hit Parade rehearsal, and gone over to that date, and it dawned on me that one of my dear friends on the Hit Parade, who had also worked with Count Basie, was Jimmy Nottingham, so I said, "Gee, I think, if you're stuck, why don't you call Jimmy Nottingham and see if he's there, and he'll come over" -- because everybody goes for a little taste after rehearsal. Well, they did. They called and they got Jimmy Nottingham. And when this record was released, Jimmy Nottingham was so indebted to me that he was included on that great date, that over the years, I never could buy a drink around him, and Jimmy just passed away this past year, and I won't forget his work on this album -- he's listed on the back as contributing, "I Want a Little Girl" -- it says Jimmy Nottingham replaces Joe Newman on trumpet and Seldom Powell replaced Frank Wes on tenor sax.
And the final sum up of this record, this album,

was that Ertegun, the owner of Atlantic Records, has told me since then, in all sincerity, that they were just about to go under bankruptcy the time -- Atlantic Records -- he owned Atlantic Records with his brother, Nesuhi Ertegun, who also supervised that date.

And he told me that they were going in a receivership, and this one album bailed him out completely, and put them back on their feet and they went on -- after that, I believe they had such artists as Ella Fitzgerald and they climbed and went on to great heights, and this is one of the biggest recording companies of all time at this day and age.
Of course, they're in all other things -- modern rock and pop and so forth now.

Milt, we're getting low on tape. However, before we run out of this side, I'll have to get to Louis Armstrong. Eventually, I got to know Louis Armstrong well, such as being on the performance and closing of the Storyville Show, we were on the Timex show in Miami. He did a couple of numbers with us, the Bob Crosby Band, when I was with the Bob Crosby Band on the same show, and actually, it was the Lawson-Haggard Jazz Band -- Crosby just fronted it. Gene Krupa and Lionel Hampton did bits on that show with us.
It was exciting for me because I finally got to play behind Louis. When we did that Storyville show, the closing of Storyville, for CBS, which I told about in
great detail -- after rehearsal, Louis asked Bobby Hackett and Lou Stein and myself, we all lived on Long Island, he asked us to his house to relax in Corona.

And when we got there, he had his right hand man put on a bunch of records, and we settled back and listened to Louis, and he played nothing but Bobby Hackett records. Well, we sort of hinted that we'd like to hear some of his records.

Then when I was with the Peanuts Hucko Quartet at the Roosevelt Grill, Louis had been real sick towards the end, and he was recuperating. He came down with his wife, Lucille, to hear us. Peanuts had been with Louis for a long time -- he did some of those lengthy world wide trips with him. He made some movies with him, and that was a few years back, and Louis got up for nostalgia's sake, I couldn't believe it -- and he was a little bit weak, but he had that beautiful grin, and he came up on the bandstand and sang "Hello Dolly", "Blueberry Hill" and he did "Rocking Chair" and Peanuts sang with him, feeding in that Jack Teagarden, what Jack Teagarden did on that original record, he talked back and forth, and then he capped it all off with "Sleepy Time Down South".

Afterwards, he had Lou McGarity and Peanuts and myself over to his table and he said, "Lucille, by my judge and witness; when I reorganize and I get to feel better, I want these three boys in my band" -- and he says,
"You tell that to Joe Glaser for me".

Well, however, Louis never did recuperate enough to have that band; however, to this day, I'm so proud that he asked me. Joe Glaser called me to join Louis when I was on the Hit Parade -- I couldn't afford to leave New York with the work I was doing, I was always sorry later on in life.

I had a pass to the funeral when Louis passed away, and well, you couldn't get into the church without one. I was just too emotional to go, so I sat at home here only two and a half miles away from the church and watched it on television.
Tommy

Just in closing in this incident, Tommy Young told me a wonderful story -- a couple of wonderful stories, well, he told me a thousand wonderful stories, but the one that comes to mind is about Louis. One comes to mind -- when they made the picture, I think it was "High Society" -- if you ever remember watching Louis Armstrong's band, you'll see his drummer who looks a little strange back there, and it's Barrett Deems, and the damn producers insisted that he wear blackface, and that's a beautiful thing if you knew Barrett Deems. However, the other story that comes to mind is about Barrett Deems -- is Louis Armstrong had figured he was surrounded by blacks, and that's just the thing he took for granted, and when, of course, to the uninitiated,

Barrett Deems is white, and there was one time in the dressing room, we were sitting around drinking and everything, and Trummy was sitting there, he said Louis looked at his manager, and he said, "Do me a favor; go tell that nigger on drums to play softer behind my playing -- my singing" -- and I think that was worth a chuckle.

Milt, the University of Wyoming wrote me in great length and asked me if they could have any of my papers, drums, pictures or memorabilia -- I can't pronounce that one -- for their archives, and their music department and if I would leave some of them on my demise, and so I wrote them and told them they could have a lot of things, and it was up to my family to send them whatever may be important for their archives.
By the same token, anything that might be important musically, I would be more than happy to see that they went to the Smithsonian Institute.

In conclusion, Milt, for now, the last few years of concerts and credits, I think when we get together, after looking over the notes that I have, you and I can cover some of the things, if you're interested in my hobbies and my vast collection of antiques and guns and knives and bayonets, sword collections, my Civil War replicas and relics, and well, not replicas - I have some original relics, and bullets from the major battlefields from the War of the States, and I have a 13 star flag, which went down

with our troops from Maine, in the Battle of -- oh, Lord, I don't know which one off hand, I've got a buggy whip that was my grandfather's from Wild Bill Hickock, Buffalo Bill, that is; and I have many valuable antique trinkets and collections -- a lot of them came from my aunt from the early 1800's. A lot of these things are from my family.

I don't know what anything is worth, because I've never had an expert evaluate my complete collections, but if you want to get into that later on, I'd be more than happy if you think it's of any interest to this article -- because of my cataract operations in 1963 and so on ...
About the cataracts, to mention that, I might say in my left eye I have 20/20 vision and I can read the fine print in most any contract at 500 paces!

I have a bit about my religious views that you might want to get into later on. And another thing, about my -- when I was in high school, I majored in art, pen and ink especially, and I did a whole series of pictures of pen and inks when I was with Bobby Hackett in 1950 at the Nick's in the Village, and there are only a very few copies of these originals that I have given -- there are 10 actually finished that I have given to people who are close acquaintances and very soon I'm gonna have some prints made, and I'm gonna try to sell them for only one thing, for one of my pet charities. You know, I'm so -- I think so much of that
Hector sheriff's department down in Texas, I would like to sell some of those drawings so that I can contribute to that fund, their charitable fund, along with some church contributions.

So Milt Hinton, until we get together next time, you go over some of these notes, and -- that we've put together, and we'll have, I hope, the final long interview to sew up this whole evaluation of my life.
(END OF REEL 5)

segments.title: Opening of the Smithsonian interview, 1979
segments.summary: Interview header; Milt Hinton opens Reel 1 in 1979 and asks Leeman for his name and address.

segments.title: Birth in Portland, Maine; parents and mother's piano career
segments.summary: Leeman gives his birth date, his father Merle (a teamster) and mother Margaret Webb; the parents divorce around 1918-19 and his talented pianist mother pursues a career.

segments.title: Hinton explains the oral history project's purpose
segments.summary: Hinton explains that the Smithsonian wants family background so future generations know the jazz pioneers; Leeman says family shaped him as a drummer.

segments.title: Leeman's middle name, Spencer
segments.summary: Hinton asks about names; Leeman reveals his unused middle name Spencer, after a grandfather.

segments.title: Grandparents and a step-grandfather who laid telephone wire out west
segments.summary: Raised by his father's parents; his mother's father, a Webb sea captain, was lost at sea and her mother remarried Charles Weaver, who left him the revolver that began his gun collecting.

segments.title: Half sister and Uncle Clifford, a Bower-trained drummer
segments.summary: Half sister Pauline; Leeman was named for his uncle Clifford Francis Leeman, a New England Conservatory drummer who played with the Boston Symphony and gave up music for insurance.

segments.title: Father's remarriage and living with grandparents in Portland
segments.summary: His father remarries around 1920 and builds a house nearby, but Leeman stays with his grandparents and goes through Portland schools.

segments.title: Aunt Marion starts him on piano
segments.summary: Missing a mother's love but well cared for, Leeman starts piano at six or seven with his aunt and longs for drums, using his uncle's practice pad and homemade xylophone.

segments.title: Xylophone and drum lessons with Howard Shaw
segments.summary: He studies xylophone and Bower rudiments with Howard 'Dick' Shaw but never practices much, and plays popular sheet music on the xylophone around 1928-29.

segments.title: Tom Robbins's banjo band and clown uniforms at age 14
segments.summary: Banjo virtuoso Tom Robbins organizes a banjo band with marimba; Leeman tours theatres at 13-14 in clown uniforms until his father fetches him from Dover, New Hampshire.

segments.title: Hearing name bands at Archer Pier and Fry's Hall
segments.summary: As a teenager in Maine he hears McKinney's Cotton Pickers, Claude Hopkins, Whiteman and Casa Loma in person, which he calls his musical training; he was too shy to approach them.

segments.title: Joining Dan Murphy's Musical Skippers in 1933
segments.summary: A local bass player recommends him to territory bandleader Dan Murphy, whose naval-uniformed young band included Jimmy Blake and Ray Conniff.

segments.title: Pay and the road trip from Boston to Sioux City
segments.summary: Hired at $25 a week in Boston, he travels west by car with the band, photographed in uniform at Buffalo, and reaches Sioux City wide-eyed.

segments.title: Tom Archer's ballrooms and Lawrence Welk's trailer band
segments.summary: The Tom Archer agency books a string of Midwest ballrooms; Leeman recalls following Lawrence Welk's six-piece polka band, which lived in a trailer and paid $75 a week.

segments.title: Arriving in Kansas City in spring 1934
segments.summary: After playing Denver, where they followed Bennie Moten's band, the Murphy band reaches Depression-era Kansas City, wide open with crime and jazz.

segments.title: Boots Castle takes him to hear Basie at the Reno Club
segments.summary: A woman called Boots Castle guides him to the Reno Club on 12th Street, where he hears the Basie band with Lips Page, Buster Smith and Jimmy Rushing.

segments.title: Meeting Lips Page in Kansas City
segments.summary: Boots Castle introduces Leeman to Oran 'Lips' Page, whom he found gracious and the most beautiful of men.

segments.title: Joe Keys, Basie's forceful lead trumpet
segments.summary: Leeman recalls trumpeter Joe Keys, who played out of tune but forcefully led the section and read well from Basie's little book.

segments.title: Sitting in with Basie on brushes before Jo Jones
segments.summary: Basie, unhappy with his drummer, asks Leeman to sit in; he plays brushes while out of work with the stranded Murphy band.

segments.title: The Sunset Club: Pete Brown, Pete Johnson, Joe Turner and the Rex Stewart session
segments.summary: Lips Page takes Leeman to the black Sunset Club, where he is the only white musician admitted; he hears Pete Brown, Pete Johnson and Joe Turner and sees Lips challenge Rex Stewart.

segments.title: Pete Brown and the all-night jam sessions
segments.summary: Asked what Pete Brown sounded like, Leeman can only say he was wonderful; drummers wore out in the long jams so he was called to fill in.

segments.title: Returning to the Reno Club and hearing Jo Jones
segments.summary: Back after six months, Leeman hears the Basie band with Jo Jones, finds the music overwhelming and is told to play brushes on the next set.

segments.title: Watching Basie build the band: Lester Young, Freddie Green, Walter Page
segments.summary: He was there the night Hammond and Goodman called, and saw Basie add Lester Young, a guitarist, Hershel Evans and Walter Page.

segments.title: The unhired regular drummer while Jo Jones came in late
segments.summary: Jo Jones arrived late each night so Leeman held the drum chair at the start of the evening, until he felt he could never play like Jo and Basie insisted he keep going.

segments.title: Boots, Fairland Park and Andy Kirk's band
segments.summary: Boots takes him to Fairland Park to hear Andy Kirk's Twelve Clouds of Joy with Mary Lou Williams, John Williams and Ben Thigpen.

segments.title: Teddy Wilson's record date featuring Boots Castle
segments.summary: Teddy Wilson cuts a Kansas City date with Harry James, Gene Krupa and Harry Goodman, featuring Boots singing 'The Hour of Parting'; Leeman was not on it.

segments.title: Breakfasts and garden jam sessions around Kansas City
segments.summary: Boots takes him to private-home breakfasts with Lips and garden sessions where he played brushes on cardboard beside Mary Lou Williams.

segments.title: Importance of recording the Kansas City years
segments.summary: Leeman and Jo Jones never talk about Kansas City because no one would understand; Hinton stresses the importance of the record and Leeman calls it a hot bed of jazz.

segments.title: Acceptance by black musicians and Leeman's racial outlook
segments.summary: Leeman says he had no racial problems; black musicians took him under their wing, and Ellington and Basie were his idols.

segments.title: Leeman's ethnic background and family tree
segments.summary: He describes his German, English and Indian ancestry and his family-tree research.

segments.title: Hank Biagini band after Kansas City; John Best and Les Robinson
segments.summary: After the Murphy band broke up, Leeman joins Hank Biagini with trumpeter John Best and altoist Les Robinson and comes to New York.

segments.title: Biagini's background and Artie Shaw approaches the sidemen
segments.summary: Biagini came from the Detroit Graystone ballroom; during a Roseland matinee Artie Shaw asks Leeman, Best and Robinson to join his new band.

segments.title: Rehearsing the new Artie Shaw band for $65 a week
segments.summary: Shaw, a studio clarinetist, recruits Leeman, Best and Robinson for a 14-piece band; rehearsals begin on 49th Street and they are paid $65 against $25-30 before.

segments.title: Fletcher Henderson charts help launch the Shaw band
segments.summary: Hinton asks who Fletcher Henderson was; Leeman says Henderson's arrangements, also behind Goodman's band, helped start Shaw's orchestra.

segments.title: Shaw's Boston ballroom years and Jerry Gray's arrangements
segments.summary: The Shaw band plays New England ballrooms and schools while Shaw searches for a style, teaches Les Robinson lead alto, and Jerry Gray arranges 'Begin the Beguine'.

segments.title: Wanting to play Basie-style drums in Shaw's band
segments.summary: Leeman has Jo Jones and Basie in mind but Shaw wants something different, and nobody in the east knows the Kansas City band.

segments.title: Billie Holiday joins Shaw; Leeman's first wife Selma Cord
segments.summary: Sy Schribman arranges for Billie Holiday to join the white band, and Shaw hires Leeman's wife Selma Cord as the band singer.

segments.title: Segregation on the road with Billie Holiday
segments.summary: Shaw's band refuses hotels that exclude anyone; on the southern tour Billie is made to eat in kitchens, so Leeman and others join her there, and a girls' college would not let her sing.

segments.title: Playing drums for Shaw: rhythm section struggles and the tom-tom
segments.summary: Leeman struggles to make Shaw's rhythm section swing like Basie and uses a small Chinese tom-tom behind Shaw's choruses, an idea from Goodman's 'Sing, Sing, Sing'.

segments.title: Begin the Beguine session and the Lincoln Hotel sensation
segments.summary: The Spring 1938 sessions produce 'Begin the Beguine', 'Back Bay Shuffle' and 'Indian Love Call'; the hit saves the band, which reopens the Lincoln Hotel and films a short.

segments.title: Making a 1945 film with Hinton and Cab Calloway's band
segments.summary: Hinton and Leeman recall appearing in the same film, Leeman with Woody Herman and Hinton with Cab Calloway, and drummer J.C. Heard.

segments.title: Illness ends his Shaw job; Buddy Rich takes over
segments.summary: Leeman is hospitalized for hemorrhoids and sent home to Maine; Shaw signs Buddy Rich, Glenn Miller calls, and he recalls Chick Webb and Ella next door at the Roseland.

segments.title: New England territory bands: Mal Hallett and Joe Haymes
segments.summary: Leeman describes famous territory bands such as Mal Hallett's and Joe Haymes's, which trained young players like Pee Wee Irwin and Johnny Mince.

segments.title: Mal Hallett's comeback band with Gene Krupa
segments.summary: Leeman saw Hallett's theatre band with Frankie Carle, Toots Mondello and Gene Krupa playing loud brushes.

segments.title: Jack Teagarden fails to show in Portland
segments.summary: An anecdote of seeing Hallett's band at the Key Theatre in Portland, where Teagarden was drunk and George Troup fell off the stand.

segments.title: Ballrooms and Battles of Music with Shaw
segments.summary: Territory bands played for the Schribmans' ballrooms and colleges; Leeman describes Battles of Music, Shaw against Bunny Berigan and Red Norvo.

segments.title: Glenn Miller's offer in 1939 and the Maurice Purtle hire
segments.summary: Asked about leaving the business, Leeman says he was too weak after illness in May 1939, and Glenn Miller hired Maurice Purtle instead.

segments.title: Tommy Dorsey hires him after the Dartmouth Battle of Music
segments.summary: Dorsey, needing a drummer after Dave Tough, hires him because Shaw's band beat Dorsey's at the Dartmouth Winter Carnival; Leeman starts June 19, 1939.

segments.title: Inside the Dorsey band: arrangers and the Clambake Seven
segments.summary: He learned from Dorsey, playing brushes in the Clambake Seven with Yank Lawson, with Jimmie Mundy, Paul Weston and Dean Kincaid writing for the band.

segments.title: Babe Russin and shared Basie-Ellington tastes
segments.summary: Tenor saxophonist Babe Russin was the first in the band to mention Lester Young and shared Leeman's love of Basie and Ellington over Dorsey's style.

segments.title: Tommy Dorsey as a bandleader and the vocalists
segments.summary: Leeman stayed six or seven months; he describes Dorsey as beautiful to those he liked, hotheaded but quick to apologize, and says Sinatra joined as he left.

segments.title: No black musicians in Dorsey's band; Shavers and Teddy Wilson
segments.summary: Leeman says Charlie Shavers was the first black musician Dorsey hired, years after Teddy Wilson and Lionel Hampton joined Goodman, helped by John Hammond.

segments.title: Start of Reel 2
segments.summary: Reel 2 header of the Smithsonian interview.

segments.title: Leaving Dorsey after seven months; Buddy Rich replaces him
segments.summary: Leeman quits in November, tired of one-nighters and strict time-keeping; Buddy Rich takes the drum chair and Charlie Barnet calls him.

segments.title: Joining Charlie Barnet and the freedom to play
segments.summary: Barnet gives him complete freedom, which Leeman, who knew the Ellington book by heart, uses to develop his own style.

segments.title: Building a drumming style from Jo Jones, Chick Webb, Catlett and Sonny Greer
segments.summary: Leeman says drummers compile ideas from others: Zutty Singleton, Chick Webb, Sid Catlett, Baby Dodds, Jo Jones's hi-hat trick and Sonny Greer's way of pushing a band.

segments.title: Barnet's band: Ellington arrangements and records
segments.summary: After the Barnet library burned, Ellington sent arrangements; Leeman played as if he had always known the book and they cut 'Blue Juice' and 'Charleston Alley'.

segments.title: Woody Herman and the 'World on a String' date with Hodges and Brown
segments.summary: With Woody Herman, Leeman recommends borrowing Ellington men while Duke's band was off, and Johnny Hodges and Lawrence Brown join the session.

segments.title: Sitting in with Duke Ellington's band at the Zanzibar
segments.summary: Friendship with Ben Webster leads Leeman to sit in for the ailing Sonny Greer on the last sets at the Zanzibar.

segments.title: The Chinese cymbal and 'Back Bay Shuffle'
segments.summary: Leeman explains buying a 24-inch Chinese cymbal at Bill Mather's drum shop and using it on 'Back Bay Shuffle' for steady cymbal time; it became his trademark.

segments.title: Ben Webster and other players adopt the Chinese cymbal sound
segments.summary: Ben Webster loved the rivet cymbal, and Dizzy Gillespie and Kenny Dorham later had drummers use one; Leeman says it suits tenor sax.

segments.title: Called up for the draft and then exempted
segments.summary: Leeman gives up his Woody Herman job and apartment for induction at Fort Dix, but a new rule exempts fathers over thirty and he does not go.

segments.title: His son Bobby Leeman, pianist for Dionne Warwick
segments.summary: Son Bobby, born in 1940, studied at the New England Conservatory, overcame problems, accompanied Dionne Warwick and died suddenly of pneumonia.

segments.title: Second marriage, children and family life
segments.summary: Leeman talks about his wife Irene, their children and the loss of a daughter at 17; he and Hinton praise their wives and the family life Leeman always wanted.

segments.title: Blizzard in Waterloo, Iowa with Dan Murphy
segments.summary: In 36 degrees below zero with pot-belly-stove ballrooms, Leeman, wearing a bearskin coat sent by his father, is made to pack the truck.

segments.title: Packing drums and playing in freezing and sweltering venues
segments.summary: Hinton and Leeman compare playing with mittens and gloves in cold warehouses, and Leeman recalls a 115-degree Dorsey broadcast in a tobacco warehouse.

segments.title: Paying dues and the unrecognized talent
segments.summary: Hinton asks Leeman to explain to young people what musicians went through; Leeman says nothing was easy and much talent never got recognition.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: A 1944 Hollywood film and roommate Ernie Caceres
segments.summary: Leeman recalls a small part in a film with Charlie Barnet and sharing a room with Ernie Caceres, an underrated clarinetist and baritonist he recommended to Woody Herman.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Joining Raymond Scott's integrated CBS radio band
segments.summary: After leaving Woody, Leeman wins the drum job in Raymond Scott's CBS band with Ben Webster, Charlie Shavers and Milt Yaner, while Hinton and Leeman discuss who integrated CBS.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Charlie's Tavern and the Roseland building on 7th Avenue
segments.summary: The band ran to Charlie's Tavern between radio sets, and Hinton and Leeman pin down where the building, Roseland and A&R studios stood.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Charlie Shavers invites him into John Kirby's reorganized band
segments.summary: Shavers tells Leeman that John Kirby is reorganizing for The Aquarium; Leeman recalls the original Kirby band of Buster Bailey and Russell Procope.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Ben Webster in Kirby's band at the Aquarium
segments.summary: Ben Webster makes up his own parts in Kirby's band, which has Ram Ramirez, Buster Bailey, Shavers and George Johnson, and Leeman and Hinton sort out the personnel.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Tripling jobs: CBS show, Roxy Theatre and the Aquarium
segments.summary: Leeman, Webster and Shavers do the radio show and four Roxy shows daily, then walk three blocks to the Aquarium until four in the morning.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Wartime pay for the triple workload
segments.summary: Leeman earned $150 for the radio show, $175 at the Roxy and $175 from Kirby, a fabulous sum then, though he got only a few hours of sleep.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: John Kirby as bassist and leader
segments.summary: Leeman describes Kirby as a friend who took Charlie Shavers's advice on his business affairs, and recalls his earlier marriage to Maxine Sullivan and the 'biggest little band' billing.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: The Kirby sextet's quality and the Barnet battle at the 1939 World's Fair
segments.summary: Leeman praises the band's impeccable musicians and Shavers's difficult book, recalling the Kirby group nearly outswinging Barnet's 16 pieces with O'Neil Spencer on drums.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Dizzy Gillespie struggles with Shavers's book and Ben Webster's knife
segments.summary: Shavers leaves for Dorsey and sends Dizzy to Kirby's band; Dizzy mutters 'salt peanuts' behind Ben's solos until Ben pulls out a knife.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Emmett Berry replaces Dizzy in Kirby's band
segments.summary: Shavers brings in trumpeter Emmett Berry, whom Leeman praises as a swinging reader who later worked with Basie.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Emmett Berry reads Shavers's book better than Dizzy
segments.summary: Leeman says Emmett Berry played the difficult Kirby book more reliably than Dizzy, who wanted to do his own thing, and 'Coney's Special' came into the book.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Kirby recordings and a brief spell with Jimmy Dorsey
segments.summary: Leeman made only a couple of Muzak sides with Kirby that carry another drummer's credit, then spent three or four months with Jimmy Dorsey.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Father's death and building a house in Maine, 1945-47
segments.summary: After his father died in 1945 he went home to Maine, designed and built a house with insurance money, and then John Kirby called him back to the Aquarium in 1947.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Glen Gray's band through Bobby Hackett
segments.summary: Hinton walks through the chronology; Bobby Hackett got Leeman into Glen Gray's band, which went to Texas before he quit.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Charlie Barnet's reorganized band of 1948
segments.summary: Leeman rejoins Barnet's new band, suggests Eddie Safranski from Kenton's band and records with it for six or seven months.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Getting Chubby Jackson and Ralph Burns hired
segments.summary: Hinton sorts out dates; Leeman says he got Chubby Jackson into Barnet's band in 1940 and recommended Ralph Burns to Woody Herman.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Barnet's black-and-white band and the Apollo Theatre
segments.summary: Barnet's integrated band was the first white band to play the Apollo, 21 times, with Trummy Young, Peanuts Holland, Clark Terry and Doc Severinsen in different editions.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Barnet band personnel and records 1940-42
segments.summary: Leeman lists Billy May, Bill Miller, Lena Horne, Howard McGhee, Peanuts Holland, Dizzy and Eddie Safranski, and the head arrangements 'Comanche War Dance' and 'Night and Day'.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Apollo shows with the Cotton Club dancers and Harlem hits
segments.summary: Barnet's band backs the Cotton Club dancers at the Apollo and records 'Tappin' at the Tapper' and 'East Side, West Side', jukebox hits in Harlem.

segments.chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
segments.title: Preferring small bands: Hackett invites him to Nick's
segments.summary: Tired of moving brass sections, Leeman found the pleasure of subtle small-band drumming with Kirby, and in late 1949 Bobby Hackett offers him a job at Nick's.

segments.title: Nick's club in Greenwich Village
segments.summary: Leeman describes Nick's on 10th Street and 7th Avenue, its two pianos, Hank Duncan and Sidney Bechet.

segments.title: Bobby Hackett's band at Nick's: Billy Maxted, Phil Olivella, Andy Russo
segments.summary: The Hackett group had pianist Billy Maxted, clarinetist Phil Olivella and trombonist Andy Russo, a new world for Leeman.

segments.title: Playing jazz rather than 'Dixieland' at Nick's
segments.summary: Hackett disliked the word Dixieland; the band played traditional tunes in its own way for the crowd that came to hear them.

segments.title: Leading an integrated band at Nick's
segments.summary: Leeman later led the Nick's group himself for two or three years, with permission to use Buck Clayton, Herb Hall and Cutty Cutshall.

segments.title: Pee Wee Erwin takes over as leader at Nick's
segments.summary: Pee Wee Erwin became leader when Hackett was busy, and Leeman and Hinton praise him as a trumpeter and person.

segments.title: Raymond Scott and his brother Mark Warnow on the Hit Parade
segments.summary: Leeman is offered a job on the Hit Parade after Raymond Scott took over his late brother Mark's conducting post, and Hinton praises their role in popular music.

segments.title: Raymond Scott's quintet, Mitch Miller and Alec Wilder
segments.summary: Hinton and Leeman recall Raymond Scott's famous quintet and big band with Mitch Miller and Lou Shoobe, and the quintet playing the Jack Benny Show theme.

segments.title: Working the Hit Parade in radio and early television
segments.summary: Leeman did the Hit Parade on Saturday for $180, but Nick's would not let him off, so he quit and became a freelance New York studio musician for six and a half years.

segments.title: Joining Eddie Condon's band and its rhythm section
segments.summary: Condon hires Leeman, letting him send subs on Saturdays; he praises Gene Schroeder, Bob Casey and Walter Page, whom he recommended, and Condon's unamplified guitar.

segments.title: Condon's front line: Wild Bill Davison and Edmund Hall
segments.summary: Leeman praises Wild Bill Davison, who brings him to Switzerland annually, and Edmund Hall as soloists he loved to play behind.

segments.title: Playing behind soloists rather than soloing
segments.summary: Leeman explains he plays for the soloist and follows phrases, calls Buddy Rich the greatest soloist, and says he knew every breath Wild Bill would take.

segments.title: Condon's band and its Columbia albums
segments.summary: Leeman says the Condon band never had a bad moment, made two Columbia albums including 'Jammin' at Condon's', and alternated with guest house sets.

segments.title: Advice to young drummers, rock and Saturday Night Live
segments.summary: Asked how he would pass his knowledge to young musicians, Leeman says today's drummers lack bands to learn in, does no hard rock though he played on early rock records, and describes NBC musicians admiring his cymbals.

segments.title: The Lawson-Haggart band and its 30 albums
segments.summary: Leeman calls the Yank Lawson-Bob Haggart band a mutual admiration society where he never had a bad night across nearly thirty albums.

segments.title: Offer to help young musicians; age 65 with the World's Greatest Jazz Band
segments.summary: Leeman gives his phone number, says he wants to help anyone interested, and says he still plays strongly for an hour and a half at age 65.

segments.title: Playing best with friends: Lesberg, Holley, Barnes, Pizzarelli, Ellis
segments.summary: Leeman says he is getting better with age and names bassists and guitarists he loved working with, such as George Barnes, Bucky Pizzarelli and Herb Ellis.

segments.title: Dick Gibson as jazz patron and philanthropist
segments.summary: Hinton and Leeman credit Dick Gibson for his private jazz parties in Colorado, which Leeman has played every year, and for helping down-and-out musicians and reviving Joe Venuti.

segments.title: Start of Reel 3
segments.summary: Reel 3 header of the Smithsonian interview.

segments.title: The first Gibson jazz party with Ralph Sutton and Teddy Wilson
segments.summary: Gibson hires Ralph Sutton, Cutty Cutshall, Wild Bill Davison, Edmund Hall and Jack Lesberg plus Teddy Wilson's trio for an invitation-only Labor Day party, with the band traveling to Aspen by bus.

segments.title: Cooking stuffed grape leaves at the jazz party
segments.summary: Leeman explains how he came to cook stuffed grape leaves for Gibson's wife Mattie, after learning how from a neighbor.

segments.title: Giving up drinking after seven years of sobriety
segments.summary: Leeman, who started drinking at 14, quit cold turkey about seven years earlier because it was killing him, helped by his wife, Ralph Sutton and Dick Gibson, and learned he could play without it.

segments.title: Warming up for concerts like an athlete
segments.summary: Leeman explains he arrives two hours early to warm up his hands and feet with exercises and caffeine, comparing drumming to athletics.

segments.title: Leeman's letter after the first five-hour session
segments.summary: Hinton introduces a taped note in which Leeman says the first session was exhausting but fruitful, and thanks the Smithsonian.

segments.title: Using scrapbooks and notes to add 'Thoughts at Random'
segments.summary: Leeman explains that each band has a scrapbook and that he will use notes to add omissions and corrections to the tapes.

segments.title: Pat Bolen's Louis Armstrong records in high school
segments.summary: His next-door neighbor Pat Bolen played Armstrong's Hot Five records, his first introduction to jazz.

segments.title: The Casa Manana battle of music with Duke Ellington's band
segments.summary: Barnet planned to get Ellington's band drunk at a battle of music in California, but Duke's band out-drank them and they managed only 'Pompton Turnpike'.

segments.title: Davie Tough and Baby Dodds as influences
segments.summary: Leeman names Catlett, Zutty Singleton, Davie Tough and Baby Dodds, whom he heard at the Three Deuces in 1939, and describes Dodds's rolls, open bass drum and tricks.

segments.title: Zutty Singleton and the Shaw 'Blues' sides with the 25-inch cymbal
segments.summary: Leeman knew Zutty from 1936 and shows his influence on the Shaw 'A and B Blues' record, where he used the giant Chinese cymbal that sold out Bill Mather's shop.

segments.title: George Wettling's tuning, taste and humor
segments.summary: Leeman admires Wettling's tuned drums and humorous solos, and recalls following him in Shaw's first band and battles of music with Berigan's band.

segments.title: Sid Catlett and Buddy Rich the greatest soloist
segments.summary: Leeman introduces Catlett as a king of the drum throne, calls Buddy Rich the greatest soloist, and tells the story of Rich's reply to the Queen of England.

segments.title: Sid Catlett's listening, shows and dancers
segments.summary: Leeman first met Catlett with Louis Armstrong and watched him on 52nd Street; he admired his listening and his love of playing for tap dancers, as Leeman did for Barnet's revues.

segments.title: Chick Webb's tuning and Leeman's piccolo snare
segments.summary: Leeman says Chick Webb and Catlett tuned drums for a high sound, which led him to prefer a four-inch deep piccolo snare.

segments.title: Gene Krupa and Benny Goodman's impact on drummers
segments.summary: Krupa broke down traditions and helped drum equipment sales grow through his association with Goodman.

segments.title: Ray McKinley's sound and a short job in his band
segments.summary: Leeman admires McKinley's tuning and swing and recalls joining his band for five or six weeks.

segments.title: Opportunities to learn then versus music schools today
segments.summary: Leeman says students have good schools but not the chance to hear great artists, and Hinton thanks him.

segments.title: The Dorsey band's first flight, to Toronto in 1939
segments.summary: The Dorsey band became the first to fly as a group, on a chartered plane to the Canadian Exposition.

segments.title: The demo that became 'I'll Never Smile Again'
segments.summary: A woman in a wheelchair gave Leeman and Carmen Mastren a demo, and after a week or two they got Dorsey to hear 'I'll Never Smile Again'.

segments.title: Andy Peretti bitten by Frank Buck's monkey at the World's Fair
segments.summary: At the Flushing Meadows World's Fair, Frank Buck's ape bit Dorsey trumpeter Andy Peretti, who lisped his complaint, and the band broke up laughing.

segments.title: Playing with Don Byas, Slam Stewart and Erroll Garner on 52nd Street
segments.summary: At the Three Deuces in late 1944 Leeman plays in trios with Don Byas and Clyde Hart and with Slam Stewart, Erroll Garner and Harold West during the wartime blackout.

segments.title: Cooking Slum Gullion for 54 musicians at the Three Deuces
segments.summary: Leeman and Harold West swap sets on Sundays so each can cook; Leeman's pot of Slum Gullion feeds musicians including Charlie Parker and Dizzy, while West tops him with soul food.

segments.title: Hinton explains 'feed the kitty'
segments.summary: Hinton explains for the record the tip box tradition and asks Leeman to talk about Harold West and Clyde Hart.

segments.title: Harold West's early death and Clyde Hart's tuberculosis
segments.summary: Leeman says West died young from drug overdoses, and Clyde Hart, who was sick with tuberculosis, died the night after the Three Deuces engagement.

segments.title: The Famous Door hires Ben Webster to play Dixieland
segments.summary: With bop everywhere, the Famous Door wants a Dixieland band, so Ben borrows arrangements and rehearses at Eddie Barefield's studio with Buck Clayton and Bennie Morton.

segments.title: Monk's disastrous rehearsal and the end of Dixieland
segments.summary: Thelonious Monk comes to the rehearsal and it goes badly, so Kenny Kersey is hired; Ben drops the Dixieland charts after two sets and the band just plays jazz.

segments.title: The Famous Door closes and Leeman takes kitchen items
segments.summary: The club's management tells the band to take what they want before receivership, and Leeman takes pots and a meat cleaver.

segments.title: Kenny Kersey's piano prank and the meat cleaver mix-up
segments.summary: During the last night, pianist Kenny Kersey lifts the piano with his feet and Ben glares at Leeman, who later runs for the meat cleaver and is tackled by bandmates who think he is after Kersey.

segments.title: Ben Webster as a person and shared western tastes
segments.summary: Leeman calls his time with Webster a musical romance despite Ben's heavy drinking, and says they bonded over western boots, a Mexican saddle and horseback riding.

segments.title: The Bengazi club and the Dunbar Hotel in Washington
segments.summary: Ben takes Leeman to the black Bengazi nightclub in Washington, with Sonny Wright and Teddy Sturgis, and they stay at the Dunbar Hotel where Ben protects the only white guest.

segments.title: Ben in cowboy gear, with his dog, riding at Rock Creek Park
segments.summary: Ben buys western boots, a Stetson and a stray dog and books six o'clock rides at a stable in Rock Creek Park, and Leeman cooks daily at friends' houses.

segments.title: Leeman falls jumping a horse and plays with five broken ribs
segments.summary: After a night of playing and partying, Leeman tries a show jump on a Mexican saddle, breaks five ribs and plays the rest of the engagement taped up.

segments.title: Ben's rifle and bow, and the Bellevue incident
segments.summary: Ben takes up a Winchester and bow and arrows, and in New York he is taken to Bellevue for sighting a rifle from his Harlem window until Sid Catlett gets him released.

segments.title: Joining Sidney Bechet's quartet at Jimmy Ryan's
segments.summary: At Jimmy Ryan's across from the Three Deuces, Bechet takes Leeman with Kenny Kersey and Vic Dickenson; he was strict with drummers but seemed pleased.

segments.title: The Bechet album recorded at the Rendezvous Club in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Leeman describes a French bootleg LP of the Bechet quartet with Kenny Kersey and Vic Dickenson, and how he adapted to Bechet's New Orleans style of snare and press rolls.

segments.title: Working with so many black musicians: Leeman's view
segments.summary: Leeman says black musicians liked his playing first, quoting Dan Morgenstern that Condon ignored race as if it did not exist.

segments.title: Swing born in black bands; talent in all colors
segments.summary: Leeman says black bands like Henderson's and Hopkins's were swinging before Goodman, that he felt accepted as an equal, and that great and mediocre musicians come in all colors.

segments.title: His son Chris's remark about people of all colors
segments.summary: Leeman's wife recalls their two-and-a-half-year-old Chris saying that if God made people all the same the world would be monotonous.

segments.title: Leeman's progress report on his research
segments.summary: Leeman says he has worked five days at ten to twelve hours daily on his notes, is a third of the way done, and apologizes for repeating superlatives.

segments.title: Start of Reel 4
segments.summary: Reel 4 header; Hinton introduces tape four and Leeman's continued Condon story.

segments.title: The Condon band of 1951: packed house and Chicago style
segments.summary: Leeman joined in 1951 with Wild Bill Davison, Edmund Hall, Cutty Cutshall, Gene Schroeder and others, playing straight-down-the-middle jazz and requested traditional songs to jammed rooms.

segments.title: Recording with Edmund Hall and Walter Page for Decca
segments.summary: Edmund Hall asks Leeman to record at Decca with Ralph Sutton and Walter Page, and Leeman later fails to recognize his own brushes on playback.

segments.title: Freelance work in early television and radio
segments.summary: On the strength of the Hit Parade, Leeman is hired as a freelance on the Perry Como, Jack Benny, Steve Allen and Telephone Hour shows, and works on 'You Are There' with Louis Armstrong.

segments.title: Studio and album credits: Joe Turner, Peggy Lee and others
segments.summary: Leeman lists albums he made including Joe Turner Sings the Blues, Billy Butterfield and Bob Crosby albums, Peggy Lee's 'Lover' and a Paul Whiteman album.

segments.title: Forming the Lawson-Haggart band at Lou Stein's house
segments.summary: Yank Lawson proposes a group with Bob Haggart; they demo with Lou Stein and Cutty Cutshall, and Milt Gabler signs the band to Decca.

segments.title: The first Decca date and the series of albums
segments.summary: The first album with 'Jump for Joy' and 'Kisses and Jubilation' pleased Milt Gabler and began a series of twenty to thirty albums.

segments.title: Lawson-Haggart concerts and Dick Gibson's World's Greatest Jazz Band
segments.summary: Leeman describes concert tours with Lawson and Haggart, and how Gibson formed the World's Greatest Jazz Band from their arrangements, with Morey Feld on drums when Leeman was ill.

segments.title: Playing the White House Rose Garden in 1976
segments.summary: The World's Greatest Jazz Band plays for President Ford's Bicentennial salute alongside Ella Fitzgerald, and Leeman recalls his western outfit in the photograph.

segments.title: Enlarged Lawson-Haggart band and its free recording style
segments.summary: Lawson and Haggart augment the band with Butterfield, Hucko, Bud Freeman and Lou McGarity, give everyone freedom, and keep a first sight-read take of 'Tiger Rag'.

segments.title: Cozy Cole: first hearing him with Stuff Smith
segments.summary: Cozy Cole took Leeman to hear Stuff Smith's band, and Leeman praises Cole's studied technique, his snare roll and his later career with Armstrong.

segments.title: Newport Festivals and the New Jersey Jazz Society
segments.summary: Leeman plays the first Newport Festival with Condon, who conducted under an umbrella in the rain, and later New York Newport and Waterloo Village concerts.

segments.title: Meeting Bobby Hackett at Boston's Theatrical Club
segments.summary: Leeman first heard Hackett leading a small band in Boston with Brad Gowans, before Hackett went to Nick's in New York.

segments.title: Hackett friendship: Condon's Tuesday sessions and Jackie Gleason parties
segments.summary: Leeman sorts out dates, saying Hackett did not hire him until 1949-50, and recalls Condon's jam sessions, Gleason's private parties and Whiteman radio dates.

segments.title: Roosevelt Grill house band with Jack Lesberg
segments.summary: At Gibson's Roosevelt Grill, Leeman and Lesberg are the house rhythm section behind Joe Venuti, Buck Clayton and Peanuts Hucko, and later back Bobby Hackett.

segments.title: The Hackett-Dickenson Roosevelt Grill album and Hank O'Neal's liner notes
segments.summary: Leeman recommends the 1977 Chiaroscuro album recorded in 1970 and reads liner notes saying the tunes are not Dixieland but tasteful swing.

segments.title: Hackett proposes him for Masonry and dies
segments.summary: Hinton recalls the Roosevelt Grill; Leeman says Hackett proposed him for the Masons, with Paul Whiteman signing, and mourns Hackett's death.

segments.title: Playing presidential inaugural balls from Roosevelt to Carter
segments.summary: Leeman recalls six inaugural balls starting with Roosevelt's in 1940 with Barnet, Nixon's with Condon's band, and Carter's in 1977, and the Marine trumpeters taking over ruffles and flourishes.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Ben Webster's humor and storytelling
segments.summary: Leeman adds that Ben Webster was a champion storyteller who built tales slowly to a climax, much as he built his solos.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Awards from the New Jersey Jazz Society and Portland's musicians' local
segments.summary: Leeman describes his bronze plaque from the New Jersey Jazz Society, the fourth musician so honored, and another from his hometown local 364 in Portland.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Homecoming concert in Portland, Maine
segments.summary: Leeman returns to Portland as guest performer, meets old classmates and visits his birthplace and the Cape Elizabeth house he designed.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Growth of Gibson's parties: the Jerome Hotel in Aspen
segments.summary: The second Aspen party outgrew its dining room; Leeman suggested adding the Lawson-Haggart band, and he has kept Gibson's handwritten set lists since 1962.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Gibson parties move to Vail and the Broadmoor Hotel
segments.summary: The parties moved to Vail, back to Aspen, and then to the Broadmoor in Colorado Springs, growing to hundreds of guests and 67 musicians.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Gibson's set sheets as a study resource
segments.summary: Leeman offers the Smithsonian sixteen years of written set lists, valuable for students to see how Gibson mixed different musicians and styles.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Returning to Tommy Dorsey whenever he fought with Buddy Rich
segments.summary: Leeman clarifies that he worked with Dorsey off and on for years, and in 1947 Dorsey recalls him for a Christmas show at the Capitol after a fight with Buddy.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: First wife leaves with their son
segments.summary: On Christmas Day 1947 Charlie Shavers tells Leeman that his first wife has emptied their Maine house and left with their son, and Shavers looks out for him.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: New Year's Eve firecracker prank
segments.summary: Leeman and Shavers set off a firecracker in the alley below the dressing room, bringing police into the theatre until Dorsey scolds the band.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Cooking in the dressing room with Charlie Shavers
segments.summary: After buying burners and food on 8th Avenue, Leeman and Shavers cook between shows until the aromas draw complaints and Dorsey tells them to stop.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Rhapsody in Blue with Walter Gross and Dorsey's $20 bet
segments.summary: Dorsey's band plays the full Rhapsody in Blue with twenty violinists and pianist Walter Gross, and Dorsey and Gross bet $20 each night on whether he will make mistakes.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: The 1958 Paramount Theatre engagement with Sinatra and the Dorsey brothers
segments.summary: Leeman declines a contract but plays four weeks at the Paramount behind Frank Sinatra, with Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey reunited and Joey Bishop on the bill.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Doubling on Jackie Gleason's summer show and Elvis Presley's debut
segments.summary: Between Paramount shows the band cabs to Gleason's CBS show, where Leeman sees Elvis Presley's first major television appearance.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Sardi's meals and Leeman's last record date with Tommy Dorsey
segments.summary: Leeman and Shavers order from Sardi's instead of cooking, and after a Paramount show they cut a four-side session at Victor Studios, his last association with Dorsey.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Deaths of Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey
segments.summary: Tommy Dorsey chokes on food and dies, and about a year later Jimmy dies of cancer; Leeman sends a telegram to his hospital room.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Charlie Shavers's technique and unrecognized warmth
segments.summary: Leeman sums up how Dorsey grew to love Shavers, who lived near him in Corona, and regrets that Shavers's technical brilliance and early death kept him from full recognition.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Start of Reel 5
segments.summary: Reel 5 header of the Smithsonian interview.

segments.chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
segments.title: Wrapping up Charlie Shavers and his love of Roy Eldridge
segments.summary: Leeman says Shavers loved Louis Armstrong and Roy Eldridge records, and he and Ben Webster called each other frog.

segments.title: Leeman's research progress and his biography with Harlan Kenny
segments.summary: After seven and a half hours of tapes Leeman takes a break to cook chowder, and says he has worked 80 to 90 hours on notes and is also working on a biography with Professor Harlan William Kenny.

segments.title: Odessa jazz party founded by Dr. Fulcher
segments.summary: Leeman is hired again for Gibson's 1979 party, his 17th, then explains how Dr. Jim Fulcher founded the invitation-only Odessa, Texas jazz party.

segments.title: How the Odessa jazz party works
segments.summary: Leeman describes the six-day invitation-only party held in west Texas, with 20 to 25 players, four-hour nights and lavish hospitality from wealthy sponsors.

segments.title: Odessa party musicians: Flip Phillips, Buddy Tate, Dave McKenna and Teddy Wilson
segments.summary: Leeman lists the bassists, trumpeters, trombonists, reed players, pianists and vibes at a recent party and praises Teddy Wilson's breakneck tempos.

segments.title: Friendship with Dr. Jim Fulcher: hunting, bourbon and Ben Webster records
segments.summary: Leeman recalls hours with Fulcher, who loved Ben Webster and owned a vast record collection, and counted Leeman among his favorite drummers.

segments.title: Honorary sheriff and deputy commissions from Odessa and beyond
segments.summary: Fulcher has the Odessa sheriff swear in Leeman and others as honorary deputies, with Stetsons and silver buckles, and Leeman collects commissions in several counties given his love of law enforcement.

segments.title: Sworn in as special assistant to the Cumberland County DA
segments.summary: At his Portland concert in December 1978 the district attorney swears Leeman in and gives him a Miranda warning card.

segments.title: Fulcher's illness and death in 1977
segments.summary: Fulcher kept hiring musicians from his sickbed despite strokes, told the crowd to listen, and died in 1977; Leeman feels his presence still.

segments.title: Midland and Manassas parties as spin-offs of Gibson's
segments.summary: Max Christianson starts a Midland party in 1977 with some Odessa players, and Leeman notes other offshoots in New Jersey and Manassas, Virginia.

segments.title: How Milt Hinton got the nickname 'Judge'
segments.summary: Leeman asks and Hinton explains that his nickname began when he arrived early at studios and greeted everyone, echoing his grandmother's story of a jailed man and the judge.

segments.title: Pee Wee Erwin and the Kings of Jazz tours
segments.summary: Leeman recalls working with Pee Wee Erwin from 1950 and touring Britain, Scandinavia and Germany with the Kings of Jazz, with Privin, Hyman, Holley, Hubble, Davern and Mince.

segments.title: Wild Bill Davison and the Swiss festival in Bern
segments.summary: Davison brought Leeman to the Bern festival in 1976; they played Geneva and Zurich and Leeman praises his driving trumpet at age 73 and the old Condon drinking days.

segments.title: Joe Turner's 'The Boss of the Blues' session with Kansas City veterans
segments.summary: Called to a Carnegie Hall rehearsal-room date, Leeman finds Joe Turner, Pete Johnson, Pete Brown, Lawrence Brown and Freddie Green, the only white player, in a record later ranked among the best.

segments.title: Lawrence Brown's solo, Jimmy Nottingham, and how the album saved Atlantic
segments.summary: On day two Leeman recommends Jimmy Nottingham when trumpeter Joe Newman is missing, and Ahmet Ertegun later says the album rescued Atlantic Records from receivership.

segments.title: Playing behind Louis Armstrong on 'The Closing of Storyville'
segments.summary: Leeman finally plays behind Armstrong on the CBS Storyville show and at his Corona house, where Louis plays only Bobby Hackett records.

segments.title: Armstrong's invitation at the Roosevelt Grill and his funeral
segments.summary: Armstrong sits in with Peanuts Hucko's quartet and says he wants Leeman in his band, but Leeman could not leave New York; he watches the funeral on television.

segments.title: Barrett Deems in blackface and Louis's remark
segments.summary: Trummy Young tells of Armstrong's white drummer Barrett Deems being made to wear blackface in 'High Society' and of Louis forgetting he was white.

segments.title: Offers to donate papers to the University of Wyoming and the Smithsonian
segments.summary: Leeman says the University of Wyoming asked for his memorabilia and that he would like important items to go to the Smithsonian.

segments.title: His antique, gun and Civil War collections
segments.summary: Leeman describes his collections of antiques, guns, swords and Civil War relics, many from his family, and notes his 1963 cataract operations.

segments.title: Pen-and-ink drawings sold for charity
segments.summary: Leeman says he majored in art in high school, drew a pen-and-ink series at Nick's in 1950, and plans to sell prints for a sheriff's charity.

segments.title: Closing of Reel 5
segments.summary: Leeman signs off to Milt Hinton, hoping a final interview will sew up the evaluation of his life.
